principality-of-heitersheim.t: The seat of the Knights of Saint John's Grand Priory of Germany, whose grand priors ruled a tiny principality in the Breisgau.
principality-of-heitersheim.o: The Order of Saint John, the Knights Hospitaller, acquired Heitersheim near Freiburg in the 13th century, and from 1505 it was the residence of the order's Grand Prior of Germany. In 1548 Emperor Charles V raised the grand prior to a prince of the empire, making Heitersheim a small principality.
principality-of-heitersheim.r: The grand prior governed Heitersheim and a few neighbouring villages directly and oversaw the order's commanderies in Germany, which sent knights and revenues to Malta. The principality lay within the sphere of Further Austria, and the Habsburgs disputed its full independence. It remained Catholic.
principality-of-heitersheim.e: In 1806 Baden annexed Heitersheim, and the Grand Priory was dissolved. The priors' castle, the Malteserschloss, survives as a convent and museum.

principality-of-blankenburg.t: Harz principality of a Brunswick prince whose daughter became mother of Empress Maria Theresa.
principality-of-blankenburg.o: The County of Blankenburg in the Harz had passed to the dukes of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel in 1599. Duke Anthony Ulrich gave it to his younger son Louis Rudolph, and in 1707 Emperor Joseph I raised it to a principality, giving Louis Rudolph a seat among the princes of the Empire.
principality-of-blankenburg.r: Louis Rudolph ruled the small Lutheran territory from Blankenburg Castle, which he rebuilt, with a court theatre and gardens. The principality's prestige came from dynastic marriages: his daughter Elisabeth Christine married the future Emperor Charles VI and became mother of Maria Theresa, while another daughter married the son of Peter the Great.
principality-of-blankenburg.e: In 1731 Louis Rudolph inherited the Principality of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, and Blankenburg was reunited with it. It remained a Brunswick possession and became part of the Duchy of Brunswick.

principality-of-schaumburg-lippe.t: Tiny north German state at Bückeburg that survived from the Thirty Years' War to 1918, famed for a soldier-count's military academy.
principality-of-schaumburg-lippe.o: When the counts of Schaumburg died out in 1640, their lands were divided in 1647. Philip, a younger brother of the Count of Lippe, received a share including Bückeburg and Stadthagen, founding Schaumburg-Lippe, while the rest went to Hesse-Kassel and Brunswick-Lüneburg.
principality-of-schaumburg-lippe.r: Count William, in the 18th century, was a military reformer who built the island fortress of Wilhelmstein in the Steinhuder Meer and ran a school for officers where Gerhard von Scharnhorst trained. He also commanded allied forces in Portugal in 1762. The princely title came in 1807. The economy relied on farming and sandstone quarries, and the princes became wealthy landowners.
principality-of-schaumburg-lippe.e: Schaumburg-Lippe joined the German Confederation and in 1871 the German Empire as one of its smallest states. Prince Adolf II abdicated in November 1918, and it continued as the Free State of Schaumburg-Lippe.

principality-of-schwarzburg-rudolstadt.t: A small Thuringian principality ruled from the Heidecksburg above Rudolstadt, whose last prince was the last German monarch to abdicate in 1918.
principality-of-schwarzburg-rudolstadt.o: The counts of Schwarzburg were among the oldest noble houses of Thuringia. After the death of Count Günther XLI in 1583 and a period of joint rule, the Treaty of Stadtilm of 1599 divided the County of Schwarzburg between brothers, creating the Rudolstadt and Sondershausen lines.
principality-of-schwarzburg-rudolstadt.r: The counts, raised to princes in 1710, ruled two separate blocks of territory, the Upper Lordship around Rudolstadt and part of the Lower Lordship in northern Thuringia, and gradually shook off Saxon overlordship. The Lutheran court rebuilt the Heidecksburg palace in Baroque style after a fire in 1735. Schiller first met Goethe in Rudolstadt in 1788.
principality-of-schwarzburg-rudolstadt.e: Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt joined the German Confederation and the German Empire. Its last prince, Günther Victor, who had ruled both Schwarzburg states since 1909, abdicated in November 1918, the last German monarch to do so. In 1920 it merged into the Free State of Thuringia.

pharsalus.t: Thessalian city of Phthiotis, long ruled by aristocratic families, whose plain saw Caesar's victory over Pompey in 48 BCE.
pharsalus.o: Pharsalus stood on a hill above the plain of the Enipeus in southern Thessaly, in the region Greek myth linked to Achilles's Phthia. It became a city in the Archaic period and one of the leading members of the Thessalian League with Larissa and Pherae.
pharsalus.r: Pharsalus was dominated by aristocratic families such as the Echecratidae. In the 370s BCE Polydamas governed the city and was forced to submit to Jason of Pherae. Daochus, a Pharsalian, served Philip II as tetrarch of Thessaly and set up a family monument at Delphi.
pharsalus.e: Pharsalus passed under Macedonian rule, was freed by Rome in 196 BCE and came under Roman control by 146 BCE. In 48 BCE Julius Caesar defeated Pompey nearby at the Battle of Pharsalus.

principality-of-achaea.t: Most successful crusader state in Greece, a French chivalric society in the Peloponnese whose story is told in the Chronicle of the Morea.
principality-of-achaea.o: In 1205 William of Champlitte and Geoffrey of Villehardouin, crusaders of the Fourth Crusade, conquered the western Peloponnese after defeating local Greeks at the Olive Grove of Koundouros. Geoffrey I took control after Champlitte left, and his family ruled for three generations under the nominal suzerainty of the Latin Empire.
principality-of-achaea.r: The principality was a model feudal state, divided into twelve baronies, such as Karytaina, Akova and Patras, whose lords sat in the prince's council. Its laws were codified as the Assizes of Romania. The court at Andravida and the port of Clarentza were famed for French culture, and the castle of Chlemoutsi guarded the coast. Greek archons kept their lands.
principality-of-achaea.e: Captured at Pelagonia in 1259, William II of Villehardouin ceded Mistras and Monemvasia to Byzantium, creating the base of the Despotate of the Morea. Angevin, Navarrese and Zaccaria rulers followed. Thomas Palaiologos annexed the rest of the principality in 1430-1432.

principality-of-wales.t: The Welsh state built by the princes of Gwynedd and recognised by England in 1267, the high point of native Welsh political independence.
principality-of-wales.o: Llywelyn ap Iorwerth, Llywelyn the Great, made Gwynedd dominant in Wales, and at Aberdyfi in 1216 the other Welsh rulers accepted his overlordship. His grandson Llywelyn ap Gruffudd took the title Prince of Wales, which Henry III recognised in the Treaty of Montgomery in 1267.
principality-of-wales.r: The principality was a feudal overlordship over lesser Welsh lords such as those of Powys Fadog and Powys Wenwynwyn. Its princes ruled from Gwynedd's courts, including Aber Garth Celyn, and used Welsh law, stone castles such as Dolwyddelan and a growing chancery.
principality-of-wales.e: Llywelyn's refusal to do homage to Edward I led to wars in 1277 and 1282. He was killed near Cilmeri in 1282, and his brother Dafydd executed in 1283. The Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 annexed the principality to the Kingdom of England.

principality-of-koknese.t: A small Orthodox principality on the Daugava, vassal of Polotsk, swallowed by the crusading Bishopric of Riga in 1208.
principality-of-koknese.o: Koknese, called Kukenois by the Germans, was a fortified centre on the Daugava in what is now Latvia, inhabited by Latgalians and Selonians. By the late 12th century it was ruled by a prince of Rus' origin, Vyachko, as a tributary of the Principality of Polotsk. It is known almost entirely from the chronicle of Henry of Livonia.
principality-of-koknese.r: The principality controlled a stretch of the Daugava trade route between Polotsk and the Baltic and collected tribute from the surrounding Baltic peoples. Its prince and his retinue were Orthodox Christians, while most of the population remained pagan. When German crusaders founded Riga in 1201, Koknese came under pressure from Bishop Albert.
principality-of-koknese.e: In 1205 Vyachko gave half his land to the bishop in return for protection. Quarrels with German knights followed, and in 1208 he burned his castle and fled to Rus'. The bishop built a stone castle on the site, and Vyachko died defending Tartu against the crusaders in 1224.

principality-of-hereti.t: A small Christian principality between Georgia and Caucasian Albania whose Queen Dinar is remembered for bringing it into the Georgian Orthodox church.
principality-of-hereti.o: Hereti lay along the Alazani and Iori rivers and around Shaki, a borderland between Kartli and the old Caucasian Albania. In the 9th century, as Arab power waned, a local dynasty with ties to the former Mihranid Principality of Albania established its own rule, sometimes called the kings of the Rans.
principality-of-hereti.r: Its population mixed Georgians, Armenians and Caucasian Albanians, and its church long followed the anti-Chalcedonian Armenian tradition. In the 10th century Queen Dinar, of Georgian Bagratid descent, converted the principality to Georgian Orthodoxy. Its rulers fought the Emirate of Tbilisi and competed with Kakheti, controlling farmland and routes to the Caspian.
principality-of-hereti.e: Hereti was absorbed by the Principality of Kakheti in the late 10th century, and around 1010 the two formed the Kingdom of Kakheti-Hereti. The name survived as a province of the Georgian kingdom.

principality-of-brandenburg-bayreuth.t: The Franconian margraviate of the Hohenzollerns, ruled from Kulmbach and Bayreuth and made a rococo showcase by Margravine Wilhelmine.
principality-of-brandenburg-bayreuth.o: When the Hohenzollern rulers of the Burgraviate of Nuremberg divided their Franconian lands in 1398, the territory 'above the mountains' around Kulmbach and the Plassenburg went to John III. After the family gained the Margraviate of Brandenburg in 1415, its Franconian principalities were usually ruled by younger sons with the title of margrave.
principality-of-brandenburg-bayreuth.r: Margrave Albert Alcibiades devastated Franconia in his wars of the 1550s. The territory was Lutheran, and the court moved from Kulmbach to Bayreuth in the early 17th century. Margravine Wilhelmine, sister of Frederick the Great, and her husband Frederick made Bayreuth a cultural centre, building the Margravial Opera House and founding the university at Erlangen in 1743.
principality-of-brandenburg-bayreuth.e: In 1769 Bayreuth passed to Charles Alexander, margrave of the Principality of Brandenburg-Ansbach, who in 1791 ceded both principalities to the Kingdom of Prussia. Napoleon gave Bayreuth to the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1810. Richard Wagner later built his festival theatre in the town.

pre-islamic-mecca.t: The sanctuary town of the Kaaba, governed by the clans of Quraysh, whose trade and pilgrimage made it the birthplace of Islam.
pre-islamic-mecca.o: Arab tradition credits Qusayy ibn Kilab with gathering the Quraysh clans in Mecca in the 5th century and taking control of the Kaaba, a shrine already visited by pilgrims from across western Arabia. He distributed the hereditary offices of the sanctuary: guarding the Kaaba, giving water and food to pilgrims and holding the war banner.
pre-islamic-mecca.r: Mecca had no king. Clans such as Hashim, Makhzum, Umayya and Abd al-Dar shared power through an assembly of elders. The town lived on the pilgrimage, the sacred months that protected trade, nearby fairs such as Ukaz and caravans to Syria and Yemen. The Kaaba housed images of many deities, Hubal chief among them, and Allah was recognised as a high god.
pre-islamic-mecca.e: Muhammad, of the clan of Hashim, began preaching around 610, met growing opposition and left for Medina in 622. After years of war, Mecca surrendered to the Islamic state of Medina in 630; the idols of the Kaaba were destroyed and the town became the holiest city of Islam.

provisional-government-of-schleswig-hols.t: Rebel German government set up in Kiel in 1848 to free Schleswig and Holstein from Denmark, which fought the First Schleswig War and lost.
provisional-government-of-schleswig-hols.o: In March 1848, as revolutions spread across Europe, Denmark's new liberal government moved to tie Schleswig more closely to the kingdom. German nationalists in the duchies responded by forming a provisional government at Kiel on 24 March, led by Wilhelm Hartwig Beseler and Prince Frederick of Noer, claiming both duchies for the German Confederation.
provisional-government-of-schleswig-hols.r: The government raised a Schleswig-Holstein army and received support from Prussia and the German Confederation, whose troops fought the Danes in 1848-1849. It governed from Kiel with the backing of the German-speaking estates, while Danish-minded inhabitants of northern Schleswig opposed it. Great-power pressure forced Prussia to make peace with Denmark in 1850.
provisional-government-of-schleswig-hols.e: Fighting alone, the Schleswig-Holstein army was defeated at Isted (Idstedt) in July 1850. Under pressure from Austria and Prussia, the government dissolved in early 1851, and Danish rule was restored. The London Protocol of 1852 confirmed the settlement, but the dispute reignited in the war of 1864.

pashalik-of-vidin.t: Rebel domain of Osman Pazvantoğlu on the Danube, who defied the Ottoman sultan and let loose raiders across Bulgaria and Wallachia.
pashalik-of-vidin.o: Osman Pazvantoğlu, a janissary from Vidin, opposed Sultan Selim III's military reforms and seized control of Vidin around 1794. He gathered disbanded janissaries and kardzhali bandits, and in 1798 defeated a large Ottoman army sent to besiege the town. Unable to remove him, the sultan pardoned him and appointed him pasha of Vidin.
pashalik-of-vidin.r: Pazvantoğlu ruled as a warlord with his own army and treasury, and conducted his own diplomacy with Russia and France. His bands raided much of Bulgaria and crossed into Wallachia, burning Craiova in 1800. He backed the janissary dahije who seized power in the Pashalik of Belgrade, whose abuses helped provoke the Serbian uprising of 1804.
pashalik-of-vidin.e: Pazvantoğlu died in 1807, and his successors soon returned Vidin to Ottoman control. His career showed the weakness of central authority under Selim III; Bulgarian memory recalls the kardzhali years as a time of terror.

principality-of-leiningen.t: A Palatinate county ruled by the Leiningen family from the Haardt hills, raised to a principality in 1779 before being swept away by the French.
principality-of-leiningen.o: Count Emich I of Leiningen appears around 1128, with castles in the Haardt hills of the Palatinate. The original line died out in 1220, and the lands passed through a sister to the Saarbrücken family, who took the Leiningen name. The family split in 1317 into Leiningen-Hardenburg and Leiningen-Dagsburg.
principality-of-leiningen.r: The counts ruled scattered territories in the Palatinate and Alsace, with castles at Hardenburg and Altleiningen. They were often in rivalry with the Electoral Palatinate. The Hardenburg line moved its residence to Dürkheim in the 18th century and was raised to princely rank in 1779.
principality-of-leiningen.e: French revolutionary forces annexed the left bank of the Rhine in the 1790s. In 1803 the princes received former church lands at Amorbach in Franconia, but these were mediatised in 1806 and divided between Baden, Bavaria and Hesse. Queen Victoria's half-brother Carl was a prince of Leiningen.

principality-of-yuryev-polsky.t: A small appanage of the Vladimir-Suzdal lands, best known for the richly carved Cathedral of Saint George.
principality-of-yuryev-polsky.o: Yuri Dolgoruky founded Yuryev-Polsky in 1152 in the open fields, the polye, between Vladimir and Pereslavl-Zalessky. When Vsevolod the Big Nest's sons divided his lands, Sviatoslav Vsevolodovich received Yuryev in 1212 and it became a separate appanage.
principality-of-yuryev-polsky.r: It was a small agricultural principality whose rulers were closely tied to Vladimir. Sviatoslav built the Cathedral of Saint George between 1230 and 1234, whose walls are covered with carved stone reliefs of saints, beasts and plants. The town was sacked by the Mongols in 1238.
principality-of-yuryev-polsky.e: Sviatoslav's descendants held the principality as a minor appanage. It came under the control of the Grand Duchy of Moscow in the first half of the 14th century, and by around 1340 its separate princely rule had ended.

provisional-government-of-lithuania-1941.t: Lithuanian government formed during the June Uprising of 1941, which hoped to restore independence but was dissolved by the Germans after six weeks.
provisional-government-of-lithuania-1941.o: When Germany invaded the Soviet Union on 22 June 1941, the Lithuanian Activist Front launched the June Uprising against Soviet rule. On 23 June it proclaimed restored independence on Kaunas radio and formed a Provisional Government. Its intended head, Kazys Škirpa, was held in Berlin, so Juozas Ambrazevičius served as acting prime minister.
provisional-government-of-lithuania-1941.r: The government tried to reverse Soviet nationalisation and re-establish Lithuanian institutions, but the Germans did not recognise it. It also issued anti-Jewish regulations while killings of Jews by German units and Lithuanian collaborators began, a record that remains deeply controversial.
provisional-government-of-lithuania-1941.e: The Germans set up their own civil administration within Reichskommissariat Ostland, and on 5 August 1941 the Provisional Government dissolved itself rather than become a German instrument. Lithuania remained under German occupation until 1944 and then became the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic again.

principality-of-novosil.t: One of the Upper Oka principalities, founded by a son of Mikhail of Chernigov and caught between Lithuania and Moscow.
principality-of-novosil.o: After Mikhail of Chernigov was killed at Batu's camp in 1246, his lands were divided among his sons. Semyon Mikhailovich received Glukhov and Novosil on the upper Oka, and Novosil became the senior seat of a group of small principalities known as the Upper Oka principalities.
principality-of-novosil.r: These were frontier lands, open to raids from the steppe and the Golden Horde. Novosil itself was ruined in the 14th century, and the princes moved their seat to Odoyev, so the line became known as the Odoyevsky. Related branches ruled Belyov and Vorotynsk. They usually served the Grand Duchy of Lithuania while bargaining with Moscow.
principality-of-novosil.e: In the late 15th century the Upper Oka princes went over to Ivan III, and the peace of 1494 between Moscow and Lithuania confirmed their lands as part of the Grand Duchy of Moscow. The Odoyevsky and Vorotynsky princes became prominent Russian nobles.

principality-of-anhalt-kothen.t: One of the Anhalt principalities of central Germany, home of the Fruitbearing Society and of the court where Johann Sebastian Bach wrote much of his instrumental music.
principality-of-anhalt-kothen.o: Anhalt was partitioned in 1603 among the sons of Prince Joachim Ernst, and Köthen fell to Ludwig, who founded the line of Anhalt-Köthen. Ludwig was a learned prince who in 1617 co-founded the Fruitbearing Society (Fruchtbringende Gesellschaft), the first society devoted to refining the German language.
principality-of-anhalt-kothen.r: The principality was a small Calvinist state in the Saale-Elbe region, living from agriculture. Its court is best known for Prince Leopold, a music lover who employed Johann Sebastian Bach as Kapellmeister from 1717 to 1723, when the Brandenburg Concertos and much chamber music were composed. In 1665 the line of Anhalt-Plötzkau inherited Köthen, continuing it under a new branch.
principality-of-anhalt-kothen.e: Köthen became a duchy in 1807 under Napoleon's patronage and joined the German Confederation. When its last duke died without heirs in 1847, the territory passed to Anhalt-Dessau and Anhalt-Bernburg, and was absorbed into the united Duchy of Anhalt by 1863.

principality-of-masserano.t: A tiny papal fief in northern Piedmont ruled by the Ferrero-Fieschi family until it was sold to the kings of Sardinia in 1767.
principality-of-masserano.o: Masserano and Crevacuore, small towns in the hills between Biella and the Sesia valley, belonged to the Fieschi family and then to the Ferrero, who took the Fieschi name. In 1598 Pope Clement VIII raised them to a principality held as a fief of the Holy See, giving the family sovereign status.
principality-of-masserano.r: The Ferrero-Fieschi princes governed a few thousand subjects, minted coins and kept a small court, while often serving foreign rulers as soldiers and diplomats, especially Spain. Surrounded by the Duchy of Savoy, the state survived through papal protection and its rulers' connections abroad. Little else is recorded of its government.
principality-of-masserano.e: The House of Savoy, now kings of the Kingdom of Sardinia, long sought to absorb the enclave. In 1767 the prince ceded his sovereignty to Charles Emmanuel III, ending the principality.

praisos.t: East Cretan city of the Eteocretans, a pre-Greek people whose language survives in a few undeciphered inscriptions.
praisos.o: Praisos stood on hills in the interior of eastern Crete. Herodotus and Strabo say its people were Eteocretans, 'true Cretans' descended from the island's pre-Greek inhabitants, and the settlement continued from the end of the Bronze Age into the Iron Age.
praisos.r: Inscriptions from Praisos, written in the Greek alphabet between the 6th and 3rd centuries BCE, record a non-Greek language that remains undeciphered. The city controlled the sanctuary of Diktaean Zeus for a time and quarrelled with Itanos. It had harbours on both coasts of eastern Crete.
praisos.e: Praisos was destroyed by its neighbour Hierapytna c. 145 BCE, which took over its land. Its inscriptions are the main evidence for the Eteocretan language.
praisos.re: Cretan religion; cult of Diktaean Zeus

principality-of-hatuqwai.t: A small princely Circassian tribe of the western Caucasus foothills, known mainly from 18th- and 19th-century Russian and travellers' accounts.
principality-of-hatuqwai.o: The Hatuqwai were one of the smaller aristocratic Adyghe tribes of Circassia, living between the Belaya and Laba rivers near the Temirgoy. Little is known of their early history; they appear as a distinct community in sources of the 18th century.
principality-of-hatuqwai.r: Like other princely Circassian groups, they were ruled by princes and nobles over free peasants and serfs, following the Adyghe code of conduct and living by farming, horse breeding and livestock. They usually acted in alliance with the neighbouring Temirgoy and shared in the wider Circassian struggle against Russia.
principality-of-hatuqwai.e: The Russian Empire conquered their lands in the final campaigns of the Russo-Circassian War, completed in 1864. Almost all Hatuqwai were expelled to the Ottoman Empire, where their descendants were absorbed into the Circassian diaspora.

principality-of-boisbelle.t: A sovereign enclave in Berry, exempt from royal taxes, where Henry IV's minister Sully built the planned town of Henrichemont.
principality-of-boisbelle.o: Boisbelle was a lordship in Berry whose holders had long claimed sovereignty, a privilege tolerated by the French crown. In 1597 Maximilien de Béthune, later duke of Sully, Henry IV's chief minister, bought it and confirmed its status as a principality.
principality-of-boisbelle.r: Sully founded the town of Henrichemont in 1608, named after the king, on a regular grid around a central square, hoping to attract Protestant settlers and artisans. Its inhabitants paid no royal taxes, which drew some settlers, though the town never grew as planned. The Béthune family ruled the enclave for over 150 years.
principality-of-boisbelle.e: In 1766 the Duke of Sully's descendants sold the principality to Louis XV, ending its sovereignty, and it became part of the Kingdom of France.
ru: Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully

principality-of-halberstadt.t: Former prince-bishopric in the Harz foreland turned into a Brandenburg-Prussian principality by the Peace of Westphalia.
principality-of-halberstadt.o: The Bishopric of Halberstadt, founded around 804, had become Lutheran during the Reformation and was ruled by administrators. At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 it was secularised and given to Brandenburg as compensation for its claims to Pomerania, becoming the Principality of Halberstadt.
principality-of-halberstadt.r: The principality was governed by Brandenburg-Prussian officials through a provincial government, with the cathedral chapter kept as a Protestant institution. It was a fertile grain-growing region with a sizeable garrison. In the 18th century the poet Johann Wilhelm Ludwig Gleim lived there as cathedral secretary, gathering a circle of writers.
principality-of-halberstadt.e: After Prussia's defeat in 1806, Halberstadt was given to the Kingdom of Westphalia in 1807. It returned to Prussia in 1815 and became part of the Province of Saxony; the town is now in Saxony-Anhalt.

principality-of-bari.t: A short-lived Lombard principality carved out of Norman Apulia by a local strongman before Roger II brought it to heel.
principality-of-bari.o: In the weak reign of Duke William II of the Duchy of Apulia and Calabria, the citizen Grimoald Alferanites took power in Bari in 1119 and called himself prince. Bari, the old seat of Byzantine government in Italy, had since 1087 housed the relics of Saint Nicholas, which made it a major pilgrimage centre.
principality-of-bari.r: Little is known of Grimoald's government beyond his alliances with Venice and with other rebellious Apulian barons. He relied on Bari's port, its merchant community and the prestige of the Basilica of San Nicola. He submitted to Roger II of Sicily in 1129 when Roger took over Apulia.
principality-of-bari.e: Grimoald joined a baronial revolt against Roger II, who captured Bari in 1132 and sent him as a prisoner to Sicily. Bari was absorbed into the Kingdom of Sicily.

principality-of-hohenlohe-schillingsfurs.t: Franconian principality of a Catholic Hohenlohe branch, whose family later produced a German chancellor.
principality-of-hohenlohe-schillingsfurs.o: The Hohenlohe family ruled lands in north-eastern Württemberg and western Franconia from the Middle Ages and divided into many lines. The Catholic Waldenburg branch included Schillingsfürst, on a hill near Rothenburg, and in 1744 its head was raised to the rank of prince of the Empire.
principality-of-hohenlohe-schillingsfurs.r: The principality was small, Catholic and rural, governed from a baroque palace at Schillingsfürst, which still houses a falconry. It belonged to the Franconian Circle and shared the Hohenlohe family's collective vote. Its princes served the emperors in court and army posts.
principality-of-hohenlohe-schillingsfurs.e: In 1806 the principality was mediatised and placed under the Kingdom of Bavaria. The family remained prominent: Chlodwig zu Hohenlohe-Schillingsfürst was Bavarian prime minister and German chancellor from 1894 to 1900.

principality-of-lichtenberg.t: Detached Saar-area exclave of Saxe-Coburg, given at Vienna and sold to Prussia after political unrest.
principality-of-lichtenberg.o: The Congress of Vienna promised the Duke of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld territory for his services against Napoleon. In 1816 he received a district around St. Wendel on the upper Nahe and Blies, far from Coburg, which was named the Principality of Lichtenberg in 1819 after the castle near Kusel.
principality-of-lichtenberg.r: The principality had about 25,000 inhabitants, Catholic and Protestant, living from farming and small crafts. It was governed by Coburg officials who were unpopular, and the region was touched by the radical democratic movement around the Hambach Festival of 1832. Unrest in St. Wendel in 1832 required troops to restore order.
principality-of-lichtenberg.e: Duke Ernest I found the distant territory hard to govern and sold it to Prussia in 1834 for an annual payment. It became the district of St. Wendel in the Rhine Province and is now part of Saarland.

provisional-government-of-milan.t: The government formed by the Milanese after the Five Days of 1848 drove out the Austrians, which merged Lombardy with Piedmont before Radetzky returned.
provisional-government-of-milan.o: From 18 to 22 March 1848 the people of Milan fought the Five Days, barricade battles that forced Marshal Radetzky's Austrian garrison to leave the city. A provisional government headed by the mayor Gabrio Casati took power, while the democrat Carlo Cattaneo led the council of war during the fighting.
provisional-government-of-milan.r: The provisional government governed Lombardy and called on Charles Albert of the Kingdom of Sardinia, who declared war on Austria. Moderates led by Casati favoured union with Piedmont, while republicans such as Cattaneo and Giuseppe Mazzini wanted to delay the question. A plebiscite in May and June approved fusion with Piedmont.
provisional-government-of-milan.e: After the Piedmontese defeat at Custoza in July 1848, Radetzky reoccupied Milan on 6 August, and Lombardy returned to the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia.

principality-of-wallachia.t: Romanian principality between the Carpathians and the Danube, home of Mircea the Elder and Vlad the Impaler, which united with Moldavia to form Romania.
principality-of-wallachia.o: Romanian voivodeships such as the Voivodeship of Litovoi and the Voivodeship of Seneslau were united under Basarab I in the early 14th century; tradition dates the founding to about 1310. In 1330 Basarab defeated Charles I of Hungary at Posada, securing independence.
principality-of-wallachia.r: The voivode (prince) ruled with boyars, and the throne was elective within the ruling family, which bred constant rivalry. Mircea the Elder (1386–1418) fought the Ottomans at Rovine, and Vlad III fought them in 1462. From the 15th century Wallachia paid tribute to the Ottomans but kept its own rulers and Orthodox church. Michael the Brave briefly united Wallachia, Transylvania and Moldavia in 1600. From 1716 to 1821 the Ottomans appointed Phanariot Greek princes.
principality-of-wallachia.e: After the Treaty of Adrianople in 1829 Wallachia came under Russian protection. In 1859 both it and the Principality of Moldavia elected Alexandru Ioan Cuza as prince, creating the United Principalities, which became Romania.

principality-of-erfurt.t: Thuringian city-state that Napoleon kept as his personal domain, scene of his 1808 congress with Tsar Alexander I.
principality-of-erfurt.o: Erfurt, long ruled by the Electorate of Mainz, passed to Prussia in 1802. After defeating Prussia at Jena in October 1806, Napoleon did not give Erfurt to any of his allies but kept it as a domain reserved to himself, the Principality of Erfurt, administered by French governors.
principality-of-erfurt.r: Erfurt was governed directly by French officials and garrisoned by French troops, with the Petersberg citadel as its stronghold. From September to October 1808 Napoleon held the Congress of Erfurt there, meeting Tsar Alexander I to renew their alliance and receiving Goethe in a famous audience. The city lived from trade, crafts and garden produce.
principality-of-erfurt.e: After the defeat at Leipzig, Erfurt was besieged by Prussian troops and its French garrison surrendered in 1814. The Congress of Vienna returned the city to Prussia in 1815, as part of the Province of Saxony.

principality-of-the-hevelli.t: A Slavic principality on the Havel centred on Brandenburg, whose last prince bequeathed his land to Albert the Bear and so began the March of Brandenburg.
principality-of-the-hevelli.o: The Hevelli, also called Stodorani, were West Slavic settlers of the Havel lands west of modern Berlin from the 7th or 8th century. Their chief stronghold was Brenna, the later Brandenburg an der Havel. In 928 to 929 the East Frankish king Henry the Fowler captured it in winter across the frozen marshes.
principality-of-the-hevelli.r: The Hevelli were governed by princes from Brenna, controlling river crossings and fortified settlements on the Havel and Spree. German rule after 929 was lost in the Great Slav Rising of 983, and the Hevelli joined, and later stood apart from, the Lutician Federation. The last prince, Pribislav-Henry, became a Christian and ruled as a German ally.
principality-of-the-hevelli.e: Pribislav-Henry named Albert the Bear his heir; on his death in 1150 Albert took Brandenburg, securing it in 1157 after a fight with the Slavic prince Jaxa of Köpenick. The Hevelli lands became the core of the Margraviate of Brandenburg.

parthenopean-republic.t: The Neapolitan republic of 1799, whose idealistic leaders were crushed by Cardinal Ruffo's peasant army and executed in their hundreds.
parthenopean-republic.o: After the Kingdom of Naples attacked the French in Rome in late 1798 and was defeated, King Ferdinand IV fled to Sicily. French troops under General Championnet fought their way into Naples, and on 23 January 1799 local patriots proclaimed a republic named after Parthenope, the ancient Greek name for the city.
parthenopean-republic.r: The republic was led by intellectuals and liberal nobles such as Carlo Lauberg and the jurist Francesco Mario Pagano, who drafted a constitution. Eleonora Fonseca Pimentel edited its newspaper, the Monitore Napoletano. It tried to abolish feudalism, but had little support among the poor and peasants, and depended on French troops, who withdrew in May.
parthenopean-republic.e: Cardinal Fabrizio Ruffo's Sanfedisti army retook Naples in June 1799. The surrender terms were broken with Nelson's backing, and over a hundred republicans, including Pagano, Pimentel and Admiral Francesco Caracciolo, were executed.

prince-bishopric-of-bamberg.t: Franconian church state founded by Emperor Henry II, whose cathedral holds the Bamberg Horseman and whose bishops staged notorious witch trials.
prince-bishopric-of-bamberg.o: Emperor Henry II founded the diocese of Bamberg in 1007 and endowed it richly; he and his wife Kunigunde are buried in its cathedral. The bishops gathered lands in Upper Franconia, and after the extinction of the counts of Andechs-Meranien in 1248 they consolidated a territory and ruled it as imperial princes.
prince-bishopric-of-bamberg.r: The cathedral chapter elected the prince-bishops. The Romanesque-Gothic cathedral, with the Bamberg Horseman and the tomb of Pope Clement II, symbolises the see's standing. Under Johann Georg II Fuchs von Dornheim the territory suffered one of the worst witch persecutions in Germany between 1626 and 1631. In the baroque era Lothar Franz von Schönborn built the New Residence.
prince-bishopric-of-bamberg.e: The prince-bishopric was secularised in 1802 and annexed by Bavaria, ending more than eight centuries of episcopal rule. Bamberg became an archdiocese in 1817, and its largely intact old town is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
ru: Johann Georg II Fuchs von Dornheim

prince-bishopric-of-sion.t: A prince-bishopric in the Valais, Switzerland, whose bishops held the county granted in 999 until the people of the Upper Valais took power from them.
prince-bishopric-of-sion.o: Sion, in the Rhône valley, had been a bishopric since the 6th century. In 999 King Rudolf III of Burgundy granted the bishop the county of Valais, making him a temporal lord. When Burgundy passed to the Empire in 1032, the bishops became imperial princes.
prince-bishopric-of-sion.r: The bishops faced the counts of Savoy, who held the lower Valais, and the growing power of the German-speaking communes (Zenden) of the upper valley. Cardinal Matthäus Schiner, bishop from 1499, was a leading diplomat of the Swiss in the Italian Wars. The Carolina document claimed Charlemagne had granted the county.
prince-bishopric-of-sion.e: The seven Zenden gradually reduced the bishop's power and in 1613 to 1634 forced bishops to renounce temporal sovereignty, making the Valais a republic allied with the Swiss Confederacy. The Valais became a Swiss canton in 1815, and the bishops of Sion remain spiritual heads.

perinthus.t: Samian colony on the Sea of Marmara that, with Byzantium, defeated Philip II's siege of 340 BCE.
perinthus.o: Colonists from Samos founded Perinthus c. 602 BCE on a promontory on the north shore of the Propontis, in Thrace. They soon fought off attacks by Megarian settlers from neighbouring colonies.
perinthus.r: Perinthus traded with the Thracian interior and along the Propontis route to Byzantium. It resisted the Persian general Megabazus c. 512 BCE but was conquered. Later it paid tribute in the Delian League. In 340 BCE Philip II besieged the city with towers and rams, but Persian satraps and Byzantium helped it hold out.
perinthus.e: Perinthus kept its independence under Hellenistic kings and the Odrysian Kingdom's influence. When Rome made Thrace a province in 46 CE, it became the provincial capital, later renamed Heraclea; it is modern Marmara Ereğlisi.

palace-state-of-phaistos.t: Minoan palace centre of the Mesara plain in southern Crete, famous for its grand staircases and the enigmatic Phaistos Disc.
palace-state-of-phaistos.o: Phaistos stands on a ridge above the Mesara, the largest plain of Crete, which had been settled since the Neolithic. Around 1950 BCE its first palace was built around a paved central court, and Phaistos became the leading power of southern Crete. After destructions in the 18th century BCE the palace was rebuilt on a grander scale.
palace-state-of-phaistos.r: Phaistos controlled the agricultural wealth of the Mesara and probably the nearby port of Kommos, which traded with Egypt and the Levant. Its archives of clay sealings and Linear A tablets reveal a developed palace bureaucracy. Finds include fine Kamares ware pottery and the stamped clay Phaistos Disc, whose script is still undeciphered. The nearby villa of Ayia Triada was closely linked to it.
palace-state-of-phaistos.e: The palace was destroyed c. 1450 BCE and its role passed largely to Ayia Triada and to Knossos, which came to dominate Crete under Mycenaean rulers. Phaistos later revived as a Greek city-state, described separately as Phaistos. The site was excavated by Italian archaeologists from 1900.

principality-of-uglich.t: An appanage principality on the upper Volga, split off from Rostov and bought by Ivan Kalita of Moscow.
principality-of-uglich.o: Uglich on the upper Volga belonged to the Rostov lands. In 1218 Konstantin Vsevolodovich of Rostov gave it to his son Vladimir, who became the first prince of a separate Uglich line.
principality-of-uglich.r: The principality was small, with its wealth drawn from Volga trade and farming. It was sacked by the Mongols in 1238. Its prince Roman Vladimirovich, who died in 1285, was later venerated as a saint for his charity to the poor. Like other small appanages of the north-east, Uglich depended on the grand princes and the Golden Horde.
principality-of-uglich.e: After its line declined, the principality was acquired by Ivan I Kalita of the Grand Duchy of Moscow around 1328, one of his famous purchases of land. Uglich later became the scene of the death of Tsarevich Dmitry in 1591.

prince-bishopric-of-meissen.t: An Ottonian bishopric among the Sorbs of the middle Elbe whose territory was gradually absorbed by the Wettin rulers of Saxony.
prince-bishopric-of-meissen.o: Otto I founded the bishopric of Meissen in 968 as part of his reorganisation of the eastern frontier under Magdeburg. It served the conversion of the Sorbs and the Slavic lands between the Saale and the Bóbr. The bishops shared the castle hill of Meissen with the margraves of Meissen.
prince-bishopric-of-meissen.r: The bishops held scattered lands around Stolpen, Wurzen and Mügeln and governed a diocese that reached into Lusatia. The Gothic cathedral of Meissen, begun around 1260, rose beside the margraves' Albrechtsburg. Benno of Meissen, bishop in the late 11th century, was canonised in 1523; his relics were moved to Munich during the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-meissen.e: The Wettin dukes and electors steadily controlled the see. After Saxony became Lutheran, Bishop Johann IX von Haugwitz resigned in 1581 and the territory was annexed to the Electorate of Saxony. A Catholic remnant in Upper Lusatia continued at Bautzen and became the modern Diocese of Dresden-Meissen.

principality-of-kostroma.t: A short-lived Volga appanage whose only prince, Vasily, rose to become grand prince of Vladimir.
principality-of-kostroma.o: Kostroma on the Volga was a town of the Vladimir-Suzdal lands. In 1246, after the death of Yaroslav Vsevolodovich, his youngest son Vasily received Kostroma as his own appanage.
principality-of-kostroma.r: Vasily of Kostroma was an active prince who fought the Lithuanians and the Novgorodians. In 1272 he became grand prince of Vladimir with the approval of the Golden Horde, ruling from Kostroma rather than moving to Vladimir. The principality was a small Volga land with little else recorded.
principality-of-kostroma.e: Vasily died in 1276 without sons, and Kostroma passed back to the grand princes of Vladimir. It later became part of the Grand Duchy of Moscow. The Ipatiev Monastery near the town later played a part in the election of Michael Romanov in 1613.

principality-of-bryansk.t: A forest principality on the Desna that inherited the senior role in the Chernigov lands after the Mongol sack, before falling to Lithuania.
principality-of-bryansk.o: Bryansk on the Desna was a town of the Principality of Chernigov. After the Mongols destroyed Chernigov in 1239 and Prince Mikhail was killed in 1246, his son Roman Mikhailovich made Bryansk his seat, and it became the leading principality of the old Chernigov lands.
principality-of-bryansk.r: Protected by thick forests, Bryansk recovered more quickly than the open lands to the south. Roman Mikhailovich, who ruled until the 1280s, fought off Lithuanian raids and allied by marriage with the princes of Galicia-Volhynia. From the early 14th century princes of the Smolensk line held the town, and it was torn by disputes between pro-Lithuanian and pro-Horde factions.
principality-of-bryansk.e: Around 1356 Algirdas of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania took Bryansk and later gave it to his son Dmitry. It remained Lithuanian until the Grand Duchy of Moscow took it in 1500.

palatinate-sulzbach.t: Small Wittelsbach duchy in the Upper Palatinate, a centre of religious tolerance and Hebrew printing whose line inherited the Palatinate and Bavaria.
palatinate-sulzbach.o: Sulzbach was split from Palatinate-Neuburg in 1614 as an appanage for Augustus, and in 1656 his son Christian August gained full sovereignty over it as a duchy. Christian August converted to Catholicism in 1655 but kept his Protestant subjects' rights.
palatinate-sulzbach.r: Christian August introduced the simultaneum, letting Catholics and Lutherans share churches, and allowed Jews to settle. Sulzbach became a centre of learning: the Christian Kabbalist Christian Knorr von Rosenroth served at court, and Hebrew printing presses flourished from 1669. The duchy's economy relied on iron ore and smelting in the Upper Palatinate.
palatinate-sulzbach.e: Charles Theodore of Sulzbach inherited the Electoral Palatinate in 1742, merging Sulzbach into it. In 1777 he also inherited the Electorate of Bavaria, and the Sulzbach line thus united the Wittelsbach lands.

principality-of-catalonia.t: The union of Catalan counties under the House of Barcelona, a land of parliaments, merchant cities and its own laws within the Crown of Aragon.
principality-of-catalonia.o: Catalonia grew out of the counties of the Marca Hispanica, gradually gathered under the County of Barcelona. In 1162 Alfonso II inherited both Barcelona and the Kingdom of Aragon, and the Catalan counties became one constituent of the Crown of Aragon. The name Principality became usual in the 14th century.
principality-of-catalonia.r: Catalonia was governed under the Usatges of Barcelona and its Corts, whose standing committee, the Generalitat, was created in 1359. Barcelona's merchants traded across the Mediterranean under the Consulate of the Sea. Catalan literature flourished with Ramon Llull and Ausiàs March, while the Black Death and civil war of 1462-1472 brought decline.
principality-of-catalonia.e: The Reapers' War of 1640 led to the loss of Roussillon to France in 1659. Siding with the Habsburg claimant in the War of the Spanish Succession, Barcelona fell in 1714, and the Nueva Planta decree of 1716 abolished Catalonia's institutions.

prince-bishopric-of-eichstatt.t: A Franconian church principality on the Altmühl, founded on the see of Saint Willibald, that became a showcase of Catholic Baroque.
prince-bishopric-of-eichstatt.o: Saint Boniface made his kinsman Willibald the first bishop of Eichstätt in the 740s. For centuries the bishops held little secular land, but in 1305 they inherited much of the lordship of the extinct counts of Hirschberg, laying the foundation of a territorial principality along the Altmühl valley between Franconia and Bavaria.
prince-bishopric-of-eichstatt.r: The prince-bishop, elected by the cathedral chapter, governed from Eichstätt and the hilltop Willibaldsburg, where Johann Conrad von Gemmingen laid out the garden recorded in the Hortus Eystettensis of 1613. The territory belonged to the Franconian Circle and lived from farming, forests and limestone quarrying. It remained Catholic, and after the Swedish sack of 1634 the city was rebuilt in Baroque style by architects such as Gabriel de Gabrieli.
prince-bishopric-of-eichstatt.e: In 1802 the prince-bishopric was secularised. Its lands went to Bavaria, then largely to Ferdinand of Tuscany's Electorate of Salzburg, before passing to the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1805. The diocese survives, and Eichstätt is home to Germany's only Catholic university.

principality-of-minsk.t: A small principality of the Polotsk lands whose town grew into the capital of modern Belarus.
principality-of-minsk.o: Minsk first appears in the chronicle in 1067, when the sons of Yaroslav the Wise sacked it during their war with Vseslav of Polotsk and defeated him on the Nemiga river. After Vseslav died in 1101 his son Gleb received Minsk, which became a separate principality.
principality-of-minsk.r: Gleb Vseslavich made Minsk a power in its own right and fought Kiev and Vladimir Monomakh until he was captured and died in Kiev in 1119. Afterwards the principality was a minor appanage of the Polotsk dynasty. Little is known of its later rulers or institutions, and it lived in the shadow of Polotsk and the growing Grand Duchy of Lithuania.
principality-of-minsk.e: By the early 14th century Minsk was dependent on Lithuania, and around 1326 a Prince Vasily of Minsk appears as a vassal of Gediminas. It was absorbed into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

prince-bishopric-of-chur.t: Alpine church state ruled by the bishops of Chur, one of the oldest sees north of the Alps, whose temporal power was broken by the leagues of Graubünden.
prince-bishopric-of-chur.o: A bishop of Chur is recorded in 451, making it one of the oldest dioceses north of the Alps. Carolingian and Ottonian kings granted the bishops immunities, tolls and lands in Rhaetia, controlling routes to the Alpine passes. In 1170 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa raised the bishop to the rank of an imperial prince, giving the church a recognised secular principality.
prince-bishopric-of-chur.r: The bishops governed estates in the Rhine valley, the Engadine and the Vinschgau from their court in Chur, with officials in castles along the pass roads. Romansh, German and Lombard dialects were all spoken in their lands. To resist episcopal power, the subjects formed the League of God's House in 1367, which later joined the Grey League and the League of the Ten Jurisdictions in the Three Leagues.
prince-bishopric-of-chur.e: The Ilanz Articles of 1524 and 1526 stripped the bishop of most secular authority and handed it to the communes of the Three Leagues. The bishops kept a few rights and the title of prince until 1803, and the Catholic diocese of Chur continues today.

principality-of-kozelsk.t: A tiny appanage of the Chernigov lands whose town held out against the Mongols for seven weeks in 1238.
principality-of-kozelsk.o: Kozelsk on the Zhizdra river, a tributary of the Oka, was a small town of the Chernigov land, first mentioned in 1146. It became the seat of a separate appanage in the early 13th century under a junior branch of the Olgovichi princes.
principality-of-kozelsk.r: The principality was small and poor, but its fortified town became famous in 1238 when Batu's army, returning from the north, besieged it for seven weeks. The defenders, led in the name of the child prince Vasily, killed many attackers before the town fell and everyone was slaughtered. The Mongols reportedly called it the evil town.
principality-of-kozelsk.e: Rebuilt, Kozelsk passed under the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the 14th century and its princes became Lithuanian vassals. In the wars of the late 15th century it changed sides, and the peace of 1494 confirmed it as part of the Grand Duchy of Moscow.

principality-of-calenberg.t: A Guelph principality between the Deister and the Leine that grew into the Electorate of Hanover and the dynasty of Britain's Georgian kings.
principality-of-calenberg.o: The Guelph lands of the old Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg were repeatedly divided. In 1432 the territory between the Deister and the Leine, named after Calenberg castle, became a separate principality under William the Victorious, split off from the Principality of Wolfenbüttel.
principality-of-calenberg.r: Calenberg was ruled from Calenberg castle and other residences, and from 1636 from Hanover. Duchess Elisabeth, regent in the 1540s, introduced Lutheranism. The principality absorbed Göttingen in 1495 and later Grubenhagen. Duke John Frederick brought Leibniz to Hanover as librarian in 1676, and Ernest Augustus built a more centralised state.
principality-of-calenberg.e: In 1692 Emperor Leopold I made Ernest Augustus an elector, and Calenberg became the core of the Electorate of Hanover, which absorbed the Principality of Lüneburg in 1705. His son George became King of Great Britain in 1714.

principality-of-rostov.t: An appanage principality based on the ancient town of Rostov on Lake Nero, gradually bought out by Moscow.
principality-of-rostov.o: Rostov is one of the oldest towns of north-eastern Rus', first mentioned in 862 in the land of the Finnic Merya, and was long the seat of a bishop. In 1207 Vsevolod the Big Nest gave it to his eldest son Konstantin, and his descendants ruled it as a principality within the Vladimir-Suzdal lands.
principality-of-rostov.r: Rostov was a religious and commercial centre with a long tradition of chronicle writing. Its prince Vasilko Konstantinovich was captured and killed by the Mongols after the Battle of the Sit in 1238. Later the principality was split between two lines, each ruling half the town, and it became a minor power between Moscow and Tver.
principality-of-rostov.e: Moscow's influence grew through the 14th century, and the Rostov princes sold the first half of their rights to Moscow in the 15th century. In 1474 the last princes sold the remaining half to Ivan III. The town remained a great church centre, and its kremlin was built by Metropolitan Jonah in the 17th century.

principality-of-berat.t: Albanian lordship of the Muzaka family around Berat and the Myzeqe plain, a leading noble realm of late medieval Albania.
principality-of-berat.o: The Muzaka were powerful Albanian nobles of the Myzeqe plain. Around 1335 Andrea II Muzaka received the Byzantine title of despot for fighting the Angevins, and the family built a lordship in the area. Berat itself was taken by the Serbian Empire in the 1340s and only came firmly into Muzaka hands around 1372.
principality-of-berat.r: The Muzaka ruled from the fortress of Berat over Albanian peasants and herders, balancing Byzantium, the Serbs, Venice and the Balšić lords of Zeta. They joined coalitions against the Balšići and against the Ottomans; Theodore II Muzaka died fighting at Kosovo in 1389 according to tradition.
principality-of-berat.e: Ottoman pressure grew after their victory at Savra in 1385. The Ottomans took Berat in 1417, and the Muzaka lands became part of the Sanjak of Albania. The family later took part in Skanderbeg's resistance.

prince-bishopric-of-brixen.t: An Alpine prince-bishopric on the Brenner route, set up by emperors to guard the road to Italy, whose bishops ruled parts of Tyrol for nearly 800 years.
prince-bishopric-of-brixen.o: The bishopric moved from Säben to Brixen (Bressanone) around 990. In 1027 Emperor Conrad II granted Bishop Hartwig the counties of the Inn and Eisack valleys, and in 1091 the Puster valley followed, so that loyal bishops would hold the passes on the imperial road to Rome.
prince-bishopric-of-brixen.r: The bishops entrusted their counties to advocates, chiefly the counts of Tyrol, who gradually absorbed most of their power. The bishopric retained Brixen, Bruneck and scattered lands. Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, bishop from 1450, clashed bitterly with Duke Sigismund of Tyrol and was imprisoned in 1460.
prince-bishopric-of-brixen.e: The prince-bishopric was secularised in 1803 and annexed by Austria, then passed to Bavaria from 1805 to 1814, and back to Austria. After the First World War Brixen became part of Italy, and in 1964 the see moved to Bolzano, becoming the Diocese of Bolzano-Brixen.

principality-of-galicia.t: A rich principality on the upper Dniester, built around the salt trade and the town of Halych, whose boyars were famously powerful.
principality-of-galicia.o: In the 1080s three Rurikid brothers, Rurik, Volodar and Vasylko Rostislavich, took control of the towns of Peremyshl, Zvenyhorod and Terebovl in the far south-west of Rus'. Their heir Volodymyrko united these lands and in 1141 made Halych on the Dniester his capital, creating the Principality of Galicia.
principality-of-galicia.r: Galicia prospered from salt mines, which supplied much of Rus', and from trade along the Dniester to the Black Sea and with Hungary and Poland. Its landholding boyars were unusually strong and repeatedly deposed or defied their princes. Yaroslav Osmomysl, who ruled from 1153 to 1187, was praised in the Lay of Igor's Campaign as a mighty ruler.
principality-of-galicia.e: The dynasty of Volodymyrko died out with Vladimir Yaroslavich in 1199. Roman Mstislavich of the Principality of Volhynia then took Halych and joined the two lands into the Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia, though Hungary and Poland long contested Galicia.

phocaea.t: Ionian city whose daring sailors founded Massalia and explored the western Mediterranean as far as Tartessos in Spain.
phocaea.o: Phocaea, the northernmost Ionian city, was founded on a peninsula north of the Hermus c. 1000 BCE by settlers said to have come from Phocis. Its rocky territory pushed the Phocaeans to the sea, and from the 7th century BCE they sailed long distances in fast fifty-oared ships.
phocaea.r: Herodotus credits Phocaeans with opening the Adriatic, Tyrrhenian and Iberian seas. They founded Lampsacus, Massalia c. 600 BCE, Alalia on Corsica and Emporion in Spain, and won the friendship of King Arganthonius of Tartessos. When Harpagus besieged the city c. 545 BCE, most citizens sailed west; those at Alalia fought Carthaginians and Etruscans c. 540 BCE.
phocaea.e: Phocaea recovered and provided Dionysius, commander of the Greek fleet at Lade in 494 BCE. In 132 BCE it backed Aristonicus against Rome and was spared destruction only through Massalia's appeal, then joined the province of Asia.

principality-of-mozhaysk.t: A western appanage of Moscow whose prince Ivan helped capture and blind Grand Prince Vasily II during Moscow's civil war.
principality-of-mozhaysk.o: Mozhaysk, on the Moskva river west of Moscow, was taken from Smolensk in 1303. In his will of 1389 Dmitry Donskoy left it, with Vereya and Beloozero, to his son Andrei, who ruled it as an appanage within the Grand Duchy of Moscow.
principality-of-mozhaysk.r: The principality guarded Moscow's approach from Lithuania and Smolensk. During the long civil war over the Moscow throne, Andrei's son Ivan of Mozhaysk joined Dmitry Shemyaka, and in 1446 he helped seize Vasily II at the Trinity Monastery, after which Vasily was blinded.
principality-of-mozhaysk.e: When Vasily II regained power, he sent an army against Mozhaysk in 1454. Ivan fled to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and Mozhaysk was absorbed into Moscow's lands, while Vereya continued for a time under Ivan's brother Mikhail.

principality-of-sedan.t: A Protestant sovereign principality on the Meuse, ruled by the La Marck and La Tour d'Auvergne families, which sheltered Huguenots and French rebels.
principality-of-sedan.o: In 1424 Everard de la Marck acquired the lordship of Sedan on the Meuse, at the frontier between France, Luxembourg and Liège. His descendants built a great fortress there and claimed sovereignty, owing allegiance to neither the French king nor the emperor.
principality-of-sedan.r: Robert II de la Marck and his successors were also dukes of Bouillon. The princes adopted Calvinism, and Sedan became a Huguenot refuge with a Protestant academy founded in 1602. In 1591 the heiress Charlotte de la Marck married Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, father of Marshal Turenne, who was born at Sedan in 1611. Sedan's cloth industry later flourished.
principality-of-sedan.e: Frédéric-Maurice de La Tour d'Auvergne joined the conspiracy of Cinq-Mars against Richelieu, and to save his life ceded Sedan to Louis XIII in 1642. The principality was absorbed into the Kingdom of France.
ru: Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Duke of Bouillon

principality-of-pronsk.t: An appanage principality of the Ryazan land whose princes repeatedly challenged the grand princes of Ryazan.
principality-of-pronsk.o: Pronsk, on the Pronya river south of Ryazan, was a fortified frontier town facing the steppe. In the 1180s it became the seat of a separate branch of the Ryazan princely house, and for three centuries its rulers held it as an appanage of the Grand Principality of Ryazan.
principality-of-pronsk.r: Pronsk princes often fought their Ryazan cousins for the senior throne, sometimes with the help of the Golden Horde or Moscow. In 1408 Ivan Vladimirovich of Pronsk briefly drove out the Ryazan grand prince with Tatar support. Like other border lands, Pronsk suffered heavily from steppe raids and was sacked by the Mongols in 1237.
principality-of-pronsk.e: In the 15th century Pronsk was gradually reabsorbed into Ryazan, and by the 1480s its princes had lost their independent role. The territory followed Ryazan into the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1521, while the Pronsky princely family served in the Russian nobility.

principality-of-birkenfeld.t: Hunsrück exclave of the Grand Duchy of Oldenburg, ruled from the North Sea coast for more than a century.
principality-of-birkenfeld.o: At the Congress of Vienna, the Grand Duke of Oldenburg was awarded territory on the left bank of the Rhine. In 1817 he received a district of the former French Saar department around Birkenfeld in the Hunsrück, which became the Principality of Birkenfeld, an exclave hundreds of kilometres from Oldenburg.
principality-of-birkenfeld.r: The principality was governed by a regional government in Birkenfeld under Oldenburg's laws and had its own provincial council. Its people were mostly Protestant farmers, with gemstone cutting and agate working around Idar and Oberstein as a distinctive industry. After 1918 it formed a part of the Free State of Oldenburg.
principality-of-birkenfeld.e: Under the Greater Hamburg Act of 1937, Oldenburg ceded Birkenfeld to Prussia, which made it a district of the Rhine Province. It is now part of Rhineland-Palatinate.

praeneste.t: Latin hill city east of Rome, famous for its princely tombs, its bronze cistae and the oracle of Fortuna Primigenia.
praeneste.o: Praeneste, modern Palestrina, occupied a spur of the Monti Prenestini commanding the routes from Latium to Campania. In the 7th century BCE its rulers were buried in the Bernardini and Barberini tombs with gold, silver and ivory from the eastern Mediterranean, among the richest burials in Italy.
praeneste.r: Praeneste was a powerful and often independent member of the Latin League. Its workshops produced engraved bronze cistae, cylindrical boxes for toiletries such as the Ficoroni cista. The sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia, where oracles were drawn by lot, was later rebuilt on a vast terraced scale in the 2nd century BCE. Local Latin had distinct features noted by Roman writers.
praeneste.e: Praeneste fought Rome in the Latin War and lost land in 338 BCE, but remained a separate allied city until it gained citizenship after the Social War. It sheltered Gaius Marius the Younger in 82 BCE; Sulla took it, executed its men and planted a colony.

plataea.t: Small Boeotian city that defied Thebes, stood with Athens at Marathon and gave its name to the battle that ended the Persian invasion of Greece in 479 BCE.
plataea.o: Plataea lay on the northern slopes of Mount Cithaeron, on the border between Boeotia and Attica. When Thebes pressed it to join the Boeotian League in the late 6th century BCE, the Plataeans turned to Athens, traditionally in 519 BCE. That alliance shaped the rest of their history: alone among the Greeks, they sent their whole levy to fight beside the Athenians at Marathon in 490 BCE.
plataea.r: A modest farming community governed by its own citizen assembly, Plataea mattered far beyond its size. In 479 BCE the allied Greek army under the Spartan Pausanias defeated the Persian general Mardonius on its territory, and the city was charged with tending the graves of the fallen and hosting a festival of freedom, the Eleutheria. Its people spoke the Boeotian dialect and kept close cultural ties with Athens.
plataea.e: Theban aggression began the Peloponnesian War at Plataea in 431 BCE; after a famous siege the city surrendered to Sparta and was razed in 427 BCE. Restored in 386 BCE, it was destroyed again by Thebes in 373 BCE and rebuilt under Philip II and Alexander. It then belonged to the Boeotian League until Roman conquest in 146 BCE.

pogesanians.t: Prussian people between the Elbląg and Pasłęk rivers, whose land saw the founding of Elbing and fierce fighting in the Great Prussian Uprising.
pogesanians.o: Pogesania lay along the Vistula Lagoon east of the Elbląg river, in modern northern Poland. Its Prussian inhabitants lived near the old trading centre of Truso, a Viking Age emporium described by the traveller Wulfstan around 890, and they are known from Peter of Dusburg's chronicle.
pogesanians.r: Pogesanian society was led by nobles holding hillforts, with farming, fishing and the amber trade as mainstays. They kept the Prussian gods and customs, including cremation of the dead, which Wulfstan described in detail.
pogesanians.e: The Teutonic Order and the Hanseatic settlers of Lübeck founded Elbing on their land in 1237. In the Great Prussian Uprising from 1260 the Pogesanians, led by Auktume, attacked Elbing and other castles, but they were subdued by 1274. Their territory was divided between the Order and the Bishopric of Pomesania.

principality-of-serpukhov.t: An appanage of the Moscow princes south of the capital, ruled by Vladimir the Bold, hero of the Battle of Kulikovo.
principality-of-serpukhov.o: Serpukhov on the Oka guarded Moscow's southern approaches against the steppe. In 1341 Ivan I Kalita's will took effect, and his youngest son Andrei received Serpukhov and surrounding lands, including Borovsk, as an appanage within the Grand Duchy of Moscow.
principality-of-serpukhov.r: Andrei's son Vladimir the Bold, cousin of Dmitry Donskoy, was Moscow's leading general. At Kulikovo in 1380 he and the commander Dmitry Bobrok led the ambush regiment whose attack decided the battle. He built the Serpukhov kremlin and founded monasteries, and his principality served as a buffer against Tatar and Lithuanian raids.
principality-of-serpukhov.e: During Moscow's civil war Vladimir's grandson Vasily Yaroslavich supported Vasily II, but in 1456 the grand prince had him arrested and annexed Serpukhov. Vasily died in prison, and the appanage ended.

principality-of-lippe.t: Small Westphalian principality at Detmold that survived as a German state into the 20th century and played a part in Hitler's rise.
principality-of-lippe.o: The lords of Lippe held lands around Detmold and Lemgo from the 12th century, becoming counts in 1528. Though granted princely rank in 1720, they did not use the title until Count Leopold I accepted it in 1789, when the County of Lippe-Detmold became the Principality of Lippe.
principality-of-lippe.r: Princess Pauline, regent from 1802 to 1820, kept Lippe independent by joining the Confederation of the Rhine and introduced social reforms, including a nursery school. Lippe was rural and Calvinist, and many men worked seasonally as brickmakers elsewhere. A disputed succession between 1895 and 1905, involving Kaiser William II's brother-in-law, was settled by arbitration in favour of the Biesterfeld line.
principality-of-lippe.e: Lippe joined the German Empire in 1871. Prince Leopold IV abdicated in November 1918, and the state continued as the Free State of Lippe until 1947.

principality-of-nassau-diez.t: Nassau territory on the Lahn whose counts, as hereditary stadtholders of Friesland, became the House of Orange-Nassau that rules the Netherlands today.
principality-of-nassau-diez.o: Nassau-Diez arose in the 1606 partition of the lands of John VI of Nassau-Dillenburg, when Ernst Casimir received Diez on the Lahn. Ernst Casimir served the Dutch Republic as a general and became stadtholder of Friesland and Groningen, beginning his line's long connection with the northern Netherlands.
principality-of-nassau-diez.r: The German lands were small and governed from Diez and later the Oranienstein palace, while the counts spent their careers in the Dutch Republic, where they held the Frisian stadtholdership hereditarily. They were raised to princes of the Empire in 1654. John William Friso inherited part of William III's Orange claims in 1702, and his son William IV united all Nassau-Ottonian lands by 1743.
principality-of-nassau-diez.e: William IV became stadtholder of all the United Provinces in 1747. In 1806 Napoleon confiscated the German lands, which went to the Grand Duchy of Berg, and after 1815 they passed to the Duchy of Nassau and Prussia. William IV's grandson became King William I of the Netherlands.

provisional-government-of-western-thrace.t: Short-lived Muslim-led state in Western Thrace in 1913, set up by Ottoman officers to keep the region from Bulgaria after the Second Balkan War.
provisional-government-of-western-thrace.o: Bulgaria took Western Thrace in the First Balkan War. When the Second Balkan War broke out in 1913, the Ottomans retook Edirne, and Ottoman officers led by Süleyman Askerî, together with local Turkish and Pomak irregulars, drove Bulgarian forces from the region. In late August 1913 they proclaimed an independent government at Gümülcine, today Komotini.
provisional-government-of-western-thrace.r: The government had a president, ministers, a flag, stamps and an army of a few thousand irregulars, drawing on the region's Muslim majority. It was effectively run by Ottoman officers acting unofficially, and no foreign power recognised it. It lasted about two months.
provisional-government-of-western-thrace.e: By the Treaty of Constantinople in September 1913 the Ottoman government recognised Bulgarian possession of Western Thrace and withdrew support, and Bulgarian troops took over in October. The region passed to Greece after the First World War, where its Muslim minority remains.

prince-bishopric-of-merseburg.t: An Ottonian bishopric on the Saale whose bishop Thietmar wrote a famous chronicle, later absorbed into Saxony after the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-merseburg.o: Otto I founded the bishopric of Merseburg in 968 to fulfil a vow made before the Battle of Lechfeld, as a suffragan of Magdeburg. It was dissolved in 981, its lands divided among neighbours, but Henry II restored it in 1004. The bishops built a cathedral beside the royal palace at Merseburg.
prince-bishopric-of-merseburg.r: Bishop Thietmar of Merseburg, from 1009 to 1018, wrote a chronicle that is a key source on the Ottonian empire, the Slavs and early Poland. The bishops ruled a small territory along the Saale. The cathedral library preserves the Merseburg Charms, the only surviving Old High German pagan spells.
prince-bishopric-of-merseburg.e: Merseburg came under the influence of the Wettin rulers of Saxony. After the Reformation, a Saxon prince became administrator in 1561, and from 1565 the see was effectively a Saxon possession. From 1656 to 1738 it formed the Duchy of Saxe-Merseburg, before reverting to the electorate and passing to Prussia in 1815.

paris-commune.t: The revolutionary government that ruled Paris for ten weeks in 1871, and whose bloody suppression became a lasting symbol for the socialist left.
paris-commune.o: After France's defeat by Prussia and the long siege of Paris, the government of Adolphe Thiers tried to remove the National Guard's cannons from Montmartre on 18 March 1871. Parisians resisted, the government withdrew to Versailles, and elections on 26 March created the Commune.
paris-commune.r: The Commune's council, a mix of Jacobins, socialists and followers of Proudhon and Blanqui, separated church and state, abolished night work in bakeries, let workers take over abandoned workshops and postponed rents. Women such as Louise Michel played prominent roles. The Communards also pulled down the Vendôme Column.
paris-commune.e: Government troops entered Paris on 21 May, and during the 'Bloody Week' that followed thousands of Communards were killed, many by summary execution; the Communards shot hostages and burned the Tuileries. Thousands more were tried and deported to New Caledonia. The French Third Republic survived.

principality-of-abkhazia.t: A principality on the Black Sea coast ruled by the Shervashidze family, between Georgian, Ottoman and Russian power, until Russia abolished it in 1864.
principality-of-abkhazia.o: As the Kingdom of Georgia broke up in the 1460s, the Shervashidze, or Chachba, family who governed the Abkhaz coast as eristavis under the Dadiani of Mingrelia made themselves independent princes with their seat at Sukhumi and later Lykhny. Family tradition traced the line to the Shirvanshahs, a claim that cannot be verified.
principality-of-abkhazia.r: The princes ruled a society of nobles and peasants living by livestock, farming and coastal trade, including a slave trade with Ottoman ports. From the 16th century Ottoman influence grew: the coast came under Ottoman garrisons, and many Abkhaz nobles adopted Islam. Keleshbey Chachba strengthened the principality but was assassinated in 1808.
principality-of-abkhazia.e: His son Giorgi accepted a Russian protectorate in 1810. The Russian Empire abolished the principality in 1864, and after revolts many Abkhaz were deported to the Ottoman Empire in the exodus called the Mahajirstvo.

principality-of-badakhshan.t: A mountain principality of the Pamirs and upper Amu Darya, ruled by mirs from Faizabad until the Afghan Emirate absorbed it.
principality-of-badakhshan.o: Badakhshan, famed since antiquity for its lapis lazuli and rubies, was ruled in the 16th and early 17th centuries by Timurid and Uzbek governors. Around 1657 a local dynasty of mirs of the Yarid family, claiming saintly descent, established independent rule from Faizabad on the Kokcha River.
principality-of-badakhshan.r: The mirs ruled a mountainous land of Tajik farmers and herders, including Ismaili communities in the Pamirs and Sunni Muslims in the lowlands. Revenue came from mines, trade routes to Kashgar and Chitral, and tribute from vassal valleys such as Shughnan and Wakhan. The state was frequently raided by the Kataghan Khanate and the Durrani Empire.
principality-of-badakhshan.e: In 1859 the Emirate of Afghanistan made Badakhshan a vassal, and around 1881 Abdur Rahman Khan annexed it fully. The Anglo-Russian boundary settlements of the 1890s divided the region along the Panj River between Afghanistan and the Russian protectorate of Bukhara.

principality-of-dombes.t: A small sovereign principality north of Lyon, with its own parliament and mint at Trévoux, held by royal relatives until it was sold to Louis XV.
principality-of-dombes.o: The Dombes, a plateau of ponds east of the Saône, belonged to the lords of Beaujeu and then the dukes of Bourbon. After the confiscation of the Constable of Bourbon's lands in 1523 it was held by the crown, then restored in 1560 to the Bourbon-Montpensier family, who ruled it as a sovereign principality outside the Kingdom of France.
principality-of-dombes.r: The princes kept a parliament at Trévoux, minted coin and taxed separately, though in practice the land was closely tied to France. Anne Marie Louise d'Orléans, La Grande Mademoiselle, held it and in 1681 ceded it to the Duke of Maine, Louis XIV's legitimised son. Jesuits at Trévoux published the Journal de Trévoux and the Dictionnaire de Trévoux.
principality-of-dombes.e: In 1762 the Duke of Maine's son, the Count of Eu, exchanged the principality with Louis XV for lands in France, and it became part of the kingdom.

peru-bolivian-confederation.t: Andrés de Santa Cruz's union of Peru and Bolivia, which threatened the balance of power in South America and was destroyed by Chile in 1839.
peru-bolivian-confederation.o: In 1835 Peru's president Luis José de Orbegoso asked the Bolivian president Andrés de Santa Cruz for help against rebels. Santa Cruz invaded, defeated Agustín Gamarra and Felipe Santiago Salaverry in 1835 and 1836, and divided Peru into the North Peruvian Republic and South Peruvian Republic, which joined the Republic of Bolivia in a confederation.
peru-bolivian-confederation.r: The Pact of Tacna of 1837 made Santa Cruz Supreme Protector, with broad powers over foreign affairs and the army. He introduced legal codes modelled on Napoleon's and promoted trade. Chile, under the influence of Diego Portales, saw the confederation as a threat, and Chile and the Argentine Confederation of Rosas declared war in 1837. Peruvian exiles and many in Lima resented Bolivian dominance.
peru-bolivian-confederation.e: A Chilean army under Manuel Bulnes, joined by Peruvian exiles, defeated Santa Cruz at Yungay on 20 January 1839. The confederation was dissolved, and Santa Cruz went into exile. Peru and Bolivia were never united again, and Chile emerged as the leading power on the Pacific coast.
