principality-of-vyazma.t: A small appanage of the Smolensk lands on the road to Moscow, taken by Lithuania in 1403.
principality-of-vyazma.o: Vyazma, on the upper Vyazma river east of Smolensk, is first mentioned in the 13th century as a town of the Principality of Smolensk. In the mid 13th century it became a separate appanage held by a junior line of the Smolensk princes, the ancestors of the Vyazemsky family.
principality-of-vyazma.r: Its importance came from its position on the main route between Smolensk and Moscow, which made it a trading post and a frontier fortress. Little is known of its individual rulers or institutions, and it was usually subordinate to Smolensk.
principality-of-vyazma.e: Vytautas of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania took Vyazma in 1403 in the course of his conquest of the Smolensk lands, and its princes became Lithuanian vassals. The Grand Duchy of Moscow captured it in 1494, and the Vyazemsky princes entered Russian service.

priene.t: Small Ionian city near Mount Mycale, home of the sage Bias and later rebuilt as the best-preserved example of a Hellenistic grid-planned town.
priene.o: Priene was one of the twelve Ionian cities, founded by tradition by settlers from Athens and Thebes c. 1000 BCE. Its original site near the Maeander has never been found. The Panionion, the common sanctuary of the Ionian League on Mount Mycale, lay in its territory, giving Priene a role in Ionian affairs out of proportion to its size.
priene.r: In the 6th century BCE Bias of Priene, counted among the Seven Sages, advised the Ionians to emigrate to Sardinia rather than submit to Persia. Priene fell to the Kingdom of Lydia and then the Achaemenid Empire, sent 12 ships to the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE and later paid tribute in the Delian League.
priene.e: In the mid-4th century BCE the city was rebuilt on a terrace of Mycale with a strict grid; Alexander dedicated its temple of Athena Polias. It passed to Rome in 133 BCE. As the Maeander silted its harbour, Priene declined, leaving its ruins remarkably intact.
priene.re: Greek religion; cult of Athena Polias

provisional-government-of-the-french-rep.t: The government that restored the Republic after liberation, gave French women the vote and built the post-war welfare state.
provisional-government-of-the-french-rep.o: In June 1944 the French Committee of National Liberation in Algiers renamed itself the Provisional Government of the French Republic, led by Charles de Gaulle. After Paris was liberated in August 1944, it moved to the capital and declared that Vichy France had never been legitimate.
provisional-government-of-the-french-rep.r: The government included Gaullists, communists, socialists and Christian democrats from the Resistance. Women voted for the first time in 1945. It nationalised Renault, coal, electricity and major banks, created the social security system and the Monnet Plan for reconstruction, and oversaw the trials of collaborators. France gained a seat on the UN Security Council and an occupation zone in Germany.
provisional-government-of-the-french-rep.e: De Gaulle resigned in January 1946 over disputes about the constitution, and Félix Gouin and Georges Bidault led the government. After a first draft was rejected, voters approved a new constitution in October 1946, founding the French Fourth Republic.

prince-bishopric-of-wurzburg.t: Franconian church state whose bishops styled themselves Dukes of Franconia and built one of Europe's grandest baroque palaces, the Würzburg Residenz.
prince-bishopric-of-wurzburg.o: The diocese was founded in 742 by Saint Boniface, with Burkard as its first bishop. Royal grants gave the bishops wide lands on the Main, and in 1168 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa confirmed their judicial and ducal rights across eastern Franconia, the basis of their later title of Dukes of Franconia and of a territorial principality inside the Holy Roman Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-wurzburg.r: The prince-bishop was elected by the noble cathedral chapter and governed from the Marienberg fortress, later from the town below. Julius Echter von Mespelbrunn refounded the university in 1582, built the Juliusspital and drove a forceful Counter-Reformation. The 17th century saw some of Germany's worst witch trials. Under the Schönborn bishops Balthasar Neumann built the Residenz, decorated with Tiepolo's ceiling frescoes, and vineyards along the Main supported a wealthy wine trade.
prince-bishopric-of-wurzburg.e: Secularised in 1802 and given to Bavaria, the territory became the Grand Duchy of Würzburg under Ferdinand of Tuscany from 1805 to 1814 before returning to the Kingdom of Bavaria. The diocese survives, and the Residenz is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

principality-of-serbia.t: Autonomous and then independent Serbian principality of the 19th century, built by the rival Obrenović and Karađorđević dynasties on the way to a modern kingdom.
principality-of-serbia.o: After the collapse of Revolutionary Serbia in 1813, Miloš Obrenović launched the Second Serbian Uprising at Takovo in 1815. Combining fighting with negotiation, he won recognition as supreme prince in 1817, and an Ottoman decree of 1830 made Serbia an autonomous hereditary principality paying tribute, with Ottoman garrisons only in a few fortresses.
principality-of-serbia.r: Miloš ruled autocratically, but the Sretenje Constitution of 1835 and the Ottoman-imposed constitution of 1838 set up a council that curbed him. Power swung between Obrenović princes and Alexander Karađorđević, who reigned from 1842 to 1858. Michael Obrenović modernised the army and secured the departure of the last Ottoman garrisons in 1867. Peasant smallholders raised pigs for export to Austria.
principality-of-serbia.e: Serbia fought the Ottomans in 1876 to 1878, and the Congress of Berlin in 1878 recognised its independence and added Niš and Pirot. In 1882 Prince Milan Obrenović proclaimed the Kingdom of Serbia.

principality-of-polotsk.t: The oldest principality of the Belarusian lands, a Dvina trading power that kept its own dynasty and long resisted Kiev.
principality-of-polotsk.o: Polotsk on the Western Dvina was a Krivich town ruled in the 10th century by the Scandinavian Rogvolod, until Vladimir I killed him and married his daughter Rogneda. Around 987 Vladimir gave Polotsk to their son Izyaslav, whose descendants held it as a separate dynasty.
principality-of-polotsk.r: Polotsk controlled the Dvina route to the Baltic and traded with Riga and Gotland. Its princes often fought the rest of Rus', and Vseslav, called the Sorcerer, who ruled for over fifty years, even held Kiev briefly in 1068. The Cathedral of Saint Sophia and the abbess Euphrosyne of Polotsk made it a religious centre.
principality-of-polotsk.e: By the 12th century the land split into smaller principalities, including Minsk and Vitebsk, and German crusaders took its Livonian tributaries. Polotsk came under the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the early 14th century, and its separate princely rule ended in 1392 when Vytautas installed his own governors.

principality-of-oettingen-spielberg.t: A Catholic line of the counts of Oettingen in the Ries, which inherited much of the family's lands in 1731 and became princely in 1734.
principality-of-oettingen-spielberg.o: The counts of Oettingen ruled the Ries crater basin from the 12th century. In 1522 the house split into the Oettingen-Oettingen line, which became Lutheran, and the Catholic Oettingen-Wallerstein line. A Catholic branch formed at Spielberg in the 17th century inherited much of the Oettingen-Oettingen lands in 1731 and received princely rank in 1734.
principality-of-oettingen-spielberg.r: The princes ruled from Oettingen, a town long divided along its main street between Catholic and Lutheran halves, a legacy of the dynasty's split. The territory lived from farming in the fertile Ries and belonged to the Swabian Circle.
principality-of-oettingen-spielberg.e: In 1806 the principality was mediatised and placed under the Kingdom of Bavaria. The princely family of Oettingen-Spielberg still owns the residence palace at Oettingen in Bayern.

proto-kingdom-of-thinis.t: The kingdom of Thinis and Abydos, whose Dynasty 0 rulers left the earliest Egyptian writing and went on to unite Egypt.
proto-kingdom-of-thinis.o: Thinis, near Abydos in Upper Egypt, became the seat of a line of rulers in the late 4th millennium BCE. Their burials in Cemetery U at Abydos grew steadily richer, and by c. 3200 BCE the Thinite chiefs had absorbed the Proto-kingdom of Naqada and extended their reach over the Proto-kingdom of Nekhen.
proto-kingdom-of-thinis.r: Tomb U-j at Abydos, built around 3320 BCE, contained hundreds of imported Levantine wine jars and small bone labels carrying some of the earliest known Egyptian writing. Kings now wrote their names inside a serekh, a palace façade topped by the Horus falcon. These rulers, known today as Dynasty 0, ran an economy of grain, wine and prestige goods and pushed their trade into the Delta.
proto-kingdom-of-thinis.e: The Thinite line culminated in Narmer, who around 3100 BCE ruled both Upper and Lower Egypt and is usually counted as the founder of Early Dynastic Egypt. Abydos remained the burial ground of the First Dynasty kings and later became the great cult centre of Osiris.

principality-of-grubenhagen.t: Small Guelph principality in the western Harz and around Einbeck, famous for its beer, whose line died out in 1596.
principality-of-grubenhagen.o: When the sons of Albert I of Brunswick divided their inheritance around 1291, Henry I the Admirable received Grubenhagen, named after a castle near Einbeck, with lands in the western Harz around Osterode and Herzberg. This became a separate Guelph principality.
principality-of-grubenhagen.r: The principality was small, divided at times among co-rulers. Its towns included Einbeck, whose beer was exported across northern Europe, and Osterode. Silver mining in the Harz around Clausthal brought income. Philip I introduced the Reformation in the 1530s. Herzberg castle served as the main residence.
principality-of-grubenhagen.e: When Philip II died without heirs in 1596, Henry Julius of the Principality of Wolfenbüttel seized Grubenhagen, but in 1617 an imperial court awarded it to the Principality of Lüneburg. It later formed part of the Electorate of Hanover and is now in Lower Saxony.

prince-bishopric-of-minden.t: Weser valley church state founded after Charlemagne's Saxon wars and secularised into a Brandenburg principality in 1648.
prince-bishopric-of-minden.o: The diocese of Minden was founded around 800 after Charlemagne's conquest of the Saxons, on a crossing of the Weser. Its bishops gained counties and immunities from the Ottonian and Salian kings. After Henry the Lion fell in 1180 they ruled a territory along the Weser as imperial princes, though Minden itself grew increasingly self-governing.
prince-bishopric-of-minden.r: The cathedral chapter elected the bishops, who often lived at Petershagen because of friction with Minden's citizens. Their land was small, rural and hemmed in by neighbours such as the counties of Schaumburg, Ravensberg and Hoya. The city of Minden adopted Lutheranism in 1530, and in the later 16th century the see was held by Lutheran princes of the houses of Brunswick-Lüneburg and Schaumburg.
prince-bishopric-of-minden.e: At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 the see was secularised as the Principality of Minden and given to Brandenburg. It remained Prussian, apart from the Napoleonic period, and the town is now in North Rhine-Westphalia.

principality-of-kiev.t: The principality of the old capital of Rus', a prize fought over by rival princes, which later became a Lithuanian vassal state.
principality-of-kiev.o: When Mstislav the Great died in 1132, the unity of Kievan Rus' broke down. Kiev itself and its surrounding lands became one principality among many, though still senior in prestige and the seat of the metropolitan. Princes of the Monomakh and Olgovichi lines competed for its throne.
principality-of-kiev.r: Kiev changed hands dozens of times in the 12th century. The armies of Andrei Bogolyubsky sacked it in 1169, and Rurik Rostislavich and his Cuman allies sacked it again in 1203. The Mongols destroyed the city in 1240, and for a century it was ruled by minor princes and Mongol officials.
principality-of-kiev.e: Around 1362 Algirdas of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania took Kiev and gave it to his son Volodymyr. Under the Olelkovich princes it was a Lithuanian vassal state with an Orthodox court. When Semen Olelkovich died in 1470, Casimir IV abolished the principality in 1471 and made it a voivodeship.

principality-of-bzhedugh.t: A princely Circassian tribe on the lower Kuban, one of the few Adyghe groups that largely remained in their homeland after 1864.
principality-of-bzhedugh.o: The Bzhedugh were one of the aristocratic Adyghe tribes of Circassia, living along the left bank of the Kuban and the Psekups river near modern Krasnodar. They are recorded as a distinct princely community by the 16th and 17th centuries; their earlier history is not recorded separately.
principality-of-bzhedugh.r: Princes and nobles held power over free peasants and serfs. When the commoners of the Shapsugs and Natukhaj rebelled against their nobility, Bzhedugh princes backed the aristocrats and were defeated at Bziyuqo in 1796. The tribe lay close to Russian forts on the Kuban and often negotiated with Russia while trading and fighting with it.
principality-of-bzhedugh.e: The Bzhedugh came under Russian control in the course of the Russo-Circassian War, which the Russian Empire completed in 1864. More of them stayed than most Circassian groups, and they form a large part of the Adyghe population of Adygea today.

paeligni.t: Sabellic people of the Abruzzo mountains whose town Corfinium became the rebel capital of the Social War and whose Sulmo was Ovid's birthplace.
paeligni.o: The Paeligni lived in the upland basin of the Aterno and Gizio rivers in central Abruzzo, surrounded by the Marsi, Vestini and Samnites, from the early 1st millennium BCE. Ancient writers counted them among the Sabellian peoples descended from the Sabines, and they spoke a dialect close to Oscan.
paeligni.r: Their main towns were Corfinium, Sulmo and Superaequum, small hill communities that formed a league. Inscriptions in the Paelignian dialect, many in Latin letters, record local gods and priestesses. They kept sheep and controlled routes through the Apennines between Rome and the Adriatic.
paeligni.e: The Paeligni made peace and an alliance with Rome in 304 BCE, together with the Marsi and Marrucini. In 91 BCE they joined the Italian revolt, and Corfinium was renamed Italia as the capital of the rebel confederation. After the Social War they received citizenship; the poet Ovid was born at Sulmo in 43 BCE.

patriarchate-of-aquileia.t: A church principality in Friuli whose patriarchs ruled as imperial princes for over three centuries and whose parliament was among Europe's earliest.
patriarchate-of-aquileia.o: During the Investiture Controversy, Emperor Henry IV rewarded Patriarch Sigehard of Aquileia for his loyalty by granting him the county of Friuli in 1077, soon followed by Istria and Carniola. The patriarchs thus became temporal princes of the Holy Roman Empire, heirs to one of the oldest bishoprics in the Latin West.
patriarchate-of-aquileia.r: Patriarchs, usually German nobles in the early centuries and later Italians or Frenchmen, ruled from Aquileia, Cividale and from the 13th century mainly Udine. The Parliament of Friuli, bringing together clergy, nobles and towns, voted taxes and troops. The principality was constantly squeezed by the counts of Gorizia, the Duchy of Austria and the Republic of Venice; Patriarch Bertrand was murdered by Friulian nobles in 1350.
patriarchate-of-aquileia.e: Venice conquered Friuli in 1420, ending the patriarchs' temporal rule; a settlement in 1445 left them only a few towns. The patriarchate continued as a church office until 1751, when Pope Benedict XIV divided it into the archdioceses of Udine and Gorizia.

pashalik-of-scutari.t: Semi-independent Ottoman province of the Bushati family in northern Albania, whose pashas waged their own wars and defied the sultan for decades.
pashalik-of-scutari.o: Mehmed Pasha Bushati, from a powerful Shkodër family, was appointed governor of the sanjak of Scutari in 1757 and made the post hereditary in practice. The Bushatis used the weakness of central Ottoman government in the later 18th century to build an autonomous domain over northern Albania and parts of Montenegro and Kosovo.
pashalik-of-scutari.r: The pashas ruled through Albanian clan chiefs and their own armies, collecting taxes and trading with Venice and Ragusa. Mehmed built the Lead Mosque at Shkodër in 1773. Kara Mahmud Pasha Bushati expanded the domain, negotiated directly with Austria and fought the Ottoman government, but was killed fighting the Montenegrins at Krusi in 1796. Catholic and Muslim Albanians coexisted.
pashalik-of-scutari.e: Mustafa Pasha Bushati, the last ruler, joined Bosnian notables against the reforms of Mahmud II. In 1831 the grand vizier Reşid Mehmed Pasha defeated him and forced his surrender at Rozafa castle, restoring direct Ottoman rule over Shkodër.

pacajes.t: An Aymara kingdom on the southern shore of Lake Titicaca whose territory included Tiwanaku and later became a key Spanish province.
pacajes.o: The Pacajes, or Pakasa, formed one of the Aymara kingdoms that emerged around Lake Titicaca after Tiwanaku's collapse, occupying the high plain south of the lake in modern Bolivia from the 12th century. Their capital was Caquiaviri.
pacajes.r: Like other Aymara kingdoms, Pacajes was divided into two halves, Urcosuyu and Umasuyu, each with its own lords. Its economy was based on herding llamas and alpacas and farming tubers such as potatoes, freeze-dried into chuño. Pacajes lords built chullpa burial towers and kept colonies in warmer valleys to the east.
pacajes.e: Pacajes was absorbed into the Inca Empire in the mid-15th century. Under Spanish rule it became a province of the Royal Audiencia of Charcas, and its people supplied labour for the Potosí mines under the mita. Caquiaviri retains a notable colonial church.

prince-archbishopric-of-salzburg.t: Alpine church state that grew rich on salt and gold, built a baroque capital, expelled its Protestants in 1731 and employed the young Mozart.
prince-archbishopric-of-salzburg.o: Saint Rupert founded a church and monastery at the Roman town of Iuvavum around 696, and Salzburg became an archbishopric in 798. Its archbishops gained lands and immunities over the centuries, and by the early 13th century, around 1213, they were recognised as princes ruling a territory largely independent of the Duchy of Bavaria.
prince-archbishopric-of-salzburg.r: The archbishop, elected by the cathedral chapter, governed a land whose wealth came from salt at Hallein and gold and silver mines in the Gastein valley. Wolf Dietrich von Raitenau and Markus Sittikus rebuilt Salzburg in Italian baroque style, and Paris Lodron kept it out of the Thirty Years War. In 1731 Leopold Anton von Firmian expelled about 20,000 Protestants. Mozart was born there in 1756 and served Archbishop Hieronymus von Colloredo.
prince-archbishopric-of-salzburg.e: The see was secularised in 1803 as the Electorate of Salzburg for Ferdinand of Tuscany, then passed to Austria in 1805 and to Bavaria in 1810. In 1816 most of it was returned to Austria, of which it is now a federal state.

prince-bishopric-of-liege.t: A church principality on the Meuse that lasted eight centuries, grew rich on coal and arms making, and balanced its bishops against assertive townspeople.
prince-bishopric-of-liege.o: Bishop Notger (972–1008) gathered secular rights from the Ottonian emperors, including the county of Huy in 985, and turned the see of Liège into a territorial principality of the Holy Roman Empire. He rebuilt the city and its schools, and Liège became one of the leading intellectual centres of the empire.
prince-bishopric-of-liege.r: The prince-bishops shared power with the cathedral chapter and towns; the Peace of Fexhe of 1316 required the consent of the estates for major decisions. Liège mined coal from the 12th century and became famous for metalwork and weapons. Charles the Bold sacked the city in 1468. Erard de la Marck rebuilt it in the early 16th century, and the principality kept a careful neutrality.
prince-bishopric-of-liege.e: The Liège Revolution of 1789 drove out the prince-bishop and created the Republic of Liège; Austrian troops restored him in 1791. French armies annexed the principality in 1795, and its lands were later divided between Belgium and the Netherlands.

principality-of-salm.t: A Vosges principality of the Salm family around the abbey town of Senones, which voted to join France in 1793.
principality-of-salm.o: The counts of Salm, a branch of the Wild- and Rhinegraves, held lands in the Vosges around Senones and Badonviller. In 1623 Philip Otto of Salm was made a prince of the Holy Roman Empire, and the territory became a principality.
principality-of-salm.r: The principality was a small mountain land of forests, ironworks and later textile workshops. Its life centred on Senones and its Benedictine abbey, whose abbot Dom Augustin Calmet was a celebrated scholar. In 1751 the territory was reorganised and Senones became the princes' residence, with a modest court.
principality-of-salm.e: Surrounded by Revolutionary France and cut off by its blockade, the inhabitants voted to join France, and the French First Republic annexed the principality in 1793. The Salm-Salm princes received compensation in Westphalia.

phaselis.t: Phaselis, a Rhodian colony with three harbours on the Lycian coast, a trading city later held by pirates and taken by Rome.
phaselis.o: Colonists from Lindos on Rhodes founded Phaselis, traditionally in 690 BCE, on a peninsula at the border of Lycia and Pamphylia. Its position on the coastal route between the Aegean and the eastern Mediterranean made it a natural port of call.
phaselis.r: Phaselis was a Greek city governed by its citizens and a member of the Delian League. It traded timber, rose oil and other goods and had a share in the Hellenion at Naukratis in Egypt. Alexander of the Macedonian Empire wintered there in 334 and 333 BCE.
phaselis.e: In the 1st century BCE the pirate leader Zenicetes held Phaselis. The Roman general Publius Servilius Isauricus captured it in 77 BCE, and the city was then absorbed into the Roman world, later joining the Lycian League.

pellendones.t: A Celtiberian people of the upper Douro around the Picos de Urbión, living in the high country north of Numantia.
pellendones.o: The Pellendones lived around the sources of the Douro in northern Soria and southern La Rioja from about the 4th century BCE. Pliny counts them among the Celtiberians, and some ancient geographers placed Numantia in their territory rather than that of the Arevaci.
pellendones.r: They were a highland people of hillforts and herding, with towns such as Visontium and Augustobriga named by Ptolemy. Their society was probably organised in clans under local elites like that of their Celtiberian neighbours, but no details are recorded.
pellendones.e: They were drawn into the Celtiberian wars against Rome and came under Roman control after the fall of Numantia in 133 BCE, becoming part of Hispania Citerior.

principality-of-anhalt-dessau.t: The leading Anhalt principality, famed for the Old Dessauer's drill reforms and the Dessau-Wörlitz Garden Realm of the Enlightenment.
principality-of-anhalt-dessau.o: Anhalt-Dessau was created in the 1603 partition of Anhalt, with Prince John George I receiving Dessau on the Mulde near its junction with the Elbe. The line was Calvinist and closely tied to the Electorate of Brandenburg by marriage.
principality-of-anhalt-dessau.r: Leopold I, the Old Dessauer, was a Prussian field marshal who introduced the iron ramrod and cadenced marching. His grandson Leopold III Friedrich Franz was a model Enlightenment ruler who laid out the landscape gardens of Wörlitz, built schools and founded the Philanthropinum, a progressive school, in 1774. The principality became a duchy in 1807.
principality-of-anhalt-dessau.e: Anhalt-Dessau inherited Anhalt-Köthen in 1847 and Anhalt-Bernburg in 1863, after which Duke Leopold IV Friedrich ruled a united Duchy of Anhalt from Dessau. The Garden Realm is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

principality-of-orange.t: A tiny sovereign principality in the Rhône valley whose title passed to the house of Nassau and gave the Dutch royal family its name.
principality-of-orange.o: Orange was a Roman colony and later a county within the Kingdom of Arles; the troubadour Raimbaut d'Orange ruled part of it in the 12th century. In 1163 Emperor Frederick Barbarossa raised it to a principality, and it passed in 1173 to Bertrand of Baux, whose family ruled it for over two centuries.
principality-of-orange.r: The principality was a small enclave inside Provence and the Comtat Venaissin, with Roman monuments, a university founded in 1365 and its own courts. It passed to the Chalon family in 1393. René of Chalon left it to his cousin William of Nassau in 1544, and under William the Silent Orange became a refuge for Protestants.
principality-of-orange.e: Louis XIV occupied Orange several times and destroyed its fortifications. After the death of William III of England in 1702, France took it, and the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 recognised its annexation. The princes of Orange-Nassau kept the title, which the Dutch royal house still bears.

portuguese-angola.t: Portugal's West African colony centred on Luanda, for three centuries the largest source of enslaved Africans shipped to Brazil.
portuguese-angola.o: In 1575 Paulo Dias de Novais arrived on the coast with a royal charter to conquer the Kingdom of Ndongo, founding Luanda the following year. The colony grew from a coastal base through wars with Ndongo, alliances with Imbangala bands and the founding of Benguela in 1617, always driven by the demand for slaves in Brazil.
portuguese-angola.r: Governors in Luanda relied on forts along the Kwanza, African auxiliaries and trading fairs to obtain captives, and Luanda's merchants were closely tied to Brazil. The Dutch occupied Luanda from 1641 until Salvador Correia de Sa recaptured it in 1648. After the end of the slave trade in the 19th century, Portugal pushed inland, and 20th-century settlers developed coffee, diamonds and later oil.
portuguese-angola.e: Nationalist revolt began in 1961, with the MPLA, FNLA and UNITA fighting Portugal. After the Carnation Revolution of 1974, Portugal withdrew, and Angola became independent on 11 November 1975 amid a civil war between the movements.

peucetians.t: Iapygian people of central Apulia around modern Bari, whose towns such as Rubi became centres of Greek-influenced art and vase collecting.
peucetians.o: The Peucetians occupied central Apulia between the Daunians to the north and the Messapians to the south, from the early 1st millennium BCE. Greek writers explained their name through Peucetius, a son of the Arcadian Lycaon, but their culture developed from local Iron Age communities related to their Iapygian neighbours.
peucetians.r: They lived in separate fortified towns, among them Caelia, Azetium, Rubi (Ruvo di Puglia) and the site of Monte Sannace, without a known central government. Their geometric painted pottery gave way, from the 5th century BCE, to strong Greek influence: the elite of Rubi buried their dead with Athenian and Apulian red-figure vases, many from Taras. They grew cereals and olives and traded through coastal landings.
peucetians.e: The Peucetian towns came under Roman control around the end of the 4th and start of the 3rd centuries BCE during Rome's expansion into Apulia. They were later absorbed into Roman Apulia and became municipia. Collections of vases from Ruvo, such as the Jatta collection, preserve much of their material culture.

palatinate-neuburg.t: The 'Young Palatinate' on the Danube, created after the Landshut War, whose dukes inherited Jülich and Berg and then the Palatine electorate.
palatinate-neuburg.o: The Cologne arbitration of 1505 that ended the War of the Landshut Succession created a new principality from parts of the Duchy of Bavaria-Landshut for Otto Henry and Philip, the young sons of Rupert of the Palatinate. Known as the Young Palatinate, it had Neuburg on the Danube as its capital.
palatinate-neuburg.r: Otto Henry introduced Lutheranism in 1542 and rebuilt Neuburg castle in Renaissance style before becoming Elector Palatine. Wolfgang William converted to Catholicism in 1613 to strengthen his claim in the Jülich succession and won Jülich and Berg, ruling from Düsseldorf. His son Philip William became Elector Palatine in 1685, after which the Neuburg dukes ruled from Düsseldorf, Heidelberg and Mannheim.
palatinate-neuburg.e: When Elector Charles Philip, the last of the Neuburg line, died in 1742, his lands passed to Charles Theodore of Palatinate-Sulzbach, who in 1777 also inherited Bavaria. Neuburg was absorbed into the Wittelsbach lands of Bavaria.

principality-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen.t: The Catholic Swabian branch of the Hohenzollerns, ruling from Sigmaringen castle on the Danube, which later gave Romania its kings.
principality-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen.o: When Count Charles I of the County of Hohenzollern died in 1576, his lands were divided among his sons. Charles II received Sigmaringen and Veringen on the upper Danube, founding the Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen line, and the counts were raised to princes in 1623.
principality-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen.r: The princes ruled a small Catholic territory from Sigmaringen's castle on a rock above the Danube, under strong Habsburg influence since parts of their lands were Austrian fiefs. Thanks partly to Princess Amalie Zephyrine, a friend of Joséphine de Beauharnais, the principality survived the mediatisation of 1806, joined the Confederation of the Rhine and even gained territory.
principality-of-hohenzollern-sigmaringen.e: After the revolution of 1848, Prince Charles Anthony ceded his sovereignty to his Prussian cousins in 1849, and in 1850 the principality became part of Prussia. His son Carol became prince and later king of Romania, and another son's candidacy for the Spanish throne helped trigger the Franco-Prussian War of 1870.

principality-of-mstislavl.t: An appanage of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in eastern Belarus, ruled by descendants of Algirdas until 1529.
principality-of-mstislavl.o: Mstislavl, on the Sozh, was a town of the old Smolensk lands. After the Grand Duchy of Lithuania took it in the mid 14th century, it was given as an appanage to sons of Algirdas, first Karigaila and later Lingvenis, whose descendants ruled it for over a century.
principality-of-mstislavl.r: Mstislavl was a frontier principality facing Smolensk and Moscow, with a largely Orthodox Ruthenian population. Lingvenis, who ruled from about 1390 to 1431, also served as a commander in Novgorod and fought at Grunwald. His line, and later the Mstislavsky family through marriage, held the land as vassals of the grand duke.
principality-of-mstislavl.e: In 1526 Prince Fyodor Mstislavsky fled to Moscow, where his family became leading boyars. Mstislavl reverted to the grand duke, and in 1529 it lost its separate status, later becoming the Mstislavl Voivodeship.

principality-of-salerno.t: Lombard principality of southern Italy, home of the famous medical school of Salerno, conquered by Robert Guiscard in 1077.
principality-of-salerno.o: A long civil war in the Principality of Benevento ended in 849 with a formal partition: Siconulf became prince of Salerno, ruling the western half including the coast of Campania, Lucania and parts of Calabria, while Radelchis kept Benevento.
principality-of-salerno.r: Salerno was a prosperous coastal city with links to Amalfi and the Byzantine world. The Schola Medica Salernitana, the first great medical school of medieval Europe, flourished there from the 10th century, drawing on Greek, Latin and Arabic learning. Under Guaimar IV (1027–1052) the principality reached its height, controlling Amalfi, Sorrento and Capua, and he invested the Norman leaders with Apulia.
principality-of-salerno.e: After Guaimar IV was murdered in 1052, Norman power grew rapidly. Robert Guiscard, who had married Sichelgaita, sister of Prince Gisulf II, besieged Salerno and took it in 1077, making it his capital. The principality became part of the Norman Duchy of Apulia.

polemonid-pontus.t: Polemonid Pontus, a Roman client kingdom on the Black Sea ruled by Polemon I, his queen Pythodorida and their son.
polemonid-pontus.o: In 37 BCE Mark Antony made Polemon, son of the orator Zeno of Laodicea, king of part of the former Kingdom of Pontus. Polemon kept his throne after Actium by switching to Augustus and was also made king of the Bosporan Kingdom.
polemonid-pontus.r: The kingdom covered the eastern Pontic coast and inland valleys, including Trapezus and Zela. After Polemon was killed c. 8 BCE, his widow Pythodorida, a granddaughter of Mark Antony, ruled in her own name for many years. Strabo, a native of the region, praised her government.
polemonid-pontus.e: Caligula gave the kingdom to her grandson Polemon II in 38 CE. Nero deposed him in 62 CE and annexed Pontus to the Roman Empire.

principality-of-hungary.t: Hungarian state of the Árpád dynasty in the Carpathian basin, from the conquest of 895 to Stephen's coronation as king in 1000.
principality-of-hungary.o: After Pecheneg attacks drove them from Etelköz, the Hungarian tribal federation under Árpád crossed the Carpathians in 895. By 900 they had taken the whole basin, and in 907 they destroyed a Bavarian army at Pressburg, securing the conquest.
principality-of-hungary.r: For half a century Hungarian horsemen raided Europe from Saxony to Spain and Constantinople, until Otto I defeated them at the Lechfeld in 955. The grand princes then centralised power: Taksony and especially Géza, ruling from Esztergom, curbed tribal chiefs and invited Western missionaries. Géza was baptised and married his son Vajk to Gisela of Bavaria.
principality-of-hungary.e: Géza's son Vajk, baptised Stephen, defeated the pagan Koppány and was crowned king on Christmas Day 1000 (or 1 January 1001) with a crown from Pope Sylvester II, founding the Kingdom of Hungary (1000-1301).

prince-bishopric-of-geneva.t: The temporal lordship of the bishops of Geneva, whose loss to the citizens and the Reformation turned the city into the 'Protestant Rome' of Calvin.
prince-bishopric-of-geneva.o: Geneva had been a bishopric since the 4th century. In 1124 the Treaty of Seyssel between Bishop Humbert de Grammont and the Count of Geneva confirmed the bishop's lordship over the city, and Frederick Barbarossa recognised him as an imperial prince in 1162.
prince-bishopric-of-geneva.r: The bishops ruled the city through officials, while the counts of Geneva and later the dukes of Savoy held the vidomnat, an important judicial office. Citizens gained a charter of liberties from Bishop Adhémar Fabri in 1387. Geneva's fairs made it a major trading centre in the 15th century. Savoy princes increasingly held the bishopric itself.
prince-bishopric-of-geneva.e: Geneva allied with Fribourg and Bern in 1526, and in 1533 Bishop Pierre de La Baume left the city. In 1535 to 1536 it adopted the Reformation and became an independent republic. John Calvin arrived in 1536. Geneva joined Switzerland in 1815.

principality-of-capua.t: Lombard principality of northern Campania that broke away from Benevento and later became the first Norman principality in southern Italy.
principality-of-capua.o: In the civil wars of the Lombard south in the 840s, Landulf I, gastald of Capua, made his town practically independent of both Benevento and Salerno. Arab raiders destroyed old Capua in 841, and in 856 his family founded a new Capua on the site of Casilinum by the Volturno. Its rulers took the title of prince by the early 10th century.
principality-of-capua.r: Capua was ruled by quarrelsome branches of Landulf's family, who controlled northern Campania and much of the Liri valley. Pandulf Ironhead (died 981) briefly united Capua, Benevento and Spoleto under imperial patronage. Pandulf IV, called the Wolf of the Abruzzi, despoiled Monte Cassino and hired Norman mercenaries, helping the Normans establish themselves at Aversa.
principality-of-capua.e: The Norman Richard I of Aversa took Capua in 1058, and his family ruled it as princes for nearly eighty years. After Robert II of Capua resisted Roger II, the principality was absorbed into the Kingdom of Sicily in 1135.

prince-abbey-of-fulda.t: Abbey founded by a disciple of Saint Boniface, a centre of Carolingian learning, and later a baroque prince-bishopric in eastern Hesse.
prince-abbey-of-fulda.o: Sturm, a disciple of Saint Boniface, founded the monastery at Fulda in 744, and Boniface was buried there in 754. Under Abbot Hrabanus Maurus in the 9th century it became one of the great centres of learning in the Frankish realm. Its abbots gathered vast estates and were recognised as imperial princes by 1220.
prince-abbey-of-fulda.r: The prince-abbots ruled a sizeable territory in the Rhön and the Fulda valley, with the support of a powerful noble chapter. Abbot Balthasar von Dernbach led a fierce Counter-Reformation in the late 16th century. The baroque cathedral by Johann Dientzenhofer and the abbots' palace reshaped the town, and in 1752 the abbey was raised to a prince-bishopric.
prince-abbey-of-fulda.e: Secularised in 1802, Fulda went to William Frederick of Nassau-Orange, then to French control and the Grand Duchy of Frankfurt. In 1816 it passed to the Electorate of Hesse. The diocese of Fulda continues today.

phocian-league.t: Federation of the towns of Phocis in central Greece, which seized Delphi and fought the Third Sacred War against Thebes and Philip II.
phocian-league.o: The Phocians lived in the valley of the Cephissus and around Mount Parnassus, in some twenty small towns such as Elateia. By the 6th century BCE they formed a federation with a common council house, the Phokikon. Their long wars with the Thessalians included famous stratagems with chalk-whitened warriors.
phocian-league.r: Phocis guarded the path around Thermopylae and fought in 480 BCE before submitting to Persia. In 356 BCE, fined by the Amphictyony, the Phocians under Philomelus seized Delphi and used its treasure to hire mercenaries. Onomarchus twice defeated Philip II in 353 BCE but was killed at the Battle of the Crocus Field in 352 BCE.
phocian-league.e: In 346 BCE Phalaecus surrendered to Philip II. The Phocian towns were broken into villages, Phocis lost its vote in the Amphictyony and owed annual indemnities to Delphi. It later revived as a league.

prince-bishopric-of-worms.t: A small prince-bishopric on the upper Rhine whose bishops lost their city of Worms and ruled a few scattered lands from Ladenburg.
prince-bishopric-of-worms.o: Worms had been a bishopric since Roman times. Bishop Burchard of Worms, who issued a famous collection of canon law around 1020, gained wide rights over the city. In 1156 Frederick Barbarossa confirmed the bishop's possessions, and the bishops became princes of a small territory.
prince-bishopric-of-worms.r: The bishops lost control of Worms itself, which became a free imperial city; the Concordat of Worms in 1122 and Luther's appearance at the Diet of Worms in 1521 took place there. The bishops ruled scattered lands, sharing Ladenburg with the Electoral Palatinate. The see was often held together with Mainz.
prince-bishopric-of-worms.e: France annexed the left-bank lands in the 1790s, and in 1803 the remaining territories were secularised and given to Hesse-Darmstadt and Baden. The diocese itself was dissolved in 1801 and later merged into the diocese of Mainz.

principality-of-schwarzburg-sondershause.t: A Thuringian principality of the house of Schwarzburg, ruled from Sondershausen and Arnstadt, where the young Bach held his first organ post.
principality-of-schwarzburg-sondershause.o: The Treaty of Stadtilm of 1599 split the Schwarzburg lands, and Count John Günther I's line received Sondershausen and Arnstadt, forming Schwarzburg-Sondershausen alongside the Principality of Schwarzburg-Rudolstadt.
principality-of-schwarzburg-sondershause.r: The counts became princes in 1697 and ruled a Lutheran territory in two parts, the Lower Lordship around Sondershausen and the Upper Lordship around Arnstadt. Arnstadt gave Johann Sebastian Bach his first post as organist in 1703. The princes kept a court orchestra, and in the 19th century Sondershausen became known for its public concerts and music school.
principality-of-schwarzburg-sondershause.e: The principality joined the German Empire in 1871. When Prince Karl Günther died childless in 1909, Günther Victor of Rudolstadt inherited it in personal union. He abdicated in November 1918, and in 1920 the state merged into the Free State of Thuringia.

principality-of-reuss-schleiz.t: Branch of the Reuss family in Thuringia that eventually reunited the Younger Line of Reuss under its rule.
principality-of-reuss-schleiz.o: Reuss-Schleiz was created in the 1647 division of the Younger Line of the House of Reuss, centred on the town of Schleiz. The counts, descended from the medieval Vögte of Weida, Gera and Plauen, held small territories in eastern Thuringia.
principality-of-reuss-schleiz.r: The territory was small and agrarian, with textile crafts, and its counts, all named Heinrich, ruled through a Lutheran church and a small court at Schleiz. The Schleiz line was raised to princely rank in 1806, joined the Confederation of the Rhine and then the German Confederation, and shared the inheritance of Reuss-Gera when that line died out in 1802.
principality-of-reuss-schleiz.e: In 1848, after the abdication of the Prince of Reuss-Lobenstein-Ebersdorf, the Schleiz line united all lands of the Younger Line as the Principality of Reuss Younger Line, with Gera as capital. That state survived until 1918 and became part of the People's State of Reuss.

principality-of-belz.t: A small Ruthenian principality on the Polish border, passed between Volhynia, Lithuania and Masovia before joining the Polish Crown.
principality-of-belz.o: Belz, on a tributary of the Bug, was one of the Cherven towns contested between Poland and Rus'. It became the seat of an appanage of the Volhynian princes in the later 12th century, when Vsevolod Mstislavich, a brother of Roman Mstislavich, ruled there.
principality-of-belz.r: It was a border land of fortified towns and farmland, part of the Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia in the 13th century. After that state collapsed in the 1340s Belz was contested by Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, then from 1388 held as a fief by the dukes of Masovia, beginning with Siemowit IV.
principality-of-belz.e: When the Masovian line of Belz died out in 1462, King Casimir IV incorporated it into the Kingdom of Poland (1385-1569) as the Belz Voivodeship. The town later became famous as the seat of the Belz Hasidic dynasty.

principality-of-samarkand.t: The leading Sogdian city-state, ruled by ikhshids whose merchants ran Silk Road trade networks from Byzantium to China.
principality-of-samarkand.o: Samarkand, ancient Maracanda, had been the chief city of Sogdiana since Achaemenid times. After the fall of the Hephthalite Empire it emerged in the 6th century as the foremost of the Sogdian principalities under rulers with the title ikhshid, recognising the overlordship of the Western Turkic Khaganate.
principality-of-samarkand.r: The ikhshids presided over a merchant aristocracy rather than an absolute monarchy. Sogdian traders dominated caravan commerce across Asia, with communities in China and Mongolia. The famous murals of Afrasiab, painted for the ruler Varkhuman around 660, show embassies from China, Korea and the Turks. Religion was a local Zoroastrianism with fire temples and ossuary burial, alongside Buddhism, Manichaeism and Christianity.
principality-of-samarkand.e: Qutayba ibn Muslim took Samarkand for the Umayyad Caliphate in 712, and the ikhshid Ghurak ruled as a vassal while also courting the Turgesh Khaganate. After the Abbasid takeover around 750 the ikhshids lost power, and the city passed to the Samanid Empire in the 9th century.

principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.t: A papal enclave in southern Italy that Napoleon turned into a sovereign principality for his foreign minister Talleyrand.
principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.o: Benevento, a small city surrounded by the Kingdom of Naples, had belonged to the Papal States since the 11th century. In 1806 Napoleon seized it and made Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand, his foreign minister, sovereign Prince of Benevento.
principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.r: Talleyrand never visited his principality. He ruled through a governor, Louis de Beer, who introduced French-style administration and the Napoleonic Code, abolished feudal privileges and improved roads and finances. The small state continued to depend on the Napoleonic Kingdom of Naples (1806–1815) around it.
principality-of-benevento-1806-1815.e: With Napoleon's fall, Talleyrand gave up the title, and the Congress of Vienna returned Benevento to the Papal States in 1815. It remained papal until 1860.

pella.t: Pella, a Canaanite town in the Jordan Valley known to the Egyptians as Pihilu, whose rulers wrote to the pharaoh in the Amarna age.
pella.o: Pihilu stood at Tabaqat Fahl, beside a perennial spring above the Jordan Valley, inhabited since the Neolithic. In the Middle Bronze Age it became a walled town, named in Egyptian execration texts, and controlled farmland and the route from the valley into the Transjordan highlands.
pella.r: University of Sydney excavations since 1979 have uncovered fortifications, a Late Bronze Age governor's residence and a temple. In the 14th century BCE its ruler Mut-Bahlu wrote to the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom in the Amarna letters, and Akkadian tablets have been found at the site.
pella.e: The Canaanite town declined with Egyptian power in the 12th century BCE. Pella revived in the Hellenistic period and became one of the cities of the Decapolis (Levant).

patria-vieja.t: Chile's first period of self-government, from the junta of 1810 to the royalist victory at Rancagua in 1814.
patria-vieja.o: On 18 September 1810, a date still celebrated as Chile's national day, a cabildo in Santiago created a governing junta led by the elderly Mateo de Toro Zambrano, ruling in the name of the captive Ferdinand VII. It replaced the governor of the Captaincy General of Chile.
patria-vieja.r: The junta opened ports to free trade and convened the First National Congress in 1811. José Miguel Carrera seized power in a series of coups and introduced a provisional constitution, the first national flag and the newspaper Aurora de Chile, edited by Camilo Henríquez. Divisions between the Carreras and Bernardo O'Higgins weakened the patriots as the viceroy of Peru, José Fernando de Abascal, sent troops in 1813.
patria-vieja.e: The Treaty of Lircay in 1814 briefly halted the war. Royalist forces then defeated O'Higgins at Rancagua in October 1814, and the patriots fled to Mendoza. The Reconquista lasted until Chacabuco in 1817.

principality-of-murom.t: An old principality on the Oka, home of the legend of Peter and Fevronia, later absorbed into Moscow's growing realm.
principality-of-murom.o: Murom, named after the Finnic Muroma tribe, is mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 862. Vladimir I's son Gleb, later venerated as a saint, held it in the early 11th century. It became the seat of the descendants of Yaroslav Sviatoslavich of Chernigov, and around 1127 split from the neighbouring Grand Principality of Ryazan to form a separate principality.
principality-of-murom.r: Murom was a frontier town on the Oka, close to Volga Bulgaria and the forest peoples, and lived from trade and farming. Its princes were usually overshadowed by Vladimir-Suzdal. The tale of Prince Peter and the peasant healer Fevronia, venerated as patrons of marriage, is set here, as is the epic hero Ilya Muromets.
principality-of-murom.e: The Mongols sacked Murom in 1239, and it declined into a minor dependent principality. In 1392 Vasily I of the Grand Duchy of Moscow bought from the Golden Horde the right to rule Murom along with Nizhny Novgorod, ending its independence.

prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.t: Small Mecklenburg church state founded during the conversion of the Obotrites and absorbed by the dukes of Mecklenburg after the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.o: The bishopric was set up by Henry the Lion during the conquest of the Slavic Obotrites, with the Cistercian monk Berno as its first bishop and its seat moved to Schwerin around 1160. After Henry's fall in 1180 the bishops held their estates as imperial princes, a status the dukes of Mecklenburg constantly disputed.
prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.r: The territory was small, consisting chiefly of lands around Bützow, where the bishops resided, and Warin. It grew through German settlement in former Slavic lands. In the 16th century the see was held by princes of the Mecklenburg house, such as Ulrich of Mecklenburg, and became Lutheran, so the bishopric functioned in practice as a Mecklenburg appanage.
prince-bishopric-of-schwerin.e: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 secularised it as the Principality of Schwerin and awarded it to the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin as compensation for Wismar, which went to Sweden. It is now part of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

principality-of-nassau-siegen.t: Iron-mining Nassau principality in the Siegerland, divided for a century between Catholic and Protestant branches of the house.
principality-of-nassau-siegen.o: After the death of Count John VI of Nassau-Dillenburg in 1606, his lands were divided and his son John VII received Siegen. Siegen was the birthplace of Peter Paul Rubens in 1577, when his parents lived there in exile.
principality-of-nassau-siegen.r: The Siegerland's iron ore and forges made it relatively prosperous. The house split confessionally: John VIII converted to Catholicism and his line held part of the land while the Reformed line held the rest, so Siegen had two castles, the Upper and Lower. Johan Maurits of Nassau-Siegen, governor of Dutch Brazil, belonged to the Reformed branch. Counts became princes in 1652 and 1664.
principality-of-nassau-siegen.e: The Reformed line died out in 1734 and the Catholic line in 1743, and the territory passed to Prince William IV of Orange-Nassau as part of Nassau-Diez. It later went to the Grand Duchy of Berg and in 1815 to the Kingdom of Prussia.

principality-of-thurn-and-taxis.t: Swabian territory acquired by the family that ran the Imperial Post, giving them a vote among the princes of the Empire.
principality-of-thurn-and-taxis.o: The Taxis family of Lombard origin had run the imperial postal service since around 1500 and became hereditary postmasters general, raised to princes in 1695. To gain a seat in the Council of Princes they needed land, so in 1785 they bought the county of Friedberg-Scheer on the Danube, raised in 1786 to a princely county.
principality-of-thurn-and-taxis.r: The Swabian territory was a small Catholic rural district; the family's wealth and power came from the Imperial Post, which carried letters across the Empire and the Netherlands. The princes lived in Regensburg, where they represented the emperor as principal commissioner at the Perpetual Imperial Diet, and from 1812 resided in the former St Emmeram Abbey.
principality-of-thurn-and-taxis.e: In 1806 the territory was mediatised under the Kingdom of Württemberg. The family kept its postal business in many German states until selling it to Prussia in 1867 and remains among the largest landowners in Germany.

principality-of-gjirokaster.t: Albanian lordship of the Zenebishi family in southern Albania, one of the last Christian powers in Epirus before the Ottoman conquest.
principality-of-gjirokaster.o: Gjon Zenebishi, an Albanian chieftain whose clan had moved into Epirus during the 14th-century Albanian migrations, took the fortress of Gjirokastër (Argyrokastron) around 1386. He extended his rule over the Drino valley and parts of Chameria, and the Byzantine court recognised him with the title of sebastokrator.
principality-of-gjirokaster.r: The lordship was a clan-based military domain built around the hilltop citadel of Gjirokastër and its villages. Gjon fought the Italian rulers of the Despotate of Epirus at Ioannina, capturing Esau de' Buondelmonti in 1399, and courted Venice, which controlled nearby Corfu. Society rested on Albanian pastoral clans and an Orthodox Greek and Albanian peasantry.
principality-of-gjirokaster.e: Repeated Ottoman campaigns under Sultan Mehmed I wore the lordship down, and Gjirokastër fell in 1418, the year Gjon died. His son Depa fled to Venetian territory and later led a failed rising in 1434. The town became the centre of an Ottoman sanjak.

principality-of-tmutarakan.t: A remote outpost of Kievan Rus' on the Taman peninsula, controlling the strait between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.
principality-of-tmutarakan.o: Tmutarakan grew out of the Khazar town of Tamatarkha, on the site of ancient Hermonassa. After Sviatoslav I broke Khazar power in the 960s, the Rus' took control, and around 988 Vladimir I gave the town to his son Mstislav as his own principality.
principality-of-tmutarakan.r: Its population of Greeks, Khazars, Alans, Kasogs and Slavs lived by trade between the steppe, the Caucasus and Byzantium. Mstislav defeated the Kasog prince Rededya in single combat in 1022, and in 1024 beat his brother Yaroslav at Listven, dividing Rus' along the Dnieper. The Tmutarakan Stone records Prince Gleb measuring the frozen strait in 1068.
principality-of-tmutarakan.e: Tmutarakan served as a refuge for exiled princes such as Oleg Sviatoslavich, who left it in 1094 to fight for Chernigov. Cut off by the Cumans, it disappears from Rus' history afterwards, probably passing to Byzantine control. Its location was rediscovered in the 18th century.

prince-provostry-of-ellwangen.t: A Benedictine abbey on the Jagst that was converted in 1460 into a provostry of noble canons whose princes ruled a sizeable Swabian territory.
prince-provostry-of-ellwangen.o: Ellwangen abbey was founded around 764 by Hariolf, later bishop of Langres, and received Carolingian protection. It built up lands along the Jagst, and its abbots held princely rank from the 13th century. In 1460 Pope Pius II converted the abbey into a secular collegiate foundation headed by a prince-provost.
prince-provostry-of-ellwangen.r: The prince-provost, often a bishop elsewhere as well, governed a considerable territory around Ellwangen with his own courts and officials and sat among the ecclesiastical princes of the Imperial Diet. The castle above the town was his residence. Witch trials between 1611 and 1618 were among the most severe in Germany, claiming several hundred victims.
prince-provostry-of-ellwangen.e: In 1802 and 1803 the provostry was secularised and annexed by Württemberg, which for some years made Ellwangen the seat of the government of its new Catholic lands. The castle and the Romanesque collegiate basilica survive.

prince-abbey-of-corvey.t: The leading Carolingian abbey of Saxony, a base for missions to the north and home of the chronicler Widukind, whose westwork is a World Heritage Site.
prince-abbey-of-corvey.o: Corvey was founded in 822 on the Weser near Höxter by monks from Corbie in Picardy, led by Adalard and Wala, cousins of Charlemagne, with the support of Louis the Pious. It was intended to anchor Christianity in newly conquered Saxony, and in 836 it received the relics of Saint Vitus from Saint-Denis.
prince-abbey-of-corvey.r: Corvey sent Ansgar on his mission to Denmark and Sweden, and its school produced Widukind of Corvey, whose Deeds of the Saxons is a chief source for the Ottonian kings. The abbots were princes of the Empire ruling a small territory around Höxter. Its Carolingian westwork, completed in 885, is one of the few surviving from the period.
prince-abbey-of-corvey.e: Corvey shrank after the Thirty Years' War. In 1792 it was raised to a prince-bishopric, but in 1803 it was secularised and given to the Prince of Orange-Nassau-Fulda, then passed to Westphalia and Prussia. The poet Hoffmann von Fallersleben, author of the German national anthem, later worked in its library.

philistine-pentapolis.t: The Philistine Pentapolis, five city-states of the southern Levant coast founded by Aegean newcomers, whose name lives on in Palestine.
philistine-pentapolis.o: Around 1175 BCE Ramesses III of the Egyptian Empire New Kingdom repelled the Sea Peoples, including the Peleset. Groups of these newcomers settled in Gaza, Ashkelon, Ashdod, Ekron and Gath, bringing Aegean-style pottery, cooking habits and pork-eating to the southern coast of Canaan.
philistine-pentapolis.r: Each city was ruled by its own lord, called seren in the Bible, and they acted together in war. The Philistines adopted the local Semitic language and gods such as Dagon, and became Israel's main rivals in the stories of Samson, Saul and David.
philistine-pentapolis.e: From the 8th century BCE the cities were vassals of the Assyrian Empire. Nebuchadnezzar II of the Chaldean Empire destroyed Ashkelon and Ekron in 604 BCE and deported their people, ending a separate Philistine identity. Greeks and Romans called the region Palaestina after them.

principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.t: Small Anhalt principality on the Elbe best remembered as the birthplace dynasty of Catherine the Great of Russia.
principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.o: Rudolf, a son of Joachim Ernst, received Zerbst in the 1603 partition of Anhalt. The town, north of the Elbe, had been a prosperous brewing centre known for its beer, and the line included the lordship of Jever in Frisia, inherited in 1667.
principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.r: The principality was Lutheran in its later period and modestly governed from a baroque palace in Zerbst. Its most famous member was Sophie Auguste Friederike, daughter of Prince Christian August, who married the future Peter III and became Empress Catherine II of Russia. Her brother Friedrich August, the last prince, lived mostly abroad and hired out soldiers to Britain during the American Revolutionary War.
principality-of-anhalt-zerbst.e: Friedrich August died without heirs in 1793. The principality was divided among the other Anhalt lines, Dessau, Bernburg and Köthen, while Jever passed to Catherine the Great and so to Russia.

principality-of-arianiti.t: Lands of the Albanian lord Gjergj Arianiti, who led an early revolt against the Ottomans and became Skanderbeg's ally and father-in-law.
principality-of-arianiti.o: The Arianiti were an old noble family of central Albania, holding lands along the Shkumbin valley and around Elbasan. In 1432 Gjergj Arianiti, who had been a hostage at the Ottoman court, led a rising against the new Ottoman land registers and defeated several Ottoman armies in the mountains between 1432 and 1436.
principality-of-arianiti.r: Little is known of how the lands were governed: they were a mountain lordship of fortified villages and clan levies rather than a state with fixed institutions, and no clear capital is recorded. Gjergj built ties through marriage, wedding his daughter Donika to Skanderbeg in 1451, and negotiated with Venice, Naples and the papacy.
principality-of-arianiti.e: Gjergj Arianiti joined the League of Lezhë in 1444, though he later quarrelled with Skanderbeg. He died in 1462, and the family's lands fell to the Ottomans in the following years. His descendants, the Arianiti Comneni, settled in Italy.

prince-bishopric-of-lausanne.t: A Swiss prince-bishopric on Lake Geneva whose bishops ruled Lausanne and its surroundings until Bern conquered Vaud and introduced the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-lausanne.o: The bishops of the Avenches area moved their seat to Lausanne around 600. In 1011 King Rudolf III of Burgundy granted Bishop Henry the county of Vaud, establishing the bishop as a temporal lord. After 1032 the bishops became princes of the Holy Roman Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-lausanne.r: The prince-bishops ruled Lausanne and estates such as Lavaux, famous for vineyards, while the counts of Savoy dominated the rest of Vaud. The Gothic cathedral of Lausanne was consecrated in 1275 in the presence of Pope Gregory X and King Rudolf I. The townspeople gradually won rights of self-government.
prince-bishopric-of-lausanne.e: In 1536 Bern conquered Vaud from Savoy, took Lausanne and expelled the bishop, introducing the Reformation after the Lausanne Disputation in which Calvin and Farel spoke. Vaud remained Bernese until 1798 and became a Swiss canton in 1803.

principality-of-kabarda.t: The most powerful Circassian principality, on the plains of the central North Caucasus, an early ally of Muscovy and a major regional power.
principality-of-kabarda.o: Kabarda formed in the 15th century when Circassian princes, traditionally descended from the semi-legendary Inal, settled the plains along the Terek, Malka and Baksan rivers. Its princes extended their power over neighbouring Ossetians, Ingush, Balkars and Abazins. Russian and Ottoman sources speak of Kabarda as a distinct country from the 16th century.
principality-of-kabarda.r: Kabarda was ruled by an aristocracy of princes and nobles who held peasants and serfs, with assemblies settling major questions. Prince Temryuk Idarov allied with Ivan IV of Russia, who married his daughter Maria in 1561. Kabardians bred famous horses and set standards of etiquette admired across the region. Their forces defeated a Crimean army at Kanzhal in 1708.
principality-of-kabarda.e: Divided into Greater and Lesser Kabarda, it became a battleground between Russia and the Crimean Khanate. Russian forts from 1763 and the campaigns of General Yermolov after 1818 broke its independence, and by 1825 it was annexed to the Russian Empire.
