prince-abbey-of-kempten.t: Benedictine abbey in the Allgäu whose prince-abbots ruled a sizeable territory and rebuilt Kempten in baroque splendour after the Thirty Years War.
prince-abbey-of-kempten.o: The Benedictine abbey of Kempten was founded in the mid 8th century near the old Roman town of Cambodunum and enjoyed the patronage of Charlemagne's wife Hildegard. It gathered estates throughout the Allgäu, and from 1213 its abbots were recognised as princes of the Empire, ruling a secular territory.
prince-abbey-of-kempten.r: The prince-abbots, drawn from the nobility, governed farmers and small towns in the Allgäu through officials and a strong territorial administration. They clashed constantly with the neighbouring Free Imperial City of Kempten, which bought its freedom from the abbey in 1525, the year their own peasants rose in the Peasants' War. After the Thirty Years War Abbot Roman Giel von Gielsberg built the Residenz and the Basilica of St. Lorenz.
prince-abbey-of-kempten.e: The abbey was secularised in 1803 and annexed by Bavaria, which merged the abbey town with the Protestant imperial city into a single Kempten. The baroque Residenz and basilica survive.

principality-of-jersika.t: An Orthodox principality of the Latgalians on the Daugava, ruled by King Visvaldis until the crusaders of Riga absorbed it.
principality-of-jersika.o: Jersika was a hill fort on the Daugava in eastern Latvia and the centre of a Latgalian principality linked to the Principality of Polotsk. By about 1200 it was ruled by a prince the German sources call Vissewalde, known in Latvian as Visvaldis, who was probably of mixed Latgalian and Rus' descent.
principality-of-jersika.r: Jersika controlled trade on the Daugava and ruled over Latgalians and Selonians, some of whom were Orthodox Christians with churches. Henry of Livonia calls Visvaldis a king. He allied with the Lithuanians against the German crusaders who had founded Riga.
principality-of-jersika.e: In 1209 Bishop Albert of Riga stormed and burned Jersika, captured Visvaldis's wife and forced him to become a vassal, receiving part of his land back as a fief. The rest of his territory passed gradually to Riga and the Livonian Order, and the principality had disappeared by about 1239.

principality-of-ratzeburg.t: Secularised bishopric east of Lübeck that became a detached province of Mecklenburg-Strelitz for more than two centuries.
principality-of-ratzeburg.o: The Bishopric of Ratzeburg, founded in the 12th century under Henry the Lion, had become Lutheran in the Reformation. At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 it was secularised and given to the dukes of Mecklenburg as the Principality of Ratzeburg, though the town of Ratzeburg itself belonged to Saxe-Lauenburg.
principality-of-ratzeburg.r: The principality was a rural area of villages and farms governed from Schönberg. It had no estates of its own, so its peasants were largely free of the noble domination typical of Mecklenburg. Under the Treaty of Hamburg in 1701 it was assigned to the new Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, from which it was separated by Mecklenburg-Schwerin.
principality-of-ratzeburg.e: Ratzeburg remained part of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, raised to a grand duchy in 1815, until the monarchy ended in 1918, then belonged to the Free State of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. Today the area forms part of the district of Nordwestmecklenburg.

principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.t: The first Serbian state, ruled by the Vlastimirović dynasty in the inland Balkans and converted to Christianity in the 870s.
principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.o: Serbs settled in the western Balkans in the 7th century. Constantine VII names Višeslav as an early prince around 780, but the state becomes clear under Vlastimir, who united Serbian tribes in the 830s and repelled an invasion by the Bulgarian khan Presian around 839–842.
principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.r: The ruling prince (knez) shared power with relatives who held districts, and dynastic quarrels were frequent. The principality lay between Byzantium and the First Bulgarian Empire, often acting as a client of one against the other. Under Mutimir the Serbs adopted Christianity in the 870s, through Byzantine missions.
principality-of-serbia-early-medieval.e: Simeon I of Bulgaria conquered Serbia in 924. Prince Časlav restored it with Byzantine help from the late 920s, but after his death in the mid-10th century the state fragmented and Byzantium took Ras around 970. Later Serbian states emerged in Duklja and Raška.

principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.t: The senior Anhalt principality, ruled from a castle above the Saale at Bernburg, whose line survived the longest among the 1603 partitions.
principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.o: When the Principality of Anhalt was divided in 1603 among the heirs of Joachim Ernst, Christian I received Bernburg. Christian was a leading Calvinist politician who directed the policy of the Protestant Union and the Elector Palatine before the defeat at the White Mountain in 1620.
principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.r: The state was small and agrarian, with silver and copper mining in its Harz exclave around Ballenstedt and Harzgerode. The ruling line was Calvinist. Branch lines split off, including Anhalt-Bernburg-Schaumburg-Hoym. Bernburg held the seniority among the Anhalt princes and was raised to a duchy in 1806, with the court later moving partly to Ballenstedt.
principality-of-anhalt-bernburg.e: The last duke, Alexander Karl, died childless in 1863, and his lands passed to Anhalt-Dessau, which thus united all the Anhalt territories into the Duchy of Anhalt. Bernburg remained a district town within Anhalt.

principality-of-galich-mersky.t: An appanage around Galich in the north-east of Rus', whose princes later fought Moscow in its great dynastic civil war.
principality-of-galich-mersky.o: Galich, on Lake Galich in the old lands of the Finnic Merya, was a town of the Vladimir-Suzdal region known for its salt springs. In 1246 it became the appanage of Konstantin, son of Grand Prince Yaroslav Vsevolodovich, and his descendants held it for over a century.
principality-of-galich-mersky.r: The principality was a remote northern land of forests and salt workings, with little recorded about its government. Its princes were minor figures in the struggles of the grand princes of Vladimir and the Golden Horde, and Galich often served as a refuge from the turmoil further south.
principality-of-galich-mersky.e: In 1363 Dmitry Donskoy of the Grand Duchy of Moscow expelled its last independent prince and annexed Galich. It was later granted to Donskoy's son Yuri, whose line fought Vasily II for the throne of Moscow in the civil war of the 1420s to 1450s.

pashalik-of-yanina.t: Virtually independent domain of Ali Pasha of Tepelena, who ruled Epirus and much of mainland Greece from Ioannina and dealt with European powers as an equal.
pashalik-of-yanina.o: Ali Pasha, an Albanian notable from Tepelena, rose through brigandage and Ottoman service, becoming governor of Trikala and then, in the late 1780s, pasha of Ioannina. By force, alliances and intrigue he extended his authority over Epirus, southern Albania, Thessaly and parts of the Peloponnese, controlling the main routes of the western Balkans.
pashalik-of-yanina.r: Ali ruled from his fortress palace in Ioannina through a personal network of officials and Albanian troops, with Greek secretaries and merchants prominent at court. Ioannina became a centre of Greek learning and trade. He negotiated with Napoleon and Britain, entertained Lord Byron in 1809, crushed the Souliotes and acquired Parga in 1819.
pashalik-of-yanina.e: Sultan Mahmud II declared Ali a rebel in 1820 and besieged Ioannina; Ali was killed in January 1822. The long campaign tied down Ottoman forces just as the Greek War of Independence broke out in 1821, helping the revolt survive.

perusia.t: Etruscan hill city above the upper Tiber, known for its gates, its family tombs and a famous siege by Octavian in 41–40 BCE.
perusia.o: Perusia, Etruscan Persna, modern Perugia, grew on a group of hills west of the Tiber, near the border with the Umbrians. It developed into a city later than the coastal centres, gaining importance from the 6th century BCE and especially in the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE, when its great walls and gates were built.
perusia.r: Perusia controlled river routes and farmland on the upper Tiber and mixed with Umbrian neighbours. Its aristocratic families buried their dead in chamber tombs with carved urns, the finest being the Hypogeum of the Volumni. The Cippus of Perugia, a stone boundary text of about 150 words, is one of the longest Etruscan inscriptions, and the Arco Etrusco gate still stands.
perusia.e: Perusia joined other Etruscan cities against Rome, made truces in 310 and 294 BCE and became a Roman ally after the wars of the early 3rd century. In the Perusine War Octavian besieged Lucius Antonius there in 41–40 BCE; the city was taken and burned. Augustus rebuilt it as Augusta Perusia.

principality-of-luneburg.t: Guelph principality of the Lüneburg Heath ruled from Celle, which embraced the Reformation early and merged into the Electorate of Hanover in 1705.
principality-of-luneburg.o: In 1269 the brothers Albert and John divided the Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg, which their father Otto the Child had received in 1235. John received the northern lands around Lüneburg and Celle, founding the Principality of Lüneburg, while Albert took the Principality of Wolfenbüttel.
principality-of-luneburg.r: The salt city of Lüneburg was wealthy and largely independent, and after the War of the Lüneburg Succession in 1371 to 1388 the dukes moved their residence to Celle. Duke Ernest the Confessor introduced the Reformation from 1527. The principality was rural, with heathland, sheep and forests. George William, the last duke of Celle, saw his daughter Sophia Dorothea marry the future George I of Great Britain.
principality-of-luneburg.e: When George William died in 1705, Lüneburg passed to his nephew and son-in-law George Louis of Calenberg and was merged into the Electorate of Hanover. It later formed part of the Kingdom of Hanover and is now in Lower Saxony.

patina.t: Patina, a Neo-Hittite kingdom of the Amuq plain whose founder called it Palistin, a name that may link it to the Philistines.
patina.o: After the Late Bronze Age collapse, a kingdom arose in the Amuq plain around Antakya, the former Kingdom of Mukish. Inscriptions of King Taita, found in the temple of the storm god at Aleppo, call it Palistin, and its capital was Kunulua, at Tell Tayinat.
patina.r: Its kings wrote Luwian hieroglyphic inscriptions and built palaces and temples in Syrian-Hittite style; a temple at Tell Tayinat yielded an Assyrian treaty tablet. Assyrians called the land Pattin or Unqi. It lived from the fertile plain and the route to the Mediterranean.
patina.e: Patina paid tribute to Ashurnasirpal II and Shalmaneser III of the Assyrian Empire. After King Tutammu rebelled, Tiglath-Pileser III captured Kunulua in 738 BCE and made the land an Assyrian province.

polyrrhenia.t: Fortified hill city of western Crete, the leading power of the island's far west in the Hellenistic period.
polyrrhenia.o: Polyrrhenia stood on a steep hill south of the Gulf of Kissamos in western Crete. Strabo says it was founded by Achaeans and Laconians, who united the scattered villages of the area. Its name, meaning rich in flocks, reflects its pastoral economy.
polyrrhenia.r: Polyrrhenia controlled the west of Crete, with harbours at Phalasarna and Kisamos at times under its influence. It had kosmoi magistrates like other Cretan cities. In the Lyttian War of 220 BCE it broke with Knossos and allied with Philip V of the Antigonid Kingdom of Macedonia. Its walls and cisterns survive.
polyrrhenia.e: Polyrrhenia came under Roman rule in the conquest of Crete in 69 to 67 BCE and continued as a town, later a Byzantine bishopric.

principality-of-starodub.t: A small appanage on the Klyazma whose princely line produced the Pozharsky family, including the liberator of Moscow in 1612.
principality-of-starodub.o: Starodub on the Klyazma, north-east of Vladimir, became the seat of Ivan Vsevolodovich, youngest son of Vsevolod the Big Nest. He is usually said to have received it from his brother Yaroslav in 1238, after the Mongol invasion, rather than in 1218.
principality-of-starodub.r: Starodub was a small forest principality within the Vladimir-Suzdal lands and later a minor player between Moscow and the Golden Horde. Its prince Fyodor Ivanovich was killed at the Horde in 1330. The family divided its land into tiny estates held by branches such as the Pozharsky, Ryapolovsky, Gagarin and Romodanovsky princes.
principality-of-starodub.e: By the mid 15th century the Starodub princes had become servitors of the Grand Duchy of Moscow, and their land was merged into Muscovite territory. Their descendant Prince Dmitry Pozharsky led the militia that freed Moscow from Polish occupation in 1612.

parisii.t: Gallic people of the middle Seine whose town Lutetia became Paris.
parisii.o: The Parisii settled on the Seine in the 3rd century BCE and controlled river traffic across the Paris basin. Caesar mentions that he held a council of Gaul at Lutetia in 53 BCE. The exact site of their oppidum is debated; excavations at Nanterre have revealed a large Gallic settlement.
parisii.r: They struck fine gold coins, among the most elegant in Gaul. Their wealth came from trade on the Seine, and Roman inscriptions later record a powerful guild of boatmen.
parisii.e: In 52 BCE they joined the revolt; the Aulercan leader Camulogenus burned Lutetia and was defeated by Caesar's legate Labienus. Under Rome Lutetia was rebuilt on the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève, where the boatmen dedicated the Pillar of the Boatmen to Jupiter. In late antiquity the town took the name of the people, Paris.

principality-of-svaneti.t: A princely domain in the high Caucasus valleys of Svaneti, home of the stone defence towers, ruled by the Dadeshkeliani family until Russia ended it in 1858.
principality-of-svaneti.o: Svaneti, the highest inhabited valleys of the Caucasus, had long been a duchy of Georgia. After the kingdom broke apart, the free communities of Upper Svaneti governed themselves, while Lower Svaneti and part of the upper valley came under the Dadeshkeliani princes by about 1600, nominally as vassals of the Kingdom of Imereti.
principality-of-svaneti.r: The Svans lived in villages of fortified stone towers, guarding treasures of medieval icons and manuscripts in their churches. Society was organised around clans, blood feuds and village assemblies, with the princes taking dues from peasants. The princes competed with the Dadiani of Mingrelia and preserved the distinct Svan language.
principality-of-svaneti.e: The Dadeshkeliani accepted a Russian protectorate in 1833. In 1857 Prince Constantine Dadeshkeliani killed the Russian governor Gagarin during a dispute and was executed, and in 1858 the Russian Empire abolished the principality.

principality-of-armenia.t: Armenia under Arab rule, when native princes governed beside the caliph's governor at Dvin and the Bagratid family rose towards kingship.
principality-of-armenia.o: As Arab armies overran the Sasanian lands, the Armenian commander Theodore Rshtuni made a treaty with Muawiya in 653 accepting Arab overlordship in return for autonomy and keeping Armenian troops. The province of Arminiya, which also took in Georgia and Albania, was established with its centre at Dvin.
principality-of-armenia.r: An Arab governor, the ostikan, sat at Dvin while a native presiding prince represented the Armenian nobility. Heavy taxes provoked revolts, notably in 774-775, which were crushed and weakened the Mamikonian house. Arab emirs settled in towns, while monasteries preserved Armenian learning. The Bagratids grew rich through lands and trade.
principality-of-armenia.e: With the Abbasid Caliphate weakening, Ashot Bagratuni was named prince of princes in 862, and around 884 the caliph sent him a crown, founding Bagratid Armenia. The period had preserved the noble houses, the church and a sense of separate identity that made this revival of Armenian kingship possible.

prince-bishopric-of-verdun.t: One of the Three Bishoprics of Lorraine, a church principality on the Meuse that passed from the Empire to France between 1552 and 1648.
prince-bishopric-of-verdun.o: Verdun, where the Carolingian empire was divided in 843, was an ancient bishopric. In 997 Emperor Otto III granted Bishop Haimo the comital rights over the city and its district, making the bishops princes of the Holy Roman Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-verdun.r: The bishops' temporal lands were small and lay along the Meuse, and they faced constant pressure from the counts of Bar and the dukes of Lorraine. The citizens of Verdun gained wide self-government and imperial-city status, limiting the bishops' power at home. The city was a trading centre, known for its sugared almonds.
prince-bishopric-of-verdun.e: Henry II of France occupied Verdun with Metz and Toul in 1552, and the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 confirmed French sovereignty over the Three Bishoprics. Verdun became part of the Kingdom of France and later a major fortress.

papal-states.t: The territories of central Italy ruled by the popes as temporal sovereigns for over a thousand years, from Pepin's donation to the capture of Rome in 1870.
papal-states.o: When the Lombards threatened Rome, Pope Stephen II won the protection of the Frankish king Pepin the Short in 754. Pepin defeated the Lombards and in 756 gave the pope the lands of the former Exarchate of Ravenna together with the Duchy of Rome. Charlemagne confirmed and extended the grant in 774.
papal-states.r: The pope ruled as an elected monarch through cardinals, legates and governors, but for centuries real control was weak, contested by Roman nobles and local lords. Innocent III expanded papal power, and Cardinal Albornoz reasserted it in the 1350s with the Egidian Constitutions. Renaissance popes such as Alexander VI and Julius II fought to bring the Romagna under control and built the new St Peter's. Ferrara (1598) and Urbino (1631) were later absorbed.
papal-states.e: Napoleon annexed the States in 1809; they were restored in 1815. In 1860 Romagna, the Marche and Umbria joined the Kingdom of Italy, and on 20 September 1870 Italian troops entered Rome. Pius IX refused to recognise the loss, and the dispute was settled by the Lateran Treaty of 1929, creating Vatican City.

principality-of-bulgaria.t: Autonomous Bulgarian principality created after the Russo-Turkish War, which united with Eastern Rumelia and proclaimed full independence in 1908.
principality-of-bulgaria.o: Russia's victory over the Ottomans led to the Treaty of San Stefano in March 1878, which created a large Bulgaria. The Congress of Berlin reduced it to an autonomous principality between the Danube and the Balkan mountains, under Ottoman suzerainty. In 1879 the Tarnovo Constitution was adopted and Alexander of Battenberg elected prince, with Sofia as capital.
principality-of-bulgaria.r: The liberal Tarnovo Constitution created a parliament elected by male suffrage, though princes and strong premiers often ruled forcefully. Unification with Eastern Rumelia in 1885 was defended by victory over Serbia at Slivnitsa. Russian anger forced Alexander's abdication in 1886, and Ferdinand of Saxe-Coburg was chosen in 1887, while premier Stefan Stambolov built a modern state and army.
principality-of-bulgaria.e: On 5 October 1908, during the crisis over Bosnia, Ferdinand proclaimed full independence at Tarnovo and took the title of tsar, creating the Kingdom of Bulgaria. The Tarnovo Constitution remained in force until 1947.

province-of-venezuela.t: The Spanish governorate of the Caribbean coast of South America, centred first on Coro and then Caracas, which grew rich on cacao.
province-of-venezuela.o: Spain founded Coro in 1527, and from 1528 the province was leased to the Welser bankers as Klein-Venedig. After the Welser lease ended in the 1540s, Spanish governors took over. Diego de Losada founded Santiago de León de Caracas in 1567, and it became the capital in 1578.
province-of-venezuela.r: The province was governed by a governor and captain-general under the Audiencia of Santo Domingo and later of Santa Fe de Bogotá. Its economy grew on cacao plantations worked by enslaved Africans, and Caracas cacao was exported to New Spain and Europe. From 1728 the Guipuzcoan Company of Caracas held a trade monopoly, provoking the revolt of Juan Francisco de León in 1749. The Creole elite, known as mantuanos, dominated society.
province-of-venezuela.e: In 1777 Charles III united the province with Cumaná, Guayana, Maracaibo and the islands of Trinidad and Margarita to form the Captaincy General of Venezuela. The province's Creole elite later led the independence movement of 1810.

prince-bishopric-of-hildesheim.t: Lower Saxon church state famed for Bishop Bernward's Romanesque art, which lost most of its land in a 1519 feud and won it back in 1643.
prince-bishopric-of-hildesheim.o: Louis the Pious founded the diocese of Hildesheim in 815. Around 1000 Bishop Bernward made the city a centre of art, building St. Michael's Church and commissioning its bronze doors and column. The bishops built up a territory between the Leine and Oker, and by the 13th century, around 1235, they ruled as imperial princes.
prince-bishopric-of-hildesheim.r: The cathedral chapter and estates shared power with the bishops. In the Hildesheim Diocesan Feud of 1519 to 1523 the see lost most of its territory to the Guelph dukes, retaining only the Small Diocese. The city of Hildesheim turned Lutheran, while the bishops stayed Catholic; Wittelsbach princes such as Clemens August of Bavaria often held the see alongside Cologne.
prince-bishopric-of-hildesheim.e: The lost lands were restored in 1643. The see was secularised in 1803 and given to Prussia, then belonged to the Kingdom of Westphalia, and in 1815 to the Kingdom of Hanover. Its cathedral and St. Michael's are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

palace-state-of-zakros.t: The easternmost Minoan palace on Crete, a harbour centre for trade with Egypt and the Levant, found unplundered with its treasures in place.
palace-state-of-zakros.o: Zakros lies in a sheltered bay at the eastern tip of Crete, a natural harbour facing Egypt, Cyprus and the Levant. A settlement existed in the Early Minoan period, and a palace was built c. 1900 BCE. The surviving palace, smaller than Knossos or Phaistos, dates mostly from the Neopalatial period after c. 1700 BCE.
palace-state-of-zakros.r: The palace followed the standard Minoan plan with a central court, storerooms, workshops, a lustral basin and a cistern room. It likely controlled trade in copper, ivory and elephant tusks, some of which were found on site. Its treasury held stone ritual vessels, including a rock-crystal rhyton, and Linear A tablets show local record-keeping.
palace-state-of-zakros.e: Zakros was destroyed by fire c. 1450 BCE and abandoned so suddenly that it was never looted. It was not reoccupied as a palace. Nikolaos Platon excavated it from 1961, recovering one of the richest collections of Minoan objects found in place.

polans-east-slavs.t: The East Slavic tribe of the middle Dnieper whose town of Kiev became the capital of Kievan Rus'.
polans-east-slavs.o: The Polans, the people of the fields, settled the wooded steppe on the middle Dnieper. The chronicle credits their legendary founder Kyi, with his brothers Shchek and Khoriv and his sister Lybid, with founding Kiev. For a time they paid tribute to the Khazars, said to have been one sword for every household.
polans-east-slavs.r: The chronicler, himself from Kiev, praises the Polans as gentle and well mannered compared with their neighbours, particularly the Drevlians. They farmed the fertile soil, and Kiev's position on the Dnieper made it a centre of trade between Scandinavia, Byzantium and the steppe. In the mid 9th century Kiev was held by the Varangians Askold and Dir.
polans-east-slavs.e: In 882 Oleg of Novgorod killed Askold and Dir and made Kiev his capital, so the Polan lands became the core of Kievan Rus'. The tribal name faded as the people of the region came to be called the Rus'.

palatinate-mosbach.t: A minor Wittelsbach duchy on the Neckar and in the Odenwald, created when King Rupert's lands were divided in 1410.
palatinate-mosbach.o: When King Rupert, Elector Palatine, died in 1410, his lands were divided among his four sons. Otto I received the territory around Mosbach on the Neckar and in the Odenwald, founding the Palatinate-Mosbach line, and in 1448 he also inherited Neumarkt in the Upper Palatinate.
palatinate-mosbach.r: The Mosbach dukes ruled a modest territory of small towns, forests and farms from Mosbach and Neumarkt, closely tied to the senior electoral line at Heidelberg. Their lands were scattered and their revenues small. Otto II, the second and last duke, never married and left no heirs.
palatinate-mosbach.e: When Otto II died in 1499, Palatinate-Mosbach passed back to the Electoral Palatinate. Mosbach remained Palatine until 1803, when it went to the princes of Leiningen and then to the Grand Duchy of Baden.

principality-of-lucca-and-piombino.t: The Tuscan principality Napoleon created for his sister Elisa Bonaparte, who governed it as an energetic reforming ruler.
principality-of-lucca-and-piombino.o: In 1805 Napoleon abolished the Republic of Lucca and joined it to the Principality of Piombino, granting the new state to his sister Elisa and her husband Felice Baciocchi. Massa and Carrara were added in 1806.
principality-of-lucca-and-piombino.r: Elisa, not her husband, held real power. She introduced the Napoleonic Code, closed many convents, reorganised schools and finances, and promoted the Carrara marble industry, founding an academy and workshops that produced busts of the Bonaparte family for all Europe. She patronised the violinist Niccolò Paganini at her court. In 1809 Napoleon also made her Grand Duchess of Tuscany, ruling from Florence.
principality-of-lucca-and-piombino.e: Elisa fled as Napoleon's empire collapsed in 1814. The Congress of Vienna gave Lucca to Maria Luisa of Bourbon as the Duchy of Lucca, while Piombino went to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany.

provisional-government-of-national-defen.t: Rival Greek government set up in Thessaloniki in 1916 by Eleftherios Venizelos, which took Greece into the First World War on the Allied side.
provisional-government-of-national-defen.o: During the First World War, King Constantine I insisted on neutrality while Prime Minister Eleftherios Venizelos wanted to join the Entente. After Venizelos was forced out, officers in Allied-held Thessaloniki launched the National Defence movement in August 1916. In September and October Venizelos formed a provisional government there with Admiral Pavlos Kountouriotis and General Panagiotis Danglis.
provisional-government-of-national-defen.r: The government, led by this triumvirate, controlled northern Greece, Crete and most of the Aegean islands with Allied support, raised an army and declared war on Bulgaria and Germany. Greece was split in two, the National Schism, while Allied pressure on Athens led to the armed clash of December 1916, the Noemvriana.
provisional-government-of-national-defen.e: In June 1917 the Allies forced Constantine I to leave the country. Venizelos returned to Athens as prime minister of a united Kingdom of Greece, which entered the war fully. The bitterness of the schism shaped Greek politics for decades.

pedi-kingdom.t: The Maroteng kingdom of the north-eastern Transvaal, which dominated its region and resisted Boer and British conquest until 1879.
pedi-kingdom.o: The Pedi Maroteng dynasty, of Sotho-Tswana origin, settled around the Steelpoort river in the 17th century. Under Thulare in the late 18th and early 19th centuries it became a paramountcy dominating many smaller chiefdoms of the region.
pedi-kingdom.r: The Pedi king ruled through royal kin and tributary chiefs, with initiation regiments forming the army. After defeat by Mzilikazi's Ndebele in the 1820s, Sekwati rebuilt the kingdom on fortified hilltops. Pedi men worked as migrant labourers in the Cape and on the diamond fields, buying guns, and Christianity divided the court in the 1860s.
pedi-kingdom.e: Sekhukhune I defeated a Transvaal Boer army in 1876, but after Britain annexed the Transvaal, a British and Swazi force stormed the capital Tsate in 1879 and captured him. The kingdom became part of the Transvaal, though the Pedi royal house survives.

prince-bishopric-of-munster.t: The largest church state in the Holy Roman Empire, scene of the Anabaptist kingdom of 1534 and of the peace talks that ended the Thirty Years War.
prince-bishopric-of-munster.o: The Frisian missionary Liudger founded a monastery at Mimigernaford around 793 and became the first bishop of Münster in 805. The bishops acquired counties across Westphalia, and after Henry the Lion fell in 1180 they ruled as imperial princes. Their lands later stretched from the Lippe to the Ems and beyond to the Dutch border.
prince-bishopric-of-munster.r: The cathedral chapter and estates kept a strong voice beside the bishop. In 1534 to 1535 radical Anabaptists under Jan van Leiden turned the city into a theocratic kingdom until Bishop Franz von Waldeck retook it after a siege. The territory remained firmly Catholic. Christoph Bernhard von Galen waged wars against the Dutch Republic, and in the 18th century the minister Franz von Fürstenberg reformed schools and founded the university.
prince-bishopric-of-munster.e: The Peace of Westphalia was negotiated partly in Münster in 1648. The see was secularised in 1802 to 1803 and divided, with the largest share going to Prussia and smaller parts to Oldenburg, Salm and Arenberg. Münster became capital of the Prussian Province of Westphalia.

principality-of-wolfenbuttel.t: Guelph principality ruled from Wolfenbüttel, home of the great Herzog August Library and the University of Helmstedt, and forerunner of the Duchy of Brunswick.
principality-of-wolfenbuttel.o: In the division of the Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg in 1269, Albert I the Tall received the southern lands around Brunswick. After further partitions the Wolfenbüttel line took shape in the 15th century, with its residence at the castle of Wolfenbüttel, as the city of Brunswick largely governed itself.
principality-of-wolfenbuttel.r: Henry the Younger was a fierce Catholic opponent of the Reformation, but his son Julius introduced Lutheranism in 1568 and founded the University of Helmstedt in 1576. Augustus the Younger built the Herzog August Library, one of the great libraries of Europe, where Lessing later served as librarian. The dukes subdued Brunswick in 1671 and moved their court there in 1753.
principality-of-wolfenbuttel.e: The principality was absorbed into the Kingdom of Westphalia in 1807. Restored in 1813, it became the Duchy of Brunswick in 1815, which lasted until 1918. The territory is now in Lower Saxony.

principality-of-nassau-usingen.t: Walramian Nassau principality in the Taunus that moved its court to Biebrich on the Rhine and co-founded the Duchy of Nassau.
principality-of-nassau-usingen.o: Nassau-Usingen was created in 1659 when the lands of Nassau-Saarbrücken were divided among the sons of Count William Louis, and Walrad received Usingen in the Taunus. Walrad, a general in Dutch and imperial service, was raised to prince in 1688.
principality-of-nassau-usingen.r: The territory was Lutheran and mostly rural, but it grew as other Walramian lines died out: Nassau-Usingen inherited Nassau-Saarbrücken and Nassau-Idstein in the 18th century. Prince Charles moved the residence to Biebrich Palace on the Rhine, near Wiesbaden, in 1744, and the spa town of Wiesbaden grew under the princes. After 1797 it lost its left-bank lands but gained Mainz territory in 1803.
principality-of-nassau-usingen.e: In 1806 Nassau-Usingen and Nassau-Weilburg united as the Duchy of Nassau within the Confederation of the Rhine, with Frederick Augustus of Usingen as duke. When he died without sons in 1816, the Usingen line ended and Nassau passed to the Weilburg line.

principality-of-pereyaslavl.t: The frontier principality of Kievan Rus' facing the steppe, home base of Vladimir Monomakh in his wars against the Cumans.
principality-of-pereyaslavl.o: Pereyaslavl, south-east of Kiev on the Trubizh river, was one of the oldest towns of Rus'. When Yaroslav the Wise died in 1054 he left it to his son Vsevolod, and it became a principality of its own, third in rank after Kiev and Chernigov.
principality-of-pereyaslavl.r: Lying on the edge of the steppe, Pereyaslavl was a military land of fortresses and earthen walls defending Rus' against the Pechenegs and then the Cumans. Vladimir Monomakh ruled here from 1094 to 1113 and led campaigns deep into the steppe. The town was briefly the seat of a metropolitan in the 11th century.
principality-of-pereyaslavl.e: Usually held by Monomakh's descendants as a stepping stone to Kiev, the principality declined in the 12th century. The Mongols sacked Pereyaslavl in 1239, and the land later passed to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. The town, now Pereiaslav, is where the Cossack Hetmanate swore allegiance to Moscow in 1654.

proto-kingdom-of-naqada.t: A predynastic chiefdom centred on Nubt in Upper Egypt, one of the early power centres whose rivalries led to the unification of Egypt.
proto-kingdom-of-naqada.o: Nubt, the Ombos of the Greeks, grew on the west bank of the Nile near modern Naqada during the Naqada I and II phases of the 4th millennium BCE. Its position opposite the Wadi Hammamat, the route to the gold-bearing Eastern Desert, brought wealth, and by c. 3500 BCE a walled town and rich graves show a ruling elite taking shape.
proto-kingdom-of-naqada.r: No written records survive, so almost everything is inferred from archaeology. Cemetery T at Naqada held large brick-lined tombs furnished with fine pottery, stone vessels, maceheads and imported goods, pointing to a hereditary chiefly class. Nubt was the cult centre of the god Set, later called 'the Ombite', and its workshops produced painted pottery traded along the Nile.
proto-kingdom-of-naqada.e: By c. 3200 BCE Nubt appears to have been eclipsed by, or absorbed into, the Proto-kingdom of Thinis, which went on to unite Egypt. The town survived as a temple centre of Set, and the Naqada culture gave its name to the whole predynastic period.

principality-of-isenburg.t: Hessian principality of the Isenburg-Birstein line that rose to sovereignty under Napoleon only to be mediatised at Vienna.
principality-of-isenburg.o: The counts of Isenburg had held lands in the Wetterau and around Büdingen since the Middle Ages, divided into many lines. The Birstein branch was raised to princely rank in 1744 under Wolfgang Ernst I, ruling from Birstein Castle in the Vogelsberg foothills.
principality-of-isenburg.r: The territory was small and agrarian, with Offenbach am Main as its most important town, where Huguenot settlers had built crafts and trade. Prince Charles joined the Confederation of the Rhine in 1806, gaining full sovereignty and absorbing the lands of other Isenburg lines, and supplied a regiment to Napoleon's army.
principality-of-isenburg.e: After Napoleon's fall Isenburg was occupied by the allies, and the Congress of Vienna mediatised it. In 1816 its lands were divided between the Grand Duchy of Hesse and the Electorate of Hesse, the princes keeping their estates.

portuguese-muscat.t: Muscat under Portuguese control, a fortified port guarding the approach to Hormuz until the Omani imams drove the Portuguese out in 1650.
portuguese-muscat.o: In 1507 Afonso de Albuquerque attacked the Omani coast and sacked Muscat, then a dependency of the Kingdom of Ormus. Muscat came under the Portuguese Empire as part of its system of forts protecting the Gulf trade and the route to India.
portuguese-muscat.r: For much of the period Muscat was governed through Hormuzi officials with Portuguese oversight and a garrison. After an Ottoman fleet under Piri Reis sacked the town in 1552, the Portuguese built the Jalali and Mirani forts in the 1580s, which still overlook the harbour. Muscat grew in importance after the Portuguese lost Hormuz in 1622 and moved their Gulf base there.
portuguese-muscat.e: The imams of the Ya'aruba dynasty took the Omani coast step by step; Sultan ibn Saif captured Muscat in 1650, ending Portuguese rule in Oman and beginning Oman's rise as a naval power.

prince-bishopric-of-montenegro.t: Mountain theocracy ruled by Orthodox metropolitans of Cetinje, which kept Montenegro self-governing against the Ottomans for more than three centuries.
prince-bishopric-of-montenegro.o: After the last Crnojević rulers left Zeta in the 1490s and the land was absorbed into the Ottoman sanjak of Scutari, the metropolitans of Cetinje became the recognised leaders of the highland clans; their secular role is traditionally dated from 1516. In 1697 the office passed to Danilo Petrović-Njegoš, whose family kept it, usually from uncle to nephew.
prince-bishopric-of-montenegro.r: The vladika was both bishop and prince, ruling a confederation of fiercely independent clans with little central administration, bound together by Orthodoxy and war against the Ottomans. From Peter the Great onwards the prince-bishops sought Russian support. Petar I defeated Kara Mahmud Pasha Bushati in 1796, and Petar II, author of the epic The Mountain Wreath, created a senate and taxes.
prince-bishopric-of-montenegro.e: When Petar II died in 1851, his nephew Danilo refused ordination and in 1852, with Russian approval, proclaimed himself secular prince, creating the Principality of Montenegro. The Petrović-Njegoš dynasty continued to rule until 1918, and the monastery at Cetinje remains the seat of the Metropolitanate.

pellene.t: Easternmost city of Achaea, a loyal Spartan ally famous for the woollen cloaks given as prizes at its games.
pellene.o: Pellene stood on a high hill in eastern Achaea, near the border with Sicyon, a short way inland from the Gulf of Corinth. It was one of the twelve Achaean cities, formed in the early Iron Age.
pellene.r: Pellene was known for its warm woollen cloaks, awarded as prizes at its local games, and for its sanctuary of Athena. Unlike most Achaean cities, it sided with Sparta at the start of the Peloponnesian War. In the 4th century BCE it was ruled at times by tyrants, including the wrestler Chaeron, who was installed with Macedonian backing.
pellene.e: Pellene joined the revived Achaean League. In 241 BCE the Aetolian League sacked it, and Aratus routed the Aetolians in its streets. It passed under Roman control in 146 BCE and later dwindled.

provisional-government-of-albania.t: First government of independent Albania, proclaimed at Vlorë in 1912 while Balkan armies occupied most of the country.
provisional-government-of-albania.o: During the First Balkan War, as Serbian, Montenegrin and Greek armies overran the Ottoman Balkans, Albanian delegates gathered in Vlorë. On 28 November 1912 they declared independence, raised Skanderbeg's flag and formed a provisional government headed by the veteran Ottoman official Ismail Qemali, with Luigj Gurakuqi among its ministers.
provisional-government-of-albania.r: The government controlled little beyond Vlorë and its surroundings, lacking an army, money or international recognition, while Durrës, Shkodër and much of the south were occupied or contested. It set up ministries, schools and a gendarmerie on paper. Its fate depended on the Conference of Ambassadors in London, which recognised Albania in 1913 but left Kosovo outside its borders.
provisional-government-of-albania.e: An International Commission of Control took over administration in late 1913, and Ismail Qemali resigned in January 1914 amid rivalry with Essad Pasha's Republic of Central Albania. In March 1914 the Great Powers' chosen ruler, Wilhelm of Wied, arrived to found the Principality of Albania.
provisional-government-of-albania.re: Sunni Islam, Orthodox and Catholic Christianity

province-of-queen-adelaide.t: A short-lived British annexation of Xhosa land between the Keiskamma and Kei rivers, reversed by London after barely a year.
province-of-queen-adelaide.o: During the Sixth Frontier War of 1834-1836, the Cape governor Sir Benjamin D'Urban proclaimed in May 1835 that the territory between the Keiskamma and Kei rivers was British, naming it after Queen Adelaide, wife of William IV. The Xhosa king Hintsa was shot while in British custody during the campaign.
province-of-queen-adelaide.r: Colonel Harry Smith governed the province from the new military headquarters of King William's Town. The plan was to expel or control the Rharhabe Xhosa, settle loyal Mfengu and open land to colonists, but it required a costly garrison and provoked continued resistance.
province-of-queen-adelaide.e: The Colonial Secretary Lord Glenelg, influenced by humanitarian critics, ordered the annexation reversed, and the province was abandoned in December 1836 in favour of treaties with Xhosa chiefs. Smith restored the idea in 1847 as British Kaffraria.

prince-bishopric-of-osnabruck.t: Westphalian church state where the Peace of Westphalia was negotiated and where, uniquely, Catholic and Lutheran bishops alternated after 1648.
prince-bishopric-of-osnabruck.o: Charlemagne founded the diocese of Osnabrück around 780 after his conquest of the Saxons. Its bishops acquired estates and comital rights between the Ems and the Weser, and in the 13th century, around 1225, they emerged as imperial princes ruling a consolidated territory free of the counts of Tecklenburg.
prince-bishopric-of-osnabruck.r: The cathedral chapter and estates held strong rights. Osnabrück and Münster hosted the negotiations of the Peace of Westphalia. Under its terms the see alternated between a Catholic bishop and a Lutheran prince of the house of Brunswick-Lüneburg; Ernest Augustus, father of George I of Great Britain, and later Frederick, Duke of York, held it. The territory was known for linen and for the writer and statesman Justus Möser.
prince-bishopric-of-osnabruck.e: In 1803 the see was secularised and given to Hanover. After the Napoleonic interlude it remained Hanoverian until Prussia annexed the Kingdom of Hanover in 1866. The Catholic diocese continues.

portuguese-mozambique.t: Portugal's East African colony for almost five centuries, from the fort at Sofala in 1505 to independence in 1975.
portuguese-mozambique.o: Portugal built a fort at Sofala in 1505 to tap the gold trade of the Zimbabwe plateau and took over Mozambique Island soon after, making it the capital and a stop on the route to India. In the 16th and 17th centuries Portuguese traders and soldiers pushed up the Zambezi to Sena and Tete, competing with Swahili merchants and the Mutapa state.
portuguese-mozambique.r: For centuries Portuguese control was limited to coastal towns and the Zambezi prazos, huge estates held by Afro-Portuguese families with private armies. The 19th-century slave trade and then forced labour and chartered companies, such as the Mozambique Company, shaped the economy. Effective occupation came only after the defeat of the Gaza ruler Gungunhana in 1895, and the capital moved to Lourenco Marques in 1898.
portuguese-mozambique.e: From 1964 FRELIMO waged a guerrilla war for independence. After the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon in 1974, Portugal negotiated withdrawal, and Mozambique became independent on 25 June 1975 under Samora Machel.

prince-bishopric-of-cambrai.t: An imperial church principality on the French border, which gave its name to the League of Cambrai and the Ladies' Peace before Louis XIV annexed it.
prince-bishopric-of-cambrai.o: Cambrai was a Merovingian bishopric whose diocese stretched across Hainaut and Brabant. In 1007 Emperor Henry II granted the county of Cambrai to Bishop Erluin, making the bishops princes of the Holy Roman Empire on its frontier with France.
prince-bishopric-of-cambrai.r: The Cambrésis was a small but rich land of cloth and linen, its name later given to the fine fabric cambric. The bishops often struggled with the townspeople and with the counts of Flanders and Hainaut. The city hosted the League of Cambrai against Venice in 1508 and the Ladies' Peace of 1529. Charles V built a citadel there in 1543.
prince-bishopric-of-cambrai.e: Cambrai became an archbishopric in 1559 under strong Spanish influence. Louis XIV captured it in 1677, and the Treaty of Nijmegen of 1678 gave it to the Kingdom of France. Fénelon was its most famous archbishop.

palatinate-zweibrucken.t: A Wittelsbach duchy in the western Palatinate whose family gave Sweden three kings and Bavaria its first king.
palatinate-zweibrucken.o: In 1453 the lands of Duke Stephen of Palatinate-Simmern were divided, and his son Louis I the Black received Zweibrücken and Veldenz, founding the Palatinate-Zweibrücken line. Louis spent much of his reign in conflict with his cousins of the Electoral Palatinate.
palatinate-zweibrucken.r: The dukes ruled scattered lands in the western Palatinate and Alsace from Zweibrücken. Wolfgang introduced Lutheranism and founded the Hornbach school in 1559, while John I later adopted Calvinism. A cadet branch, Palatinate-Kleeburg, gave Sweden three kings, beginning with Charles X Gustav in 1654, and from 1681 to 1718 Zweibrücken itself was ruled by the kings of Sweden.
palatinate-zweibrucken.e: In 1793 French armies occupied Zweibrücken, and France annexed it in 1797. Its duke Maximilian Joseph inherited the Electorate of Bavaria in 1799 and in 1806 became the first king of the Kingdom of Bavaria, whose royal house descended from Zweibrücken.

panormus.t: Phoenician and Punic city on the bay of Palermo, Carthage's chief stronghold in western Sicily until Rome captured it in 254 BCE.
panormus.o: Phoenicians settled Panormus, called Ziz ('flower') on its coins, on a promontory between two river inlets by the late 8th or 7th century BCE. Its deep natural harbour gave it the Greek name Panormos, 'all-harbour'. With Motya and Soloeis it formed the cluster of Phoenician towns in western Sicily that came under Carthaginian protection.
panormus.r: Panormus prospered from trade between Carthage, Sardinia and the Greek and Elymian towns of Sicily and served as a key Carthaginian military base: Hamilcar landed there before the battle of Himera in 480 BCE. Its necropolis shows a mixed population of Phoenicians, Greeks and Elymians. It minted coins with Punic and Greek legends and was ruled by local magistrates under Carthaginian oversight.
panormus.e: In the First Punic War Rome took Panormus in 254 BCE, and in 250 BCE the consul Lucius Caecilius Metellus defeated a Carthaginian army with elephants beneath its walls. The city became a free town of the Roman province of Sicily and later grew into Palermo, capital of the Emirate of Sicily and the Norman kingdom.

prince-bishopric-of-paderborn.t: Westphalian church state rooted in Charlemagne's Saxon wars and his 799 meeting with Pope Leo III, a Catholic bastion until 1802.
prince-bishopric-of-paderborn.o: Charlemagne held assemblies at Paderborn from 777 and met Pope Leo III there in 799, the prelude to his imperial coronation. The diocese was founded around the same time. Bishop Meinwerk in the early 11th century built up its wealth and churches. The bishops gradually acquired comital rights, ruling a territorial principality by the late 13th century, around 1281.
prince-bishopric-of-paderborn.r: The cathedral chapter and estates shared power with the prince-bishop. Lutheranism spread in the 16th century, but Bishop Dietrich von Fürstenberg restored Catholicism and founded a Jesuit university in 1614. His relative Ferdinand von Fürstenberg was a noted scholar-bishop. The territory, in the fertile Hellweg and the Egge hills, was agricultural with small towns.
prince-bishopric-of-paderborn.e: In 1802 the see was secularised and annexed by Prussia. It belonged to the Kingdom of Westphalia from 1807 to 1813 and then returned to Prussia. The diocese, raised to an archdiocese in 1930, continues.

provisional-government-of-judea.t: The rebel government of the First Jewish Revolt, which minted its own coins and held Jerusalem against Rome until the city and Temple fell in 70.
provisional-government-of-judea.o: Riots in Caesarea and the plundering of the Temple treasury by the procurator Florus led to open revolt in 66. After rebels routed the Syrian governor Cestius Gallus at Beth Horon, an assembly in Jerusalem appointed the former high priest Ananus ben Ananus and Joseph ben Gurion to lead it and sent commanders to the districts, Josephus among them to Galilee.
provisional-government-of-judea.r: The government struck silver shekels dated by years of the revolt and inscribed 'Jerusalem the Holy', a declaration of sovereignty. Its moderate priestly leadership was overthrown in 68 by Zealots allied with Idumaeans, who killed Ananus. Jerusalem then split between rival factions under John of Gischala, Simon bar Giora and Eleazar ben Simon, who fought each other and burned food stores.
provisional-government-of-judea.e: Vespasian subdued Galilee in 67 and Titus besieged Jerusalem in 70, destroying the city and the Second Temple that summer. The last strongholds, including Masada, fell by 73-74. Judea became a separate province with a legion stationed in the ruins of Jerusalem.

principality-of-correggio.t: The small Emilian state of the da Correggio lords, birthplace of the painter Antonio Allegri, called Correggio.
principality-of-correggio.o: The da Correggio family had ruled the town of Correggio, between Reggio and Carpi, since the 12th century and had been powerful in Parma. In 1452 Emperor Frederick III recognised their lands as a county, raised to a principality in 1616.
principality-of-correggio.r: The counts governed a small farming territory and a fortified town with a lively court. Veronica Gambara, poet and widow of Count Giberto, ruled as regent in the early 16th century and corresponded with leading writers. The painter Antonio Allegri, known as Correggio, was born in the town around 1489. The rulers depended on the protection of the emperor and their Este neighbours.
principality-of-correggio.e: Prince Siro da Correggio was accused of minting debased coins and was deposed by the emperor in 1630. In 1635 the principality was sold to Francesco I d'Este and joined to the Duchy of Modena and Reggio.

principality-of-salm-1802.t: Napoleonic-era principality in the Münsterland, given to two Salm princes in compensation for lands lost to France.
principality-of-salm-1802.o: The princes of Salm-Salm and Salm-Kyrburg lost their territories in the Vosges and on the left bank of the Rhine to revolutionary France. Under the settlement of 1802 and the Imperial Recess of 1803, they jointly received the districts of Bocholt and Ahaus from the secularised Prince-Bishopric of Münster, forming the Principality of Salm.
principality-of-salm-1802.r: The two princely houses held the state jointly, with Salm-Salm taking two-thirds and Salm-Kyrburg one third, and governed from Bocholt and Anholt. The territory was Catholic and agrarian. In 1806 it joined the Confederation of the Rhine as a sovereign member. The Salm-Kyrburg prince Frederick III had been guillotined in Paris in 1794, and his young son Frederick IV succeeded him.
principality-of-salm-1802.e: In December 1810 Napoleon annexed north-western Germany to secure the coast against British trade, and Salm was incorporated into France in 1811. In 1815 the territory passed to Prussia, where the Salm families remained as mediatised landowners.

prince-bishopric-of-passau.t: Danube church state at the meeting of three rivers, whose vast diocese once stretched to Vienna and whose court may have produced the Nibelungenlied.
prince-bishopric-of-passau.o: Saint Boniface organised the diocese of Passau in 739. As the Bavarian church expanded eastwards, its diocese came to cover much of today's Austria. In 1217 Emperor Frederick II recognised the bishop's secular lordship over the city and nearby lands, making Passau a prince-bishopric directly under the Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-passau.r: The cathedral chapter elected the prince-bishops, who ruled a small territory around Passau and in the Bavarian Forest, with salt trade on the Danube and Inn. The Nibelungenlied may have been composed around 1200 at the court of Bishop Wolfger von Erla. Conflicts with the citizens recurred. After a fire in 1662 Italian architects rebuilt the city and St. Stephen's Cathedral in baroque style.
prince-bishopric-of-passau.e: The prince-bishopric was secularised in 1803 and divided between Bavaria and the Electorate of Salzburg; by 1805 all of it belonged to Bavaria. The Catholic diocese of Passau continues, and the baroque old town still clusters on the narrow peninsula between the Danube and the Inn.

principality-of-philaretos-brachamios.t: A short-lived Armenian-ruled domain in the Taurus and northern Syria, built by a Byzantine general after the empire's collapse in the East.
principality-of-philaretos-brachamios.o: Philaretos Brachamios was an Armenian officer in Byzantine service. After the defeat at Manzikert in 1071 and the civil wars that followed, he gathered soldiers and Armenian refugees and made himself master of Marash, Melitene and other towns in the Taurus and Cilicia.
principality-of-philaretos-brachamios.r: Philaretos acted independently but sought recognition from Constantinople, which gave him high titles and appointed him governor in the East. At its height around 1078-1083 his domain stretched from Cilicia to Antioch and Edessa. He was a Chalcedonian Christian, which made him unpopular with many Armenians of the national church, and he is said to have considered accepting Islam to keep Seljuk favour.
principality-of-philaretos-brachamios.e: The Seljuk prince Suleiman ibn Qutalmish took Antioch in 1084, and Edessa fell soon after. Philaretos disappears from the record around 1086. Armenian lords who had served him, including the Rubenids, later formed the core of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia.

principality-of-oettingen-wallerstein.t: The Catholic line of the Ries counts of Oettingen, raised to princes in 1774, whose court at Wallerstein kept a renowned orchestra.
principality-of-oettingen-wallerstein.o: The 1522 division of the house of Oettingen gave the Wallerstein line lands in the southern Ries, with castles at Wallerstein and Harburg. While the Oettingen-Oettingen line became Lutheran, Wallerstein remained Catholic and supported the Counter-Reformation.
principality-of-oettingen-wallerstein.r: The counts, raised to princes in 1774, ruled a farming territory in the Swabian Circle from Wallerstein and Harburg castle. Prince Kraft Ernst maintained one of the finest court orchestras in Germany, employing the composer Antonio Rosetti, and the family built up a famous library rich in medieval manuscripts.
principality-of-oettingen-wallerstein.e: Mediatised in 1806, Oettingen-Wallerstein came under the Kingdom of Bavaria. Prince Ludwig of Oettingen-Wallerstein served as a Bavarian minister in the 1830s and 1840s, and the family still owns Harburg castle.

protectorate-of-peru.t: The provisional government of San Martín in Lima, which declared Peru's independence while royalist armies still held the highlands.
protectorate-of-peru.o: José de San Martín landed his Liberating Expedition, transported from Chile by Lord Cochrane, on the Peruvian coast in 1820. When the viceroy abandoned Lima in July 1821, San Martín entered the city, proclaimed independence on 28 July and on 3 August took the title of Protector of Peru.
protectorate-of-peru.r: San Martín governed with Bernardo de Monteagudo as his chief minister. The Protectorate abolished the Indian tribute and forced labour, declared that children of enslaved mothers would be born free, founded the National Library and created the Order of the Sun. Monteagudo's harsh treatment of Spaniards made him unpopular. Royalist forces still held Cusco and the highlands, and San Martín favoured a constitutional monarchy for Peru.
protectorate-of-peru.e: After his meeting with Bolívar at Guayaquil in July 1822, San Martín resigned before the first Peruvian Congress in September 1822 and left Peru. Power passed to a governing junta of the Republic of Peru.

principality-of-galilee.t: The largest lordship of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, centred on Tiberias, whose siege in 1187 drew the Frankish army to defeat at Hattin.
principality-of-galilee.o: Tancred, the Norman crusader, took Tiberias and the surrounding region soon after the capture of Jerusalem in 1099 and styled himself Prince of Galilee. When he left for Antioch in 1101, Baldwin I gave the fief to Hugh of Saint-Omer.
principality-of-galilee.r: Galilee owed the king a large contingent of knights and had its own vassals, including the Lordship of Toron, whose castle Hugh of Saint-Omer built. Its lords collected revenue from fertile farmland around the Sea of Galilee and faced Damascus across the Jordan. In the 12th century it passed to the Bures family, and through Eschiva of Bures to her husband Raymond III of Tripoli.
principality-of-galilee.e: In July 1187 Saladin besieged Eschiva in Tiberias. The royal army marched to relieve her and was destroyed at Hattin, and Galilee fell to Saladin. The title survived among exiled Frankish nobles, but the principality was never restored.

prince-bishopric-of-trent.t: An Alpine prince-bishopric on the road from Germany to Italy, best known as the host city of the Council of Trent.
prince-bishopric-of-trent.o: Trent was a bishopric from the 4th century. In 1027 Emperor Conrad II granted Bishop Udalrich II the counties of Trento, Bolzano and Vinschgau, to secure the Adige valley route between Germany and Italy. The bishops became princes of the Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-trent.r: The bishops faced their own advocates, the counts of Tyrol, who after 1363 passed to the Habsburgs and dominated the bishopric through treaties. Bishop Frederick Vanga issued an important mining code in 1208. Under Bishop Bernardo Clesio and his successor Cristoforo Madruzzo, the Council of Trent met there between 1545 and 1563, launching the Catholic Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-trent.e: The prince-bishopric was secularised in 1803 and annexed to Austria, passing to Bavaria and the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy before returning to Austria in 1815. After 1918 Trentino became part of Italy, and the see remains as the Archdiocese of Trento.

prince-bishopric-of-basel.t: A prince-bishopric on the upper Rhine whose bishops, driven out of Protestant Basel, ruled the Jura from Porrentruy until 1792.
prince-bishopric-of-basel.o: Basel had been a bishopric since the 7th century. In 999 King Rudolf III of Burgundy gave the bishop the abbey of Moutier-Grandval in the Jura, the basis of later territory. When Burgundy fell to the Empire in 1032, Basel's bishops became imperial princes, later gaining further lands in the Jura and Alsace.
prince-bishopric-of-basel.r: The bishops ruled the city of Basel until its citizens won self-government, and Basel joined the Swiss Confederacy in 1501. The Council of Basel met there from 1431, and the university was founded in 1460. With the Reformation in 1529 the bishop moved to Porrentruy, ruling a mainly French-speaking territory.
prince-bishopric-of-basel.e: French revolutionary troops occupied the territory in 1792, creating the short-lived Rauracian Republic, which France annexed in 1793. The prince-bishopric was formally dissolved in 1803. In 1815 most of its lands were given to Bern, and the Canton of Jura was created from part of them in 1979.

pomesanians.t: Prussian people on the east bank of the lower Vistula, the first to be conquered by the Teutonic Knights in the 1230s.
pomesanians.o: The Pomesanians lived in Pomesania, between the Vistula, the Nogat and the Drwęca, in what is now northern Poland. Like other Prussian groups they emerged as a distinct territory in the Viking Age, with farming villages and hillforts and contacts with Pomerania and Masovia.
pomesanians.r: They were organised in districts led by nobles rather than a single ruler, and kept the Prussian pagan cults. Their nearness to Christian Poland and Pomerania exposed them to missions and raids from the early 13th century.
pomesanians.e: The Teutonic Order, invited by Konrad of Masovia, attacked Pomesania first, founding Kwidzyn (Marienwerder) in 1233 and winning at the Sirgune river in 1234; by 1236 the land was subdued. The Pomesanians joined the Great Prussian Uprising in 1260 but were reconquered, and their land became the Bishopric of Pomesania and Order territory.

potchefstroom-republic.t: The first Boer republic north of the Vaal, founded at Potchefstroom by Andries Potgieter and forerunner of the Transvaal.
potchefstroom-republic.o: After driving the Ndebele north, Voortrekkers led by Andries Hendrik Potgieter founded Potchefstroom in 1838, the first European town north of the Vaal River. A Volksraad was formed and from 1843 the community was linked with Winburg across the river.
potchefstroom-republic.r: The republic was a loose community of cattle farmers governed by a Volksraad and commandants, prone to rivalry between leaders. Potgieter, wary of British reach, moved north to found Andries-Ohrigstad in 1845, while Andries Pretorius gained influence in the west. Labour came partly from captured children, called inboekelinge.
potchefstroom-republic.e: In the Sand River Convention of 1852 Britain recognised the independence of the Boers north of the Vaal, and the communities were gradually merged into the South African Republic.

principality-of-ferghana.t: The early medieval kingdom of the Ferghana valley, a contested prize between Tang China, the Turks and the Arab caliphate.
principality-of-ferghana.o: After the ancient Kingdom of Dayuan, the Ferghana valley was ruled by local dynasties whose kings took the title ikhshid. By the 6th century the principality was within the sphere of the Western Turkic Khaganate, and in the 7th century it was nominally attached to the Tang protectorate system.
principality-of-ferghana.r: Ferghana was a fertile valley of farming towns and pastures, famed for horses. Its rulers alternated between Turkic and local Sogdian-speaking houses, and at times the valley was split between rival kings. Chinese records list embassies to the Tang court, and Arab armies under Qutayba ibn Muslim campaigned there from 713.
principality-of-ferghana.e: Ferghana was contested between the Umayyads, the Turgesh Khaganate and Tang China until after the Battle of Talas. Its ikhshids accepted Abbasid suzerainty, and around 820 the valley passed under the Samanid Empire, ending its independence.

principality-of-pontecorvo.t: A tiny papal enclave in southern Lazio that Napoleon granted to Marshal Bernadotte, the future king of Sweden.
principality-of-pontecorvo.o: Pontecorvo, a small town on the Liri river surrounded by the Kingdom of Naples, belonged to the Papal States. In 1806 Napoleon seized it and made Marshal Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte its sovereign prince.
principality-of-pontecorvo.r: Bernadotte never visited and ruled through local administrators who applied French laws. In 1810 he was elected crown prince of Sweden and gave up the principality, which Napoleon in 1812 granted to Lucien Murat, son of King Joachim Murat of the Kingdom of Naples (1806–1815).
principality-of-pontecorvo.e: After Napoleon's fall, the Congress of Vienna returned Pontecorvo to the Papal States in 1815. Bernadotte became King Charles XIV John of Sweden in 1818.

prince-provostry-of-berchtesgaden.t: An Alpine church principality of Augustinian canons whose salt mine made it a coveted little state between Bavaria and Salzburg.
prince-provostry-of-berchtesgaden.o: Augustinian canons settled at Berchtesgaden early in the 12th century, endowed by the family of the counts of Sulzbach. Frederick Barbarossa granted the provost rights over forests and salt in 1156, and in 1380 King Wenceslaus confirmed the provostry's direct dependence on the empire; from 1559 its provosts were counted among the princes.
prince-provostry-of-berchtesgaden.r: The provost, elected by the canons, ruled a small mountain land enclosed by Salzburg and Bavaria. Its wealth came from salt, mined in the Berchtesgaden salt mine from 1517, which caused long disputes with the Prince-Archbishopric of Salzburg and Bavaria over the trade. Woodcarving became a famous local craft. For long periods Wittelsbach princes held the provostry alongside other sees.
prince-provostry-of-berchtesgaden.e: Secularised in 1803, Berchtesgaden went to the Electorate of Salzburg, then to Austria in 1805 and to the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1810. In the 20th century Hitler's Berghof stood on the Obersalzberg above the town.

principality-of-panjikent.t: A small Sogdian town-state whose excavated houses and murals give the most vivid picture of everyday life on the early medieval Silk Road.
principality-of-panjikent.o: Panjikent, on the Zarafshan River east of Samarkand, was founded in the 5th century and grew into a walled town of merchants and landowners. It was one of several principalities of Sogdiana, often under the influence of the Principality of Samarkand, and within the orbit of the Western Turkic Khaganate.
principality-of-panjikent.r: Excavations since 1946 have revealed a citadel, two temples and streets of two-storey houses whose reception halls were covered in wall paintings of epics, gods and banquets, including scenes from the Rustam cycle. Its ruler Divashtich styled himself king of Sogdiana and ikhshid of Samarkand. Its archive of documents on leather and wood was found at Mount Mugh.
principality-of-panjikent.e: Divashtich resisted the Umayyad advance, was captured at Mount Mugh in 722 and crucified. The town declined and was abandoned in the late 8th century, which preserved its ruins for archaeologists.

principality-of-aschaffenburg.t: Mainz territory on the Main formed into a principality for the archchancellor Dalberg during the Napoleonic reorganisation.
principality-of-aschaffenburg.o: Aschaffenburg had been the second residence of the archbishops of Mainz for centuries, with the large Renaissance Johannisburg palace. When the Electorate of Mainz lost its left-bank lands, the Imperial Recess of 1803 formed its remaining territories on the Main and Spessart into the Principality of Aschaffenburg for Karl Theodor von Dalberg.
principality-of-aschaffenburg.r: Aschaffenburg was the core of the Archchancellor's Electorate and Dalberg's main residence. It was Catholic and rural, with forestry in the Spessart. Dalberg promoted education, founding a school of forestry and maintaining the Mainz university's remnants as a Karlsuniversität in Aschaffenburg.
principality-of-aschaffenburg.e: In 1810 the principality became a department of the Grand Duchy of Frankfurt. After Napoleon's fall it was given to the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1814, to which it still belongs.

principality-of-pereslavl-zalessky.t: An appanage principality on Lake Pleshcheyevo, birthplace of Alexander Nevsky, bequeathed to Moscow by its last prince in 1302.
principality-of-pereslavl-zalessky.o: Yuri Dolgoruky founded Pereslavl-Zalessky, Pereslavl beyond the forests, in 1152 on the shore of Lake Pleshcheyevo, naming it after Pereyaslavl in the south. He began the Transfiguration Cathedral there, one of the oldest white-stone churches in Russia. After the death of Andrei Bogolyubsky it became a separate appanage of the Vladimir-Suzdal lands.
principality-of-pereslavl-zalessky.r: Pereslavl was a fortified town with earthen ramparts that guarded the route from Vladimir to the north. Yaroslav Vsevolodovich held it from 1212, and his son Alexander Nevsky was born there around 1220. Its princes were close kin of the grand princes of Vladimir, and the town played a part in their many succession struggles.
principality-of-pereslavl-zalessky.e: The last prince, Ivan Dmitrievich, a grandson of Alexander Nevsky, died childless in 1302 and left Pereslavl to his uncle Daniel of Moscow. This bequest was an early step in the growth of the Grand Duchy of Moscow. Peter the Great later built his first toy fleet on the lake.

principality-of-iberia.t: The rule of presiding princes over eastern Georgia between the fall of its ancient monarchy and the rise of the Bagratids, a time of Arab conquest and church building.
principality-of-iberia.o: After the Sasanian Empire abolished the Kingdom of Iberia in 580, the Georgian nobility was left without a king. In 588, with Byzantine backing, Guaram I of the Guaramid family was recognised as presiding prince, holding the Byzantine title of kouropalates, and the office passed among leading families for three centuries.
principality-of-iberia.r: The presiding princes, or erismtavari, were first among equals over regional nobles rather than true monarchs, balancing between the Byzantine Empire, Persia and later the caliphate. Stephen I built the Jvari church above Mtskheta, a model for Georgian architecture. Arab armies took Tbilisi in 645, and by 736 the city became the seat of the Emirate of Tbilisi, pushing princely power west and south.
principality-of-iberia.e: The Bagratid prince Ashot I moved the family's base to Tao-Klarjeti in the early 9th century. In 888 his descendant Adarnase IV revived the royal title, creating the Kingdom of the Iberians.

portuguese-morocco.t: Portugal's chain of fortified enclaves on the Moroccan coast, from Ceuta to Mazagan, the first European overseas expansion of the Age of Discovery.
portuguese-morocco.o: The Kingdom of Portugal captured Ceuta from the Marinid Sultanate in 1415, launching its overseas expansion. Afonso V added Ksar es-Seghir in 1458 and Arzila and Tangier in 1471. Under Manuel I the Portuguese built or seized Atlantic posts at Agadir, Safi, Azemmour and Mazagan between 1505 and 1514.
portuguese-morocco.r: The enclaves were garrison towns governed by captains, supplied by sea and living from raids, tribute from nearby tribes and trade in grain, horses and textiles, partly for the Guinea trade. Portuguese kings styled themselves lords of the Algarve beyond the sea in Africa. Life was precarious, with constant warfare against Wattasid and Saadi forces.
portuguese-morocco.e: After the Saadi Sultanate took Agadir in 1541, Portugal abandoned Safi, Azemmour and other posts. King Sebastian's disastrous invasion ended at Alcácer Quibir in 1578. Ceuta passed to Spain after 1640, Tangier went to England in 1661, and Mazagan was evacuated in 1769.

principality-of-khuttal.t: A mountain principality north of the Amu Darya, famed for its horses, whose kings resisted the Arab conquest for decades.
principality-of-khuttal.o: Khuttal lay between the Vakhsh and Panj rivers in what is now southern Tajikistan. It emerged in the 6th and 7th centuries as one of the principalities of Tokharistan under Hephthalite and then Turkic overlordship, ruled by kings with the title Khuttalan-shah, and its capital is identified with Hulbuk.
principality-of-khuttal.r: Khuttal was a land of valleys and mountain pastures known for horses and for its warrior aristocracy. Its rulers bore Turkic or Hephthalite titles and maintained ties with the Yabghus of Tokharistan, the Turgesh Khaganate and Tang China. The king al-Sabal fought the Umayyad governors in the 720s and 730s.
principality-of-khuttal.e: Khuttal accepted Abbasid suzerainty after the mid-8th century, and its local dynasty continued as vassals for a time. It later became a province of the Samanid Empire, and the palace of Hulbuk flourished under its Islamic-era governors.

pechenegs.t: Turkic nomads who dominated the Black Sea steppe for two centuries, killed Sviatoslav of Kiev and were crushed by Byzantium in 1091.
pechenegs.o: The Pechenegs lived between the Volga and the Ural until the Oghuz and Khazars drove them west around 890. Allied with the First Bulgarian Empire, they expelled the Magyars from their lands between the Dnieper and the Danube around 895 and took over the steppe north of the Black Sea.
pechenegs.r: Constantine VII describes eight tribes, each with its own chief, grouped into two wings either side of the Dnieper. Byzantium paid them to hold back the Rus' and the Bulgarians, and they controlled the Dnieper rapids, where in 972 their chief Kurya killed Sviatoslav I and made his skull into a drinking cup.
pechenegs.e: Defeated outside Kiev by Yaroslav the Wise in 1036, and pressed by the Oghuz and Cumans, many Pechenegs moved into the Balkans. In 1091 Alexios I Komnenos and his Cuman allies annihilated them at Levounion, and a final defeat in 1122 ended them as a people. Survivors settled in Hungary and Byzantium.

parisii-britain.t: East Yorkshire people known for the Arras culture of square-barrow and chariot burials, sharing their name with the Parisii of Gaul.
parisii-britain.o: The Parisii are identified with the Arras culture of the Yorkshire Wolds, which from about the 4th century BCE buried its dead under small square barrows, sometimes with dismantled two-wheeled vehicles, as at Wetwang and Garton Slack. The likeness of these burials to rites in northern Gaul, and the shared name with the Parisii of the Seine, has fuelled long debate over migration or contact.
parisii-britain.r: Society was based on mixed farming on the chalk Wolds and in the Vale of Pickering, with large cemeteries of thousands of barrows. Chariot burials of men and women, with harness fittings, mirrors and brooches, point to an elite who displayed status through horses and fine metalwork. No coinage is attributed to them and no rulers are named.
parisii-britain.e: The area came under Roman control during the campaigns of Petillius Cerialis against the Brigantes from 71. Ptolemy later listed Petuaria as their town, and an inscription from Brough-on-Humber records the civitas of the Parisi, which administered the region under Roman Britain.

principality-of-castiglione.t: A small Lombard state of a Gonzaga branch, birthplace of Saint Aloysius Gonzaga, who gave up its succession to become a Jesuit.
principality-of-castiglione.o: Castiglione delle Stiviere, south of Lake Garda, belonged to a cadet branch of the Gonzaga of Mantua. Ferrante Gonzaga, its lord, was made marquis by the emperor in 1579, and the state became a principality under his grandson Francesco in the early 17th century.
principality-of-castiglione.r: The rulers governed a few small towns and farmland as an imperial fief. Ferrante's eldest son Aloysius, born in 1568, renounced his rights to join the Jesuits and died in 1591 nursing plague victims in Rome; he was canonised in 1726 and the town became a pilgrimage centre. His brother Rodolfo was murdered in 1593 by his own subjects. Later princes faced revolts and imperial intervention.
principality-of-castiglione.e: Prince Ferdinando II was deposed after local unrest, and Austrian troops occupied the state in 1691. After long disputes over compensation for the family, the principality was finally incorporated into Austrian Lombardy in 1773.

principality-of-reuss-gera.t: The Younger Line of the house of Reuss in eastern Thuringia, whose princes all bore the name Heinrich, ruling until 1918.
principality-of-reuss-gera.o: The Reuss lords descended from the Vögte (advocates) of Weida, Gera and Plauen, who ruled the Vogtland from the 12th century. In 1564 their lands were divided into Elder, Middle and Younger Lines; the Younger Line, centred on Gera and Schleiz, later absorbed the Middle Line's lands.
principality-of-reuss-gera.r: Every male member of the family was named Heinrich and given a number, a custom said to honour Emperor Henry VI. The Younger Line's lands were repeatedly divided, producing the Principality of Reuss-Schleiz, the Principality of Reuss-Lobenstein and the Principality of Reuss-Ebersdorf. Gera grew into a centre of woollen textiles. The house was Lutheran and gained princely rank in 1806.
principality-of-reuss-gera.e: The branches of the Younger Line were reunited in 1848 as a single principality ruled from Gera, which joined the German Empire in 1871. Its last prince abdicated in 1918, and in 1919 it merged with the Elder Line into the People's State of Reuss, which joined Thuringia in 1920.

principality-of-transylvania.t: Semi-independent Ottoman vassal state in the Carpathians, famed for its religious tolerance and for princes who played the Habsburgs and Ottomans against each other.
principality-of-transylvania.o: The principality grew out of the Eastern Hungarian Kingdom. By the Treaty of Speyer in 1570, John Sigismund Zápolya renounced the Hungarian royal title and became Prince of Transylvania, ruling Transylvania and the Partium, eastern Hungarian counties, under Ottoman suzerainty with his court at Gyulafehérvár.
principality-of-transylvania.r: Princes were elected by a diet of the three privileged nations, the Hungarian nobles, the Saxons and the Székelys, and paid tribute to the sultan. Four religions were received: Catholic, Lutheran, Calvinist and Unitarian, while the Romanian Orthodox majority had no political rights. Stephen Báthory became king of Poland in 1576, and Gabriel Bethlen made Gyulafehérvár a centre of Protestant learning.
principality-of-transylvania.e: George II Rákóczi's disastrous invasion of Poland in 1657 brought Ottoman reprisals. After the Ottoman defeat at Vienna in 1683, Transylvania accepted Habsburg rule through the Leopoldine Diploma of 1691. The failure of Francis II Rákóczi's revolt ended at the Peace of Szatmár in 1711, leading to the Grand Principality of Transylvania.
principality-of-transylvania.re: Calvinist, Catholic, Lutheran and Unitarian Christianity; Orthodox
