principality-of-vitebsk.t: A Dvina trading principality split off from Polotsk, which passed peacefully to Lithuania through the marriage of Algirdas.
principality-of-vitebsk.o: Vitebsk, on the Western Dvina, belonged to the Principality of Polotsk. After the death of Vseslav of Polotsk in 1101, his sons divided his lands, and Vitebsk became the seat of its own line of princes, though the details of its early rulers are poorly recorded.
principality-of-vitebsk.r: The town lived from trade along the Dvina between Riga and the Rus' interior, and its merchants were included in the trade treaty that Smolensk made with Riga and Gotland in 1229. Rule passed among descendants of the Polotsk dynasty and sometimes to princes from Smolensk, while the influence of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania grew through the 13th century.
principality-of-vitebsk.e: Algirdas, son of Gediminas, married Maria, daughter of the last prince Yaroslav, and inherited Vitebsk in 1320. The principality became part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and an important base for Algirdas.

prince-bishopric-of-metz.t: The largest of the Three Bishoprics of Lorraine, an ecclesiastical principality of the Empire ruled from Vic-sur-Seille after Metz itself broke free.
prince-bishopric-of-metz.o: Metz had been a bishopric since Roman times and a Carolingian centre of liturgy and chant. In the late 10th century the Ottonian kings confirmed the bishops' secular lordship over the city and scattered lands in Lorraine, making them princes of the Holy Roman Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-metz.r: The bishops' territory was fragmented and lay largely around the Seille valley, with salt works at Vic and Marsal providing revenue. By the 13th century the citizens of Metz had won independence as the Free Imperial City of Metz, so the bishops ruled from Vic-sur-Seille. They often struggled with the dukes of Lorraine.
prince-bishopric-of-metz.e: In 1552 Henry II of France seized Metz, Toul and Verdun, and the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 confirmed French sovereignty over the Three Bishoprics. The bishopric then became part of the Kingdom of France.

prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg.t: The Alsatian church principality whose bishops lost their cathedral city to its burghers in 1262 but kept a territory on both banks of the Rhine until 1803.
prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg.o: Strasbourg had been a bishopric since late Roman times. In 982 Emperor Otto II granted the bishop extensive rights over the city, and later Ottonian and Salian grants added counties and estates in Alsace and the Ortenau, making the bishops princes of the Holy Roman Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg.r: The bishops began the great Romanesque cathedral under Bishop Werner in 1015. In 1262 the citizens defeated Bishop Walter of Geroldseck at Hausbergen and the city became the Free Imperial City of Strasbourg, so the bishops governed from Saverne. Their lands lay in scattered pieces across lower Alsace and the right bank of the Rhine.
prince-bishopric-of-strasbourg.e: After Louis XIV took Strasbourg in 1681 the left-bank lands came under French sovereignty, and a line of Rohan cardinals held the see. The Revolution abolished the bishops' rights in Alsace, and the right-bank remainder was secularised and given to Baden in 1803.

principality-of-hohenzollern-hechingen.t: The senior Swabian branch of the Hohenzollerns, ruling from Hechingen beneath the dynasty's ancestral castle.
principality-of-hohenzollern-hechingen.o: The 1576 division of the County of Hohenzollern gave the eldest son, Eitel Frederick IV, the ancestral Hohenzollern castle and the town of Hechingen. The counts of Hohenzollern-Hechingen were raised to princes in 1623.
principality-of-hohenzollern-hechingen.r: Eitel Frederick IV built a Renaissance residence in Hechingen and maintained a celebrated court chapel of musicians. The principality was Catholic, small and often in debt, and in the 18th century its princes fought long lawsuits with their peasants before the imperial courts. It joined the Confederation of the Rhine in 1806 and so survived mediatisation.
principality-of-hohenzollern-hechingen.e: After the 1848 revolution the last prince, Frederick William Constantine, abdicated in 1849 in favour of the King of Prussia, and in 1850 Hechingen became part of Prussia. Frederick William IV rebuilt the ancestral castle in neo-Gothic style from 1850 to 1867.

phlius.t: Small inland city of the north-eastern Peloponnese, renowned for its steadfast loyalty to Sparta and its long siege by Agesilaus.
phlius.o: Phlius occupied an upland valley south-west of Corinth, at the head of the Asopus river. Dorian settlers from Argos formed the city in the early Iron Age. It was a small agricultural state known for its wine.
phlius.r: Phlius was usually an oligarchy and a loyal member of the Peloponnesian League. A democratic faction took power in the 380s BCE, and Agesilaus II of Sparta besieged the city from 381 to 379 BCE to restore the exiles. Xenophon praised the Phliasians for their faithfulness to Sparta during Theban invasions in the 360s BCE. The dramatist Pratinas, credited with the satyr play, was a citizen.
phlius.e: Phlius joined the Achaean League in 229 BCE, after its tyrant stepped down, and passed under Roman control in 146 BCE.

palatinate-simmern.t: A Wittelsbach line in the Hunsrück that produced the Calvinist Electors Palatine, beginning with Frederick III in 1559.
palatinate-simmern.o: The 1410 division of King Rupert's lands gave his son Stephen the territories of Simmern and Zweibrücken, to which his marriage added part of the County of Sponheim. In 1453 Stephen's lands were split: Frederick I received Simmern, while Louis took Palatinate-Zweibrücken.
palatinate-simmern.r: The Simmern dukes ruled a hilly territory in the Hunsrück around Simmern together with their share of Sponheim. John II introduced the Reformation. In 1559, when the senior electoral line died out, Duke Frederick III of Simmern became Elector Palatine and made the Palatinate Calvinist, issuing the Heidelberg Catechism in 1563. Simmern itself then passed to a younger branch.
palatinate-simmern.e: Frederick III's descendants, including Frederick V, the Winter King, ruled the Electoral Palatinate until 1685. The junior Simmern branch ended with Duke Richard's death in 1598, and the duchy returned to the electorate, though a later Simmern line was briefly revived in the 17th century.

poseidonia.t: Greek colony on the Gulf of Salerno, later called Paestum, with three of the best-preserved Doric temples anywhere.
poseidonia.o: Colonists from Sybaris founded Poseidonia around 600 BCE on the plain near the mouth of the Sele river, giving Sybaris an outlet on the Tyrrhenian Sea. Named after Poseidon, the city was laid out on a grid and enclosed later by walls nearly 5 km long.
poseidonia.r: Poseidonia prospered from farming and trade with the Etruscans and native peoples. Its three Doric temples, the so-called Basilica of about 550 BCE, the Temple of Athena and the temple of about 460 BCE once called the Temple of Neptune, still stand. The sanctuary of Hera at the mouth of the Sele and the painted Tomb of the Diver of about 470 BCE are famous.
poseidonia.e: Around 410 BCE the Lucanians took over the city, which became Paistom, and Greek and Lucanian customs blended. In 273 BCE Rome founded the Latin colony of Paestum there. Malaria and silting led to its abandonment in the Middle Ages, which helped preserve the temples.

principality-of-bidache.t: A tiny sovereign lordship on the edge of the Basque Country whose Gramont lords claimed independence from France until the Revolution.
principality-of-bidache.o: Bidache, on the Bidouze river between Béarn, Navarre and the Labourd, belonged to the Gramont family. Exploiting its uncertain position on the frontier of Navarre and France, the Gramonts asserted full sovereignty over it, and the register dates the principality from 1570.
principality-of-bidache.r: The Gramonts ruled the small territory from their castle at Bidache, administering justice and taxation without royal interference, while serving the French kings at court and in war. Antoine III de Gramont was a marshal of France and diplomat under Louis XIV. The lands were rural, with Gascon and Basque speakers.
principality-of-bidache.e: The Revolution abolished the Gramonts' privileges, and in 1790 Bidache was incorporated into France and the new department of Basses-Pyrénées. The ruined castle remains.

principality-of-wales-under-owain-glyndw.t: The last attempt at an independent Welsh state, led by Owain Glyndwr, who was proclaimed Prince of Wales in 1400 and held parliaments at Machynlleth.
principality-of-wales-under-owain-glyndw.o: Owain Glyndwr, a descendant of the princes of Powys Fadog and Deheubarth, was proclaimed Prince of Wales by his followers in September 1400 after a land dispute with Lord Grey of Ruthin. His revolt quickly spread across Wales, fed by anger at English rule and taxes.
principality-of-wales-under-owain-glyndw.r: By 1404 Glyndwr held most of Wales, took Harlech and Aberystwyth castles, and summoned parliaments at Machynlleth and Harlech. He allied with France and with English rebels, the Percys and Mortimers, and in the Pennal Letter proposed an independent Welsh church and two universities.
principality-of-wales-under-owain-glyndw.e: From 1405 English forces under Prince Henry recovered ground, retaking Aberystwyth and Harlech by 1409. Glyndwr vanished around 1415. He became a lasting symbol of Welsh national identity.

principality-of-upper-hungary.t: Ottoman-backed realm of the Kuruc rebel Imre Thököly in what is now eastern Slovakia, which collapsed with the Ottoman defeat at Vienna.
principality-of-upper-hungary.o: Imre Thököly, a Lutheran noble, led the Kuruc rebels of northern Hungary against Habsburg persecution of Protestants from 1678. After a string of victories he captured Kassa and much of Upper Hungary, and in 1682 Sultan Mehmed IV recognised him as king of Upper Hungary in return for tribute; Thököly himself used the title of prince.
principality-of-upper-hungary.r: Thököly governed from Kassa through diets of the northern counties, protecting Lutheran and Calvinist worship and paying the Ottomans an annual tribute. His power rested on Kuruc troops of minor nobles, peasants and haiduks. His marriage to Ilona Zrínyi, widow of Francis I Rákóczi, brought him the great Rákóczi estates and the castle of Munkács.
principality-of-upper-hungary.e: Thököly supported the Ottoman siege of Vienna in 1683, and after its failure Habsburg armies retook his towns. In 1685 the Ottomans arrested him and Kassa fell. Ilona Zrínyi held Munkács until 1688. Thököly died in exile in Ottoman Izmit in 1705.

palace-state-of-malia.t: Minoan palace centre on Crete's north coast, one of the island's great Bronze Age palaces and the source of the famous gold bee pendant.
palace-state-of-malia.o: Malia grew from an Early Minoan settlement on a fertile coastal plain east of Knossos. Around 1950 BCE, in the Protopalatial period, a monumental palace was built around a central court, making it one of the earliest palace centres on Crete alongside Knossos and Phaistos. The palace was destroyed c. 1700 BCE, probably by earthquake, and rebuilt on a similar plan.
palace-state-of-malia.r: Its rulers are unknown, as Minoan scripts remain undeciphered, but the palace stored grain, oil and wine in large pithoi and organised craft production. The nearby Quartier Mu workshops produced seals, pottery and metalwork, and the Chrysolakkos burial complex yielded the gold pendant of two bees. Inscriptions in Cretan hieroglyphic and Linear A show an administrative system shared with other palaces.
palace-state-of-malia.e: Like most Cretan palaces, Malia was destroyed by fire c. 1450 BCE, in the wave of destructions that preceded Mycenaean dominance from Knossos. It was not rebuilt as a palace, though limited settlement continued. Excavated by French archaeologists since 1915, it is among the best-preserved Minoan sites.

principality-of-mindelheim.t: Swabian lordship briefly made a principality of the Empire for the Duke of Marlborough as a reward for Blenheim.
principality-of-mindelheim.o: Mindelheim, a Swabian lordship belonging to the Electorate of Bavaria, was confiscated by Emperor Joseph I after the Bavarian elector's defeat at Blenheim in 1704. In 1705 it was granted to John Churchill, Duke of Marlborough, as a principality, making him a prince of the Holy Roman Empire.
principality-of-mindelheim.r: Marlborough never lived there and visited only briefly; the lordship was administered by agents who collected its revenues from the town of Mindelheim and surrounding villages. Its importance was symbolic, giving the English general rank among the German princes. The population remained Catholic under a Protestant absentee prince.
principality-of-mindelheim.e: At the peace of Rastatt and Baden in 1714 the Elector of Bavaria was restored to his lands, and Mindelheim returned to Bavaria. Marlborough kept the title of Prince of Mindelheim, and the episode is remembered in the town's history.

principality-of-liechtenstein.t: Alpine principality between Switzerland and Austria, the only surviving state of the Holy Roman Empire's princely bench.
principality-of-liechtenstein.o: The Liechtenstein family, great landowners in Moravia and Austria, needed land held directly from the emperor to gain a seat in the Imperial Diet. They bought the lordship of Schellenberg in 1699 and the county of Vaduz in 1712, and in 1719 Emperor Charles VI united them as the Principality of Liechtenstein.
principality-of-liechtenstein.r: For a century the princes lived in Vienna and governed through officials. Liechtenstein became sovereign through the Confederation of the Rhine in 1806 and was a member of the German Confederation until 1866. It abolished its army in 1868, adopted the constitution of 1921, and formed a customs union with Switzerland in 1923, using the Swiss franc.
principality-of-liechtenstein.e: Franz Joseph II moved to Vaduz in 1938 and the country stayed neutral in the Second World War. It joined the United Nations in 1990 and the European Economic Area in 1995. A 2003 referendum strengthened the powers of Prince Hans-Adam II.

pale-of-calais.t: England's last foothold in mainland France, a fortified port and wool staple held for two centuries after Edward III's siege of 1346–1347.
pale-of-calais.o: After his victory at Crécy, Edward III besieged Calais for eleven months and took it in 1347; the story of the six burghers who offered their lives is famous. The English expelled much of the population and settled the town with English colonists, adding a surrounding district of marsh and forts, the Pale.
pale-of-calais.r: Calais was garrisoned by the largest standing force of the English crown. From 1363 it hosted the Staple, through which England's raw wool exports passed, and the Merchants of the Staple funded its defence. From 1536 it sent members to the English Parliament. It was a base for English armies in France for two centuries.
pale-of-calais.e: In January 1558, during a war in alliance with Spain, Francis, duke of Guise, captured Calais in a surprise winter attack. Mary I reportedly said that Calais would be found written on her heart. The Pale became part of the Kingdom of France.

peloponnesian-senate.t: Revolutionary governing body of the Peloponnese in the first year of the Greek War of Independence, dominated by the region's notables.
peloponnesian-senate.o: When the Greek revolt broke out in March 1821, Petros Mavromichalis formed the Messenian Senate at Kalamata. In May and June 1821 leading notables and clergy of the Peloponnese met at the monastery of Kaltezes and created the Peloponnesian Senate to direct the war and administer liberated territory, later based at Tripolitsa after its capture.
peloponnesian-senate.r: The senate was controlled by the Peloponnesian primates (kodjabashis), local landowners and tax-farmers who had held power under the Ottomans, with Petrobey Mavromichalis as president. It organised supplies and taxes for the siege of Tripolitsa and quarrelled with Demetrios Ypsilantis, who claimed national leadership, and with military chiefs such as Theodoros Kolokotronis.
peloponnesian-senate.e: The First National Assembly at Epidaurus in January 1822 created a central Provisional Administration, the First Hellenic Republic. The regional senate was subordinated and soon dissolved, though the rivalry between notables and military leaders continued into the civil wars of 1823-1825.

prince-bishopric-of-regensburg.t: Small Danube church state of the bishops of Regensburg, who governed a great Bavarian diocese from a Gothic cathedral but ruled only a little land.
prince-bishopric-of-regensburg.o: Saint Boniface organised the diocese of Regensburg in 739, building on an older bishop's seat in the Roman city. Its bishops were overshadowed in the city by the Bavarian dukes and the abbey of St. Emmeram, but gathered scattered lordships such as Donaustauf, Wörth and Hohenburg, which they ruled as imperial princes from the 13th century.
prince-bishopric-of-regensburg.r: The prince-bishop's secular territory was small and fragmented, while his diocese covered much of eastern Bavaria. The scholar Albertus Magnus served briefly as bishop in 1260 to 1262. The Gothic cathedral of St. Peter was built from 1273 over more than two centuries. The see remained Catholic, while the Free Imperial City of Regensburg around it turned Lutheran, and many bishops came from the Wittelsbach house.
prince-bishopric-of-regensburg.e: In 1803 the prince-bishopric was merged into the Principality of Regensburg under Karl Theodor von Dalberg, which passed to Bavaria in 1810. The diocese continues, and its cathedral choir is world famous.

principality-of-rostov-suzdal.t: The north-eastern principality of Yuri Dolgoruky, founder of Moscow, which laid the foundations of later Russian power.
principality-of-rostov-suzdal.o: The forest lands between the Volga and the Oka, once home to the Finnic Merya, were colonised by Slavs from the 10th century and ruled from Rostov. Vladimir Monomakh gave them to his son Yuri, who around 1125 made Suzdal his seat, turning the region into an independent principality.
principality-of-rostov-suzdal.r: Yuri Dolgoruky, the Long-armed, founded or fortified towns such as Yuryev-Polsky, Pereslavl-Zalessky and Dmitrov, and Moscow is first mentioned in 1147 as the place of a feast he held. Slavic settlers moved here from the troubled south. Its white-stone churches, such as the one at Kideksha, mark the start of a distinct north-eastern architecture.
principality-of-rostov-suzdal.e: Yuri fought for years to win Kiev, finally becoming its grand prince in 1155, and died there in 1157. His son Andrei Bogolyubsky moved the capital to Vladimir, and the land became Vladimir-Suzdal.

principality-of-theodoro.t: An Orthodox Greek principality in the mountains of south-western Crimea, the last remnant of Byzantine rule there until 1475.
principality-of-theodoro.o: The south-western Crimea, known as Gothia after the Goths who settled there in late antiquity, came under a local Greek-speaking dynasty in the 14th century. The fortress of Mangup, called Theodoro, became its capital. Its rulers may have been linked to the Gabras family of Trebizond, though their origins are uncertain.
principality-of-theodoro.r: The principality was a mountain state of Greeks, Goths, Alans and others, living from vineyards, farming and trade. Prince Alexios I fought the Genoese of Genoese Gazaria for the coast and built a port at Kalamita. Theodoro's princes married into the ruling families of Trebizond and Moldavia; Maria of Mangup became the wife of Stephen the Great.
principality-of-theodoro.e: In 1475 the Ottoman Empire, having taken Caffa, besieged Mangup for months. The fortress fell in December 1475 and the princely family was taken to Istanbul and killed. The Ottomans ruled the area directly, and Crimean Gothic, once spoken there, died out.

principality-of-chernigov.t: One of the largest and most powerful principalities of Kievan Rus', ruled by the Olgovichi, rivals of Kiev for the throne.
principality-of-chernigov.o: Chernigov on the Desna, in the old Severian lands, became a princely seat in 1024 when Mstislav of Tmutarakan made it his capital. Under the will of Yaroslav the Wise it passed in 1054 to his son Sviatoslav II, and the Lyubech conference of 1097 confirmed it to Sviatoslav's sons, founding the Olgovichi dynasty.
principality-of-chernigov.r: The principality stretched from the Dnieper to the upper Oka and was divided into appanages such as Novgorod-Seversky and Kursk. Its princes competed for Kiev and often allied with the Cumans. The Transfiguration Cathedral of the 1030s is among the oldest churches in Ukraine, and the Lay of Igor's Campaign celebrates one of its princes.
principality-of-chernigov.e: The Mongols sacked Chernigov in 1239, and Prince Mikhail was executed at Batu's camp in 1246. The land broke into small principalities under Mongol overlordship and in the 14th century passed largely to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

principality-of-stavelot-malmedy.t: Tiny ecclesiastical principality of the Ardennes, ruled for over a thousand years by the abbots of twin monasteries.
principality-of-stavelot-malmedy.o: Around 648 to 651 the missionary Remaclus founded twin abbeys at Stavelot and Malmedy in the Ardennes forest, on land granted by Sigebert III of Austrasia. The two houses shared a single abbot, and the community became one of the leading monasteries of the region.
principality-of-stavelot-malmedy.r: In the Holy Roman Empire the abbots became princes with a seat in the Imperial Diet, ruling a small territory between the Prince-Bishopric of Liège and the Duchy of Luxembourg. Abbot Wibald in the 12th century was an adviser to emperors, and the abbey's workshops produced masterpieces of Mosan goldsmith work such as the Stavelot Triptych.
principality-of-stavelot-malmedy.e: Revolutionary France annexed the principality in 1795 and dissolved the abbeys. In 1815 Stavelot went to the Netherlands, and later Belgium, while Malmedy passed to Prussia. Malmedy was transferred to Belgium in 1920, reuniting the two towns.

principality-of-taron.t: An Armenian principality west of Lake Van, ruled by a branch of the Bagratids, that passed peacefully to Byzantium in the 960s.
principality-of-taron.o: Taron, the plain around Mush, had long been a Mamikonian land. In the early 9th century the Bagratid Bagrat, son of Ashot Msaker, secured it as his share of the family lands, and in 826 his branch became its hereditary princes under the Abbasid Caliphate.
principality-of-taron.r: Taron was a fertile, well-watered district on routes between Armenia and Mesopotamia, and its monastery of Surb Karapet at Glak was among the most revered in Armenia. Its princes balanced between the Arab emirs, the kings of Bagratid Armenia and the Byzantine Empire; Constantine VII describes Prince Grigor visiting Constantinople and receiving a palace and pension.
principality-of-taron.e: Around 966 Grigor's sons Ashot and Grigor surrendered Taron to the Byzantine Empire in return for court titles and estates. It became a Byzantine theme, the first of the Armenian principalities to be annexed.

principality-of-albania-medieval.t: Principality of the Thopia family centred on Durrës, a leading Albanian realm of the late 14th century that ended when Durrës passed to Venice.
principality-of-albania-medieval.o: Karl Thopia, an Albanian noble claiming Angevin descent through his mother, built up lands between the Mat and Shkumbin rivers. In 1368 he took Durrës from the Angevins, ending the Kingdom of Albania (medieval), and styled himself Prince of Albania.
principality-of-albania-medieval.r: Karl ruled from Durrës and the inland town of Elbasan, rivalling Zeta under the Balšići and the Muzaka of Berat. He founded the monastery of Shën Gjon Vladimir near Elbasan. Balša II seized Durrës in 1385, and Karl called in the Ottomans, who killed Balša at Savra; Karl recovered the city soon after.
principality-of-albania-medieval.e: Karl died in 1388. His son Gjergj Thopia, weakened by Ottoman pressure, handed Durrës to Venice in 1392, and he died soon after. The remaining Thopia lands later fell under Ottoman control.

patrae.t: Achaean city at the mouth of the Gulf of Corinth, a founder of the Achaean League and forerunner of modern Patras.
patrae.o: Patrae was formed, according to Pausanias, by uniting the villages of Aroe, Antheia and Mesatis on the coast of western Achaea. It was one of the twelve Achaean cities and controlled the narrows at the entrance to the Gulf of Corinth.
patrae.r: Patrae was a modest farming and trading town in the Classical period. In 280 BCE it joined Dyme, Tritaea and Pharae in reviving the Achaean League. In 279 BCE the Patraeans were the only Achaeans to send troops against the invading Gauls, suffering heavy losses. The city had a sanctuary of Artemis Laphria.
patrae.e: Patrae passed under Rome in 146 BCE. Augustus made it a Roman colony c. 14 BCE, and it became the chief port of the region, growing into the modern city of Patras.
patrae.re: Greek religion; cult of Artemis Laphria

prince-bishopric-of-havelberg.t: A bishopric founded by Otto I among the Slavs of the Havel, lost in the revolt of 983 and refounded as a small territory that Brandenburg absorbed.
prince-bishopric-of-havelberg.o: Otto I founded the bishopric of Havelberg in 946 or 948 at a stronghold on the Havel, to convert the Slavs of the Northern March. It became a suffragan of the Archbishopric of Magdeburg in 968. The Great Slav Rising of 983 destroyed it, and its bishops lived in exile for more than a century.
prince-bishopric-of-havelberg.r: After the Wendish Crusade of 1147, Bishop Anselm of Havelberg, a noted theologian and diplomat to Byzantium, restored the see, and the cathedral was consecrated in 1170. The bishops ruled a small territory around Havelberg and Wittstock, where they built their residence, but depended on the margraves of Brandenburg.
prince-bishopric-of-havelberg.e: With the Reformation in Brandenburg, the last Catholic bishop died in 1548, and the Hohenzollern electors installed their own family as administrators. The territory was absorbed into the Margraviate of Brandenburg by 1598. The cathedral on the hill at Havelberg survives.

picentes.t: Italic people of the central Adriatic coast, said to have followed a woodpecker to their new land, whose warrior culture lasted until Rome conquered them in 268 BCE.
picentes.o: The Picentes lived in Picenum, the coastal strip and hills of the modern Marche and northern Abruzzo, from the early 1st millennium BCE. Roman tradition said they descended from Sabines who left home in a 'sacred spring' migration, guided by a woodpecker (picus), the bird of Mars. Archaeologists call their culture the Picene culture.
picentes.r: Picene society was dominated by warrior elites buried with helmets, weapons, chariots and amber from the Baltic. Their South Picene inscriptions, in a Sabellic language written in a distinctive alphabet, appear on stone stelae, and the Novilara stele in the north bears a still undeciphered text. Asculum was their main centre, and they traded across the Adriatic and with Etruria.
picentes.e: The Picentes allied with Rome in 299 BCE but revolted in 269 BCE and were conquered in 268 BCE; part of the population was moved to the Gulf of Salerno. Asculum became an allied city, and its massacre of Romans in 91 BCE began the Social War. Picenum became part of Augustus's Regio V.

principality-of-valona.t: Albanian coastal lordship around Vlorë and Kanina, founded by a governor of the Serbian Empire and lost to the Ottomans in 1417.
principality-of-valona.o: Stefan Dušan of the Serbian Empire took Valona (Vlorë) and Kanina from Byzantium around 1345. His brother-in-law John Komnenos Asen governed them, and after Dušan's death in 1355 ruled as an independent despot.
principality-of-valona.r: Its rulers held the port of Valona, the fortress of Kanina and nearby lands, trading with Venice and Ragusa and taxing traffic across the Strait of Otranto. After John's son Alexander, the city passed to Balša II of Zeta under the Balšići around 1372, and then through his widow Komita to her son-in-law Merksha Žarković and, after his death in 1414, to his widow Ruđina.
principality-of-valona.e: Ruđina had ruled only briefly when the Ottomans captured Valona and Kanina in 1417. Valona became an Ottoman port and centre of the Sanjak of Avlonya.

principality-of-brandenburg-ansbach.t: The Hohenzollern margraviate around Ansbach in Franconia, an early Lutheran state that was sold to Prussia by its last margrave in 1791.
principality-of-brandenburg-ansbach.o: The 1398 division of the lands of the Burgraviate of Nuremberg gave Frederick VI, later the first Hohenzollern elector of Brandenburg, the territory 'below the mountains' around Ansbach. From the 15th century it was usually ruled by a younger Hohenzollern son as margrave.
principality-of-brandenburg-ansbach.r: Margrave Albert Achilles, who also became elector, made Ansbach a centre of Hohenzollern power, and George the Pious introduced Lutheranism in 1528. The principality was rich in farmland and governed through a strong bureaucracy. Ansbach's Baroque residence was built in the 18th century, and the margraves hired out soldiers to Britain for the American War of Independence.
principality-of-brandenburg-ansbach.e: The last margrave, Charles Alexander, inherited the Principality of Brandenburg-Bayreuth in 1769 and in 1791 handed both principalities to his Prussian cousins before retiring to England. Prussia ceded Ansbach to the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806.

principality-of-bukhara.t: The Sogdian city-state ruled by the Bukhar Khudahs, whose queen-regent Khatun faced the Arab conquest of Transoxiana.
principality-of-bukhara.o: Bukhara, in the Zarafshan delta west of Samarkand, was ruled from the 6th or 7th century by a dynasty bearing the title Bukhar Khudah, lord of Bukhara. Tradition, recorded by Narshakhi, links its foundation to settlers and princes from the Hephthalite and Turkic period.
principality-of-bukhara.r: The Bukhar Khudahs ruled from the citadel of Bukhara over an oasis of farms and walled estates. Their silver coins, imitating the Sasanian king Bahram V, circulated widely as 'Bukhar Khudah drachms' for centuries. The regent known as Khatun ruled in the late 7th century during the Arab raids, alternately paying tribute and fighting.
principality-of-bukhara.e: Qutayba ibn Muslim captured Bukhara in 709 and installed the young Tughshada as a vassal Bukhar Khudah, building the first mosque. The dynasty kept a ceremonial role until its last members were killed around 782, and Bukhara later became the capital of the Samanid Empire.

principality-of-khachen.t: An Armenian principality in the highlands of Karabakh that survived Arab, Seljuk and Mongol overlords for nearly eight centuries and built the monastery of Gandzasar.
principality-of-khachen.o: Khachen emerged in the 9th century in the mountains of Artsakh, in the former lands of the Mihranid Principality of Albania. Its early prince Sahl Smbatean became famous for capturing the rebel leader Babak in 837 and handing him to the Abbasids. The principality took its name from the fortress of Khachen.
principality-of-khachen.r: Princes ruled from mountain fortresses such as Khokhanaberd over Armenian villages, vineyards and monasteries. The greatest, Hasan-Jalal Dawla, prince from 1214, built the monastery of Gandzasar, seat of the Catholicos of Aghvank. Khachen served as a vassal of Zakarid Armenia, the Mongols and the Ilkhanate, keeping local autonomy through skilful diplomacy and dynastic marriages.
principality-of-khachen.e: After Hasan-Jalal's execution by the Mongols in 1261, Khachen fragmented among branches of his house. Under the Safavid Empire in the early 17th century its lands were reorganised into the Melikdoms of Karabakh, ruled by descendants of the Hasan-Jalalyan family.

prince-bishopric-of-halberstadt.t: Church principality in the northern Harz foreland, founded under Charlemagne and secularised to Brandenburg at the Peace of Westphalia.
prince-bishopric-of-halberstadt.o: The diocese of Halberstadt was founded about 804 under Charlemagne to christianise the eastern Saxons. Its bishops gathered counties and estates in the Harz foreland. After the fall of Henry the Lion in 1180 freed them from his ducal power, they ruled a consolidated territory as imperial princes.
prince-bishopric-of-halberstadt.r: The cathedral chapter elected the bishop, who ruled from Halberstadt and towns such as Gröningen. Its Gothic cathedral and treasury are among the richest in Germany. From the 16th century the see was held by princes of the houses of Brandenburg and Brunswick, including Albert of Brandenburg and Henry Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, and the territory became Lutheran. In the Thirty Years War its administrator, Christian of Brunswick, fought for the Protestant side.
prince-bishopric-of-halberstadt.e: At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 the see was secularised and given to Brandenburg as the Principality of Halberstadt. It remained Prussian, apart from the Kingdom of Westphalia interlude, and is now in Saxony-Anhalt.

principality-of-beloozero.t: A northern principality on the White Lake, gateway to the fur trade, whose last princes died at Kulikovo before Moscow took it over.
principality-of-beloozero.o: Beloozero, the White Lake, is mentioned in the Primary Chronicle under 862 as the seat of Rurik's brother Sineus, in the land of the Finnic Ves. Part of the Rostov lands, it became a separate appanage in 1238 for Gleb Vasilkovich, son of the Rostov prince killed by the Mongols.
principality-of-beloozero.r: The principality was a remote, thinly settled land of forests and lakes on the routes to the north, where furs, fish and salt were gathered. Its princes depended on Rostov, the grand princes of Vladimir and the Golden Horde. Prince Fyodor Romanovich and his son were killed fighting for Dmitry Donskoy at Kulikovo in 1380.
principality-of-beloozero.e: After their deaths Moscow took control, and in his will of 1389 Dmitry Donskoy left Beloozero to his son Andrei. In 1397 the monk Kirill founded the Kirillo-Belozersky Monastery nearby, which became one of Russia's richest monasteries.

principality-of-nassau-hadamar.t: Small Nassau principality in the Westerwald that became a Catholic outpost of the house and left a baroque residence town.
principality-of-nassau-hadamar.o: Hadamar was created in the 1607 division of the lands of John VI of Nassau-Dillenburg and went to his son John Louis. John Louis converted to Catholicism in 1629 and served the emperor as a diplomat at the Peace of Westphalia, for which he was made a prince of the Empire in 1650.
principality-of-nassau-hadamar.r: After its ruler's conversion Hadamar became a Catholic enclave among Protestant Nassau lands, with a Jesuit college and Franciscan friars. John Louis rebuilt Hadamar as a planned residence town with a new palace. The economy was agrarian, with small-scale iron and wool working in the Westerwald hills.
principality-of-nassau-hadamar.e: The line died out with Prince Francis Alexander in 1711, and the territory was divided among the other Nassau-Ottonian lines, Nassau-Diez, Nassau-Siegen and Nassau-Dillenburg. Its lands later passed to the Duchy of Nassau and, in 1866, to Prussia.

prince-bishopric-of-ratzeburg.t: Small Lauenburg church state founded by Henry the Lion among the Polabian Slavs, secularised to Mecklenburg in 1648.
prince-bishopric-of-ratzeburg.o: Henry the Lion founded the bishopric of Ratzeburg in 1154 during the conquest and conversion of the Slavic Polabians, with Evermod as its first bishop. The bishops built the Romanesque brick cathedral on the island of Ratzeburg and acquired lands east of the lake. After Henry's fall they ruled these lands as an imperial principality.
prince-bishopric-of-ratzeburg.r: The territory, centred on Schönberg, was small and rural, settled by German farmers among the earlier Slavic population. The bishops were overshadowed by the dukes of Saxe-Lauenburg, who held Ratzeburg town, and by the dukes of Mecklenburg. In the 16th century the cathedral chapter turned Lutheran, and Mecklenburg princes held the see as administrators.
prince-bishopric-of-ratzeburg.e: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 secularised the see as the Principality of Ratzeburg and gave it to the Duchy of Mecklenburg. From 1701 it belonged to the Duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz and is now part of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

palmyrene-empire.t: The breakaway realm of the caravan city of Palmyra, which under Queen Zenobia briefly ruled Rome's East from Egypt to Anatolia.
palmyrene-empire.o: After the Persian king Shapur I captured the emperor Valerian in 260, the Palmyrene noble Odaenathus defeated the retreating Persians and crushed the usurpers in the East, earning from Gallienus the title corrector of the whole East. His murder in 267 left power to his widow Zenobia, regent for their young son Vaballathus.
palmyrene-empire.r: Palmyra had grown rich on caravan trade linking the Euphrates and the Gulf with the Mediterranean, and its elite blended Aramaic, Arab, Greek and Roman culture, worshipping Bel and other Semitic gods. Zenobia kept a learned court that included the rhetorician Longinus. In 270 her armies took Egypt and much of Anatolia, and in 272 Vaballathus was proclaimed Augustus, an open break with Rome.
palmyrene-empire.e: The emperor Aurelian defeated Zenobia's armies at Immae and Emesa in 272, besieged Palmyra and captured her as she fled towards Persia. When the city rebelled again in 273 it was sacked and never recovered its wealth. Zenobia was taken to Rome.

peoples-socialist-republic-of-albania.t: Enver Hoxha's communist Albania, the most isolated state in Europe, which broke in turn with Yugoslavia, the Soviet Union and China and banned all religion.
peoples-socialist-republic-of-albania.o: Enver Hoxha's Communist-led Partisans took power as German forces withdrew in November 1944 from the Albanian Kingdom (1943-1944). After elections with a single list in December 1945, the monarchy was formally abolished and the People's Republic of Albania proclaimed on 11 January 1946, with Hoxha as leader. Opponents were tried, executed or imprisoned.
peoples-socialist-republic-of-albania.r: The regime was strictly Stalinist: land was collectivised, industry nationalised and the Sigurimi secret police watched everyone. Hoxha broke with Yugoslavia in 1948, the Soviet Union in 1961 and China in 1978, leaving Albania almost alone. In 1967 it declared itself the world's first atheist state, closing all mosques and churches, and built hundreds of thousands of concrete bunkers. It was renamed the People's Socialist Republic in 1976.
peoples-socialist-republic-of-albania.e: After Hoxha died in 1985, Ramiz Alia allowed cautious change. Student protests and mass flight abroad in 1990 forced the legalisation of opposition parties, and after the first multi-party elections the country was renamed the Republic of Albania in April 1991.

powys-fadog.t: The northern half of the Welsh kingdom of Powys, ruled by Madog ap Maredudd's descendants from Castell Dinas Bran above Llangollen.
powys-fadog.o: When Madog ap Maredudd, the last king of all Powys, died in 1160, his kingdom split. The northern part passed to his grandson Madog ap Gruffydd Maelor, after whom it was named Powys Fadog, covering Maelor, Ial, Edeirnion and Cynllaith.
powys-fadog.r: Its princes usually aligned with Gwynedd's Principality of Wales against the English crown. Madog ap Gruffydd founded the Cistercian abbey of Valle Crucis around 1201, and Gruffydd ap Madog built Castell Dinas Bran around 1260.
powys-fadog.e: Powys Fadog's princes backed Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in his final war, and after his death in 1282 Edward I granted the lands to English lords. Its line survived as minor gentry; Owain Glyndwr, who led the Principality of Wales under Owain Glyndwr, descended from it.

principality-of-rugen.t: Slavic principality on the Baltic island of Rügen whose princes, once pagan Rani, became Danish vassals and founders of Stralsund before dying out in 1325.
principality-of-rugen.o: The Slavic Rani ruled Rügen from the temple fortress of Arkona, sanctuary of the god Svantevit. In 1168 King Valdemar I of Denmark and Bishop Absalon stormed Arkona, destroyed the idol and forced the Rani to accept Christianity and Danish overlordship. The native princely house kept its rule as Danish vassals, with Jaromar I as its first Christian prince.
principality-of-rugen.r: The princes held the island and a strip of the Pomeranian mainland, where Wizlaw I granted Stralsund town rights in 1234. They founded monasteries such as Bergen and Eldena and invited German settlers, so Low German gradually replaced the Slavic speech of the Rani. The court combined Danish loyalty with growing ties to the German north, and Wizlaw III composed love songs as a minnesinger.
principality-of-rugen.e: Wizlaw III died without a son in 1325, and the principality passed by inheritance treaty to the Duchy of Pomerania-Wolgast after a war of succession against Mecklenburg. Rügen stayed Pomeranian, then Swedish and Prussian, and is now part of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.

principality-of-furstenberg.t: Black Forest state of the Fürstenberg family, heirs of the Zähringen, whose court at Donaueschingen stood beside the source of the Danube.
principality-of-furstenberg.o: When the Zähringen line died out in 1218, the counts of Urach inherited part of their lands in the Baar and the Black Forest. Count Henry took the name Fürstenberg, after a castle near Donaueschingen, around 1250, founding a comital house that ruled the upper Danube and Kinzig valleys.
principality-of-furstenberg.r: The family split into several lines, and its counts served the Habsburgs as officers and diplomats. Branches were raised to princely rank in 1664 and 1716, and in 1744 the lands were reunited under Joseph Wilhelm Ernst, with Donaueschingen as residence. The territory produced timber, iron and beer, and the court library acquired manuscript C of the Nibelungenlied. It stayed Catholic.
principality-of-furstenberg.e: In 1806 Fürstenberg was mediatised and divided mainly between Baden, Württemberg and Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. The princely family kept its estates, brewery and palace at Donaueschingen, where the park spring is still presented as the source of the Danube.

pictones.t: Gallic people of Poitou who built ships for Caesar against the Veneti and gave their name to Poitiers and Poitou.
pictones.o: The Pictones held the land south of the lower Loire, around Lemonum (Poitiers), with a coastline on the Atlantic. They were among the larger peoples of western Gaul.
pictones.r: Caesar used their shipyards in 56 BCE for the fleet that defeated the Veneti. Their leader Duratius remained loyal to Rome, which split the people during the revolts.
pictones.e: In 51 BCE Duratius was besieged in Lemonum by Dumnacus of the Andecavi until Roman forces relieved him. Under Rome Lemonum, later called Pictavi, became Poitiers, a major city and bishopric, and the region kept the name Poitou.

purushanda.t: Purushanda, an Anatolian city whose ruler bore the title great king in the age of the Assyrian merchants, later humbled by Anitta of Kussara.
purushanda.o: Burushattum appears in Old Assyrian trade letters of the 20th and 19th centuries BCE as a wealthy city in south-central Anatolia, probably at Acemhöyük near Aksaray, though the identification is debated. Assyrian merchants bought silver and wool there and kept a trading house.
purushanda.r: Its ruler was the only Anatolian king the merchants called great king, suggesting overlordship over neighbouring cities. Later Mesopotamian legend made it the target of a campaign by Sargon of the Akkadian Empire to protect merchants, a story told in the text known as the King of Battle.
purushanda.e: In the 18th century BCE the king of Purushanda submitted to Anitta of Kussara, offering him an iron throne and iron sceptre. The city then lost its independence and fades from the record by c. 1700 BCE.

principality-of-arbanon.t: The first Albanian state, a principality around Krujë ruled by the Progon family under Byzantine, Serbian and Epirote overlords.
principality-of-arbanon.o: Arbanon, in the mountains around Krujë in central Albania, gained autonomy in the late 12th century as Byzantine power declined. Its first known ruler was the archon Progon, around 1190, followed by his sons Gjin and Dhimitër.
principality-of-arbanon.r: The archons ruled a Catholic and Orthodox Albanian population from Krujë, balancing Byzantium, Serbia, Venice and the papacy. Dhimitër Progoni, who styled himself panhypersebastos, married Komnena, daughter of the Serbian ruler Stefan the First-Crowned, and corresponded with Pope Innocent III. After his death around 1215, the Greek lord Gregory Kamonas and then Golem ruled.
principality-of-arbanon.e: From the 1230s Arbanon fell under the Despotate of Epirus and then the Empire of Nicaea, which took over Krujë around 1255. The area later formed part of the Kingdom of Albania (medieval).

principality-of-turov-and-pinsk.t: A principality of the Pripyat marshes in southern Belarus, known for the preacher Cyril of Turov.
principality-of-turov-and-pinsk.o: Turov on the Pripyat had been an early seat of Rus' princes, ruled by Sviatopolk, son of Vladimir I, in the late 10th century. It was long attached to Kiev, but in the late 1150s Yuri Yaroslavich, a grandson of Sviatopolk II, made it independent, founding a local dynasty.
principality-of-turov-and-pinsk.r: The principality covered the wet, wooded lands of the Dregovichs and lived from farming, fishing and river trade. Its bishop Cyril of Turov, who died around 1182, was one of the finest preachers and writers of early Rus'. Over time it split into smaller appanages based on Turov, Pinsk and other towns, and its princes became minor players.
principality-of-turov-and-pinsk.e: After the Mongol invasion its lands weakened further, and in the early 14th century they were absorbed by the Grand Duchy of Lithuania under Gediminas. Pinsk later became a Lithuanian appanage duchy.

principality-of-arches-charleville.t: A sovereign principality on the Meuse where Charles of Gonzaga founded the planned city of Charleville in 1606.
principality-of-arches-charleville.o: Charles of Gonzaga, duke of Nevers and Rethel, held the land of Arches on the Meuse, which claimed to lie outside both France and the Empire. In 1606 he founded a new town there, Charleville, named after himself, and ruled it as a sovereign principality.
principality-of-arches-charleville.r: Charleville was laid out on a regular plan around the Place Ducale, modelled on the Place des Vosges in Paris. The principality minted its own coins and attracted craftsmen with tax exemptions. Charles later became duke of Mantua in 1627, and his Gonzaga heirs ruled the principality from Italy.
principality-of-arches-charleville.e: The last Gonzaga duke, Ferdinando Carlo, died in 1708 after siding with France in the War of the Spanish Succession. Louis XIV then took the principality into the Kingdom of France, though the Condé family claimed it.

portuguese-congo.t: The Portuguese protectorate of Cabinda, an enclave north of the Congo River whose oil and separatism shape Angolan politics.
portuguese-congo.o: Portugal had traded on the Loango coast for centuries. To secure its claim against France and Leopold II, it signed the Treaty of Simulambuco with the princes and chiefs of Cabinda on 1 February 1885, establishing a protectorate over territory once ruled by the Kingdom of Ngoyo and the Kingdom of Kakongo.
portuguese-congo.r: The Berlin Conference left Cabinda separated from Portuguese Angola by a strip of land given to the Congo Free State. It was governed from Cabinda town, at first separately and from the 1920s increasingly as a district of Angola. Timber, cocoa and coffee were exported, and from the 1960s offshore oil discovered by Cabinda Gulf Oil became the enclave's main resource.
portuguese-congo.e: Separatists of the Front for the Liberation of the Enclave of Cabinda claimed independence, but the 1975 Alvor Agreement made Cabinda part of independent Angola, where it remains a province with a low-level separatist conflict.

prince-bishopric-of-brandenburg.t: An Ottonian missionary bishopric on the Havel that, after a long exile, became a small church territory absorbed by the Hohenzollern electors.
prince-bishopric-of-brandenburg.o: Otto I founded the bishopric of Brandenburg in 948 at the captured Hevelli stronghold of Brenna, as part of his eastern mission, placing it under Magdeburg in 968. In the Great Slav Rising of 983 the Slavs destroyed the see, and its bishops lived as titular exiles until the 12th century.
prince-bishopric-of-brandenburg.r: After Albert the Bear took Brandenburg in 1157, the Premonstratensian cathedral chapter was re-established, and the cathedral on the island in Brandenburg an der Havel was begun in 1165. The bishops held a small territory around Ziesar, where they built their residence, but the margraves dominated them and claimed the right to nominate bishops.
prince-bishopric-of-brandenburg.e: Brandenburg became Lutheran under Elector Joachim II from 1539, and the last Catholic bishop, Matthias von Jagow, accepted the change. The prince-bishopric was secularised and fully incorporated into the Margraviate of Brandenburg by 1571. The cathedral chapter continued as a Protestant institution.

principality-of-piombino.t: A small Tuscan coastal state with the iron mines of Elba, ruled by the Appiani and later the Ludovisi and Boncompagni.
principality-of-piombino.o: In 1399 Gherardo Appiani, lord of Pisa, sold the city to Gian Galeazzo Visconti but kept Piombino, Elba and nearby islands as his own lordship. His family ruled it as lords and, from 1594, as imperial princes.
principality-of-piombino.r: Piombino controlled the iron mines of Elba and the channel between Elba and the mainland, a strategic route for Mediterranean shipping. Its small size made it dependent on stronger powers: Cosimo I de' Medici built Portoferraio on Elba in 1548, and Spain later held Porto Longone. After the Appiani died out, the principality passed to the Ludovisi in 1634 and then to the Boncompagni-Ludovisi.
principality-of-piombino.e: In 1805 Napoleon gave Piombino to his sister Elisa, merging it into the Principality of Lucca and Piombino. In 1815 the Congress of Vienna gave it to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany.

potidaea.t: Corinthian colony on the isthmus of Pallene in Chalcidice whose revolt against Athens in 432 BCE helped trigger the Peloponnesian War.
potidaea.o: Potidaea was founded around 600 BCE by Corinth under the tyrant Periander, whose son Evagoras is named as founder. It stood on the narrow neck of the Pallene peninsula, controlling the way into it, and remained unusually close to its mother city, which still sent it annual magistrates in the 5th century BCE.
potidaea.r: A walled port city with an assembly and magistrates, Potidaea lived from trade in the northern Aegean, Macedonian timber and the produce of Pallene. It held out against the Persian commander Artabazus in 480-479 BCE and fought at Plataea. As a tribute-paying member of the Delian League it was caught between loyalty to Athens and its Corinthian ties.
potidaea.e: Ordered by Athens to pull down its walls and expel the Corinthian magistrates, Potidaea revolted in 432 BCE and surrendered after a costly siege in 430 BCE; Athenian settlers replaced its people. It later joined the Chalcidian League, was retaken by Athens in 364 BCE and was captured by Philip II in 356 BCE. Cassander refounded it as Cassandreia.

principality-of-novgorod-seversky.t: A frontier principality of the Chernigov lands, home of Prince Igor, whose failed campaign against the Cumans inspired a great epic.
principality-of-novgorod-seversky.o: Novgorod-Seversky on the Desna was an old Severian town. At the Lyubech conference of 1097 it was assigned to the sons of Sviatoslav II of Chernigov, and it became the seat of a junior branch of the Olgovichi, second only to Chernigov itself in their lands.
principality-of-novgorod-seversky.r: Its princes held a frontier zone exposed to the steppe and fought the Cumans as often as they allied with them. In 1185 Prince Igor Sviatoslavich led a raid against the Cumans that ended in his defeat and capture, the subject of the Lay of Igor's Campaign. Later princes included Dmitry Koribut, a son of Algirdas.
principality-of-novgorod-seversky.e: After the Mongol invasion the land passed to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the 14th century. In 1500 Vasily Shemyachich transferred his allegiance to the Grand Duchy of Moscow, which kept the territory by the truce of 1503. Vasily III arrested Shemyachich in 1523 and abolished the principality.

prince-bishopric-of-augsburg.t: Swabian church state of the bishops of Augsburg, who were forced out of their own cathedral city and governed instead from Dillingen on the Danube.
prince-bishopric-of-augsburg.o: The diocese of Augsburg dates from late Roman times and was led in the 10th century by Saint Ulrich, who defended the city at the Lechfeld in 955. From the late 12th century the bishops assembled a secular territory along the Lech and Danube. As the city itself won independence as the Free Imperial City of Augsburg, they moved their residence to Dillingen.
prince-bishopric-of-augsburg.r: The cathedral chapter elected the prince-bishop, who ruled scattered lands including Dillingen, Füssen and parts of the Allgäu. Cardinal Otto Truchsess von Waldburg founded the University of Dillingen in 1551, run by the Jesuits from 1563, which made the territory a Counter-Reformation stronghold. Its estates were rural, with farms, forests and small market towns.
prince-bishopric-of-augsburg.e: The territory was secularised in 1802 and annexed by the Electorate of Bavaria, ending the bishops' secular rule; the last prince-bishop, Clemens Wenceslaus of Saxony, was also Elector of Trier. The Catholic diocese of Augsburg continues today.

principality-of-thessaly.t: Greek principality in Thessaly ruled by an offshoot of the Epirote dynasty, independent of Byzantium until the Catalans and Byzantines divided it.
principality-of-thessaly.o: On the death of Michael II of the Despotate of Epirus around 1268, his illegitimate son John I Doukas received Thessaly, with its capital at Neopatras. Byzantine writers called the region Great Vlachia, after its many Vlach inhabitants. John resisted Michael VIII Palaiologos, defeating a Byzantine army at Neopatras around 1275.
principality-of-thessaly.r: John I held the Byzantine title of sebastokrator and ruled a mixed Greek and Vlach population of farmers and herders through local magnates. He allied with the Latin Duchy of Athens and the Principality of Achaea against the restored Byzantine Empire. His sons Constantine and John II continued his policies, John II marrying a daughter of Andronikos II.
principality-of-thessaly.e: When John II died without heirs in 1318, Thessaly broke apart. The Catalan Company, ruling the Duchy of Athens, seized the south and created the Duchy of Neopatras, while local lords and the Byzantines took the north.

principality-of-abasgia.t: A Byzantine-aligned principality on the Black Sea coast of Abkhazia that grew into the Kingdom of Abkhazia in the late 8th century.
principality-of-abasgia.o: The Abasgoi lived on the coast north-west of Lazica. In the mid-6th century the Byzantine Empire under Justinian I extended control over them, ended a local practice of selling eunuchs to Constantinople, and sponsored their conversion to Christianity, with a church built for them.
principality-of-abasgia.r: Local princes, called archons by the Greeks, ruled as Byzantine clients from the hill fortress of Anacopia, near New Athos. The economy rested on farming, livestock and coastal trade. Anacopia withstood an Arab siege in 737, and the victory brought Leon I recognition as hereditary ruler from Byzantium.
principality-of-abasgia.e: His nephew Leon II, whose mother was a Khazar princess, used Khazar support around 778 to throw off Byzantine authority, unite Abasgia with Egrisi and take the title king, founding the Kingdom of Abkhazia.

principality-of-taranto.t: A great southern Italian fief created for the crusader Bohemond, later held by princes so powerful they rivalled the kings of Naples.
principality-of-taranto.o: After Robert Guiscard's death the Norman inheritance was divided, and in 1088 his eldest son Bohemond received Taranto and much of the heel of Italy as compensation for losing the Duchy of Apulia and Calabria to his half-brother Roger Borsa. Bohemond soon left on the First Crusade and founded the Principality of Antioch.
principality-of-taranto.r: Taranto became a fief within the Kingdom of Sicily and then the Kingdom of Naples, often granted to royal relatives, such as the Angevin Philip I of Taranto from 1294. Its princes controlled the ports and olive and grain lands of Apulia and could field large armies. Under the Orsini del Balzo in the 15th century it covered much of southern Apulia.
principality-of-taranto.e: Prince Giovanni Antonio Orsini del Balzo, who rebelled against King Ferrante, died in 1463 without legitimate heirs. Ferrante seized his lands, and the principality was absorbed into the royal domain of the Kingdom of Naples.

principality-of-anhalt.t: Ascanian principality between the Harz and the Elbe that adopted the Reformation early and was repeatedly divided among branches of its ruling house.
principality-of-anhalt.o: Henry I, son of Duke Bernhard of Saxony of the Ascanian house, received the family's ancestral lands around the Harz and middle Elbe when his father's possessions were divided in 1212. He took the title Count, then Prince, of Anhalt, after the castle of that name near Harzgerode, founding a principality separate from Saxony.
principality-of-anhalt.r: Anhalt was repeatedly split among branches, such as Aschersleben, Bernburg, Köthen and Zerbst, each ruling small towns and farmland along the Elbe and Saale. Prince Wolfgang of Anhalt-Köthen signed the Augsburg Confession in 1530, making Anhalt an early Lutheran land, and it later turned Reformed. Joachim Ernst reunited the territories in 1570 and issued a common law code.
principality-of-anhalt.e: After Joachim Ernst's death, his sons divided Anhalt in 1603 into Anhalt-Dessau, Anhalt-Bernburg, Anhalt-Köthen, Anhalt-Zerbst and Anhalt-Plötzkau. These lines were reunited as the Duchy of Anhalt in 1863, which became a free state in 1918 and is now part of Saxony-Anhalt.
principality-of-anhalt.re: Catholicism, then Lutheranism and Reformed Protestantism

persarmenia.t: The Persian-ruled part of Armenia after the end of its monarchy, where Armenians fought to keep their Christian faith and their church took its independent path.
persarmenia.o: When the Kingdom of Armenia (Arsacid) was abolished in 428, the larger eastern part of the country, assigned to Persia by the partition of 387, became a province of the Sasanian Empire. It was governed by a marzpan, often an Armenian noble, from the city of Dvin.
persarmenia.r: Armenian noble houses kept their lands and armies, and the church remained central to society. When Yazdegerd II tried to impose Zoroastrianism, Vardan Mamikonian led a revolt that was crushed at Avarayr in 451 but secured toleration, confirmed by the Treaty of Nvarsak in 484. Councils at Dvin rejected Chalcedon, separating the Armenian church from Byzantium.
persarmenia.e: In 591 most of the province was ceded to Byzantium, and later wars returned it to contest. Arab armies took Dvin in 640, and by the 650s the region had become the Principality of Armenia under the caliphate.

principality-of-kastrioti.t: Central Albanian lordship of the Kastrioti family, the base from which Gjergj Kastrioti, Skanderbeg, launched his revolt against the Ottomans.
principality-of-kastrioti.o: The Kastrioti family appears in the late 14th century, when Pal Kastrioti held two villages including Sinë, in the Dibër region. His son Gjon Kastrioti built a lordship stretching from the Mat valley towards the Adriatic coast near Lezhë, accepting Ottoman overlordship after the 1380s while trading with Venice and Ragusa.
principality-of-kastrioti.r: Gjon ruled as a regional lord, balancing Ottoman vassalage with Venetian and Ragusan ties; he was made a citizen of Venice and granted trading rights. As the price of submission he sent his sons to the Ottoman court as hostages, among them Gjergj, who was raised a Muslim and served the sultan as a commander.
principality-of-kastrioti.e: After Gjon's death in 1437 the Ottomans absorbed his lands. In 1443 Gjergj, now called Skanderbeg, deserted the Ottoman army after the battle of Niš, seized Krujë and returned to Christianity. In 1444 he gathered the Albanian nobles in the League of Lezhë, which inherited the Kastrioti lordship.

prince-bishopric-of-lubeck.t: The only prince-bishopric to survive the Reformation in Protestant hands, ruled from Eutin by Holstein-Gottorp princes until secularised in 1803.
prince-bishopric-of-lubeck.o: Henry the Lion moved the bishopric of Oldenburg in Holstein to the new town of Lübeck in 1160, and the bishops gathered estates in eastern Holstein. After Henry's fall in 1180 they held these lands as imperial princes. Conflicts with the citizens of the Free and Hanseatic City of Lübeck led them to govern from Eutin.
prince-bishopric-of-lubeck.r: The territory was a small rural principality of lakes and estates around Eutin. After the Reformation the cathedral chapter turned Lutheran and from 1586 elected princes of the house of Holstein-Gottorp, an arrangement the Peace of Westphalia protected. One of them, Adolf Frederick, became King of Sweden in 1751. Eutin grew into a small court town of the Enlightenment, later called the Weimar of the North.
prince-bishopric-of-lubeck.e: In 1803 the see was secularised as the Principality of Lübeck and joined to the Duchy of Oldenburg, whose ruler had been its last prince-bishop. It stayed Oldenburg's exclave until the Greater Hamburg Act of 1937 merged it into Prussian Schleswig-Holstein.

principality-of-antioch.t: A Norman-founded Crusader principality in northern Syria that lasted 170 years until Baybars destroyed its capital in 1268.
principality-of-antioch.o: The First Crusade besieged Antioch from October 1097 and took it in June 1098, then defeated Kerbogha's relief army. Bohemond of Taranto, a Norman from southern Italy, kept the city for himself despite promises to return it to Byzantium, founding the principality.
principality-of-antioch.r: Antioch's princes ruled a population of Greek Orthodox, Armenians, Syriac Christians and Muslims, with Italian merchants in Latakia and the port of Saint Symeon. The Assizes of Antioch codified its law. Its army was crushed at the Field of Blood in 1119, and in the 1130s-1150s Raymond of Poitiers had to accept Byzantine overlordship. In the 13th century it was united with the County of Tripoli, and Bohemond VI submitted to the Mongols in 1260.
principality-of-antioch.e: The Mamluk sultan Baybars stormed Antioch in May 1268, killing or enslaving much of its population; the city never regained its former importance. The title Prince of Antioch survived in the house of Tripoli and later Cyprus.

principality-of-vereya.t: The last surviving appanage of the Moscow princes, bequeathed to Ivan III after its heir fled to Lithuania.
principality-of-vereya.o: Vereya, south-west of Moscow, belonged to the lands of Andrei of Mozhaysk. In 1432 his younger son Mikhail Andreyevich began to rule Vereya together with Beloozero as his own appanage.
principality-of-vereya.r: Unlike his brother Ivan of Mozhaysk, Mikhail stayed loyal to Vasily II during Moscow's civil war, and he was allowed to keep his lands after Mozhaysk was taken in 1454. He ruled a small principality of farmland and forest, dependent on the grand prince for protection and politics.
principality-of-vereya.e: In 1483 Mikhail's son Vasily, nicknamed the Daring, quarrelled with Ivan III and fled to the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. Mikhail was forced to leave his lands to Ivan III, and on his death in 1486 Vereya was absorbed into the Grand Duchy of Moscow.

prince-bishopric-of-warmia.t: A church principality in Prussia, ruled by its bishops for over 500 years, where Nicolaus Copernicus worked as a canon.
prince-bishopric-of-warmia.o: In 1243 the papal legate William of Modena divided conquered Prussia into four dioceses, one of them Warmia. Its bishop received a third of the diocese as his own territory, while the rest went to the Teutonic Order. The bishops made Lidzbark their residence and the cathedral chapter settled at Frombork.
prince-bishopric-of-warmia.r: The bishops ruled as territorial princes, with their own castles, towns and officials, and Warmia was settled by German colonists alongside Old Prussians and later Poles. Lucas Watzenrode, bishop from 1489, brought his nephew Nicolaus Copernicus to serve the chapter, and Copernicus wrote his work on the heavens at Frombork. Bishop Stanislaus Hosius made it a stronghold of the Counter-Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-warmia.e: After the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466 Warmia came under the protection of the Polish Crown, keeping wide self-government as part of Royal Prussia. The First Partition of Poland in 1772 gave it to the Kingdom of Prussia, which took over the bishops' lands. The last bishop-prince, the poet Ignacy Krasicki, kept only his spiritual office.

principality-of-smolensk.t: A wealthy Rus' principality on the upper Dnieper, long fought over by Lithuania and Moscow.
principality-of-smolensk.o: Smolensk, the old centre of the Krivichs, stood where goods were portaged between the Dnieper, the Dvina and the Volga. Rostislav Mstislavich, grandson of Vladimir Monomakh, became its prince in 1127 and made it independent of Kiev, setting up a bishopric in 1136. His descendants, the Rostislavichi, ruled it for almost three centuries.
principality-of-smolensk.r: Smolensk grew rich from trade with the Baltic, and in 1229 its prince Mstislav Davydovich made a treaty with Riga and Gotland that set rules for German merchants. Its princes were strong enough to compete for Kiev and Novgorod. The town built many stone churches, including the surviving Church of Saints Peter and Paul.
principality-of-smolensk.e: Smolensk largely escaped the Mongol sack but became a tributary of the Golden Horde. Squeezed between the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and Moscow, it was taken by Vytautas in 1395, and after a last revolt under Yury Sviatoslavich it was annexed outright in 1404. Moscow captured it in 1514.

principality-of-temirgoy.t: A princely Circassian tribe on the Laba and Belaya rivers, whose dialect became the basis of the modern Adyghe literary language.
principality-of-temirgoy.o: The Temirgoy, or Kemirgoy, were one of the aristocratic Adyghe tribes of Circassia, living along the Laba and Belaya rivers. Their princely house, the Bolotoko, rose to prominence among the western Circassians by the 16th and 17th centuries. Earlier history is not recorded separately.
principality-of-temirgoy.r: Society was ranked into princes, nobles, free peasants and serfs, bound by the Adyghe code of honour. The Temirgoy were among the strongest western tribes and often led coalitions against the Crimean Khanate and later Russia. Prince Jambulat Bolotoko led raids and negotiations with Russia in the early 19th century.
principality-of-temirgoy.e: Russia gradually forced the Temirgoy princes into submission, and the Russian Empire completed its conquest of their land in 1864. Many emigrated to the Ottoman Empire, but some remained in what became Adygea, and their dialect underlies literary Adyghe.

paulician-state.t: A fortified refuge of the dualist Paulician Christians on the upper Euphrates, which fought Byzantium alongside the Arab emirs.
paulician-state.o: The Paulicians, a Christian sect that rejected the church hierarchy and the veneration of icons and saw the material world as the work of an evil power, had been persecuted by Byzantium for generations. After Empress Theodora ordered a massacre of them around 843, the officer Karbeas fled with thousands of followers to the emir of Melitene and founded the stronghold of Tephrike (modern Divrigi).
paulician-state.r: From Tephrike and the forts of Argaous and Amara the Paulicians formed a militarised community that raided Byzantine Anatolia in alliance with Umar al-Aqta of the Emirate of Melitene. After Karbeas died in 863 his nephew Chrysocheir led even bolder raids, reaching Nicaea and Ephesus around 869, where his men stabled horses in the church of Saint John.
paulician-state.e: Basil I's forces defeated and killed Chrysocheir at Bathys Ryax in the early 870s, and Tephrike was taken around 878. The Paulicians were scattered; many were resettled in the Balkans around Philippopolis, where their ideas fed the later Bogomil movement.

principality-of-dukagjini.t: Northern Albanian lordship of the Dukagjini family, whose name survives in the customary law code known as the Kanun of Lekë Dukagjini.
principality-of-dukagjini.o: The Dukagjini were a noble family of the northern Albanian highlands who emerged as regional lords in the late 14th century. Around 1387 they held the port of Lezhë and its hinterland, between the territories of the Balšić lords of Zeta and the Kastrioti. Pressed by the Ottomans, they handed Lezhë to Venice in 1393.
principality-of-dukagjini.r: Power rested on control of mountain clans between the Drin river and the plains of Kosovo, with the family dividing lands among branches. The lords switched between Ottoman vassalage and Venetian protection, and were Catholic Christians linked to the bishoprics of the region. Highland society was governed by unwritten custom, later codified under the name of Lekë Dukagjini.
principality-of-dukagjini.e: In 1444 Pal and Lekë Dukagjini joined Skanderbeg's League of Lezhë, folding the lordship into the wider Albanian resistance. Lekë Dukagjini fought on after Skanderbeg's death until the Ottoman conquest of the late 1470s. The Dukagjini plateau and the Kanun still bear the family's name.

prince-bishopric-of-naumburg.t: An Ottonian bishopric on the Saale famed for its cathedral's lifelike founder statues, absorbed into Saxony after the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-naumburg.o: The bishopric was founded at Zeitz in 968 under Magdeburg. In 1028, with the approval of Pope John XIX and Emperor Conrad II, it moved to Naumburg, a new seat founded by the Ekkehardine margraves of Meissen. The bishops ruled lands around Naumburg and Zeitz.
prince-bishopric-of-naumburg.r: Naumburg Cathedral's west choir, made around 1250 by the anonymous Naumburg Master, holds twelve statues of the cathedral's founders, including the margravine Uta, among the finest works of Gothic sculpture. The bishops were imperial princes but leaned heavily on the Wettin rulers of Meissen.
prince-bishopric-of-naumburg.e: In 1542 the Elector of Saxony installed the Lutheran Nicholas of Amsdorf as bishop against the chapter's choice. After the last Catholic bishop, Julius von Pflug, died in 1564, the see came under Saxon administrators. From 1656 to 1718 it formed Saxe-Zeitz, and in 1815 it passed to Prussia.

prince-bishopric-of-lebus.t: Frontier bishopric on the Oder that passed from Polish to Brandenburg control and was absorbed by the Hohenzollern electors after the Reformation.
prince-bishopric-of-lebus.o: The bishopric of Lebus was founded in the early 12th century by the Polish dukes, under the archdiocese of Gniezno. When the margraves of Brandenburg seized the Land of Lebus around 1249 to 1252, the bishops came under their influence while keeping estates on both banks of the Oder. They moved their seat to Fürstenwalde in the late 14th century.
prince-bishopric-of-lebus.r: The territory was small and its bishops weak, caught between Brandenburg, Poland and Silesia. They held lands around Fürstenwalde, Lebus and Storkow and depended on the Brandenburg electors, who effectively nominated them. During the Reformation the electors installed Hohenzollern administrators, and the see became Lutheran.
prince-bishopric-of-lebus.e: After the last administrator, the bishopric was dissolved and absorbed into the Margraviate of Brandenburg in 1598. Its lands west of the Oder remain in Brandenburg, those east of it in Poland.

principality-of-waldeck.t: Small north Hessian state of the counts and princes of Waldeck, known for hiring out soldiers and for surviving as a German state until 1918.
principality-of-waldeck.o: The counts of Schwalenberg acquired Waldeck castle above the Eder in the 12th century and took its name, emerging as counts of Waldeck by about 1180. They built up a county in the uplands between Hesse and Westphalia, often under Hessian pressure, and adopted the Reformation in the 16th century. In 1625 they inherited the County of Pyrmont.
principality-of-waldeck.r: The counts, raised to princes in 1712, ruled a poor, rural land of small towns from Arolsen, where they built a baroque palace. Revenue came partly from hiring out regiments to the Dutch Republic and to Britain, including troops used in the American Revolutionary War. George Frederick of Waldeck served as a Dutch field marshal under William III.
principality-of-waldeck.e: Waldeck joined the North German Confederation and in 1868 handed its administration to Prussia while keeping its prince. The last prince abdicated in 1918; the Free State of Waldeck lost Pyrmont in 1922 and merged into Prussia in 1929. The area is now part of Hesse.

pervaneids.t: The Sinop beylik of the family of Mu'in al-Din Suleyman Pervane, the vizier who ruled Seljuk Anatolia under the Mongols.
pervaneids.o: Mu'in al-Din Suleyman, known by his title Pervane, was the most powerful man in the Sultanate of Rum in the 1260s and 1270s and conquered the Black Sea port of Sinop in 1261. After the Mongols executed him in 1277 for suspected collusion with the Mamluk sultan Baybars, his descendants kept Sinop as a hereditary domain.
pervaneids.r: The Pervane had built a madrasa in Sinop. His son and grandsons ruled the port and its hinterland as Ilkhanid vassals. The last of them, Ghazi Chelebi, was famed for naval raids against the Genoese of Caffa and the Empire of Trebizond.
pervaneids.e: After Ghazi Chelebi's death around 1322, Sinop passed to the Candarids.

populonia.t: The only major Etruscan city on the sea, and the iron-smelting centre of ancient Italy, working ore shipped from the island of Elba.
populonia.o: Populonia, Etruscan Pupluna or Fufluna, stood on the Piombino promontory facing Elba. Villanovan settlements appeared there in the 9th century BCE, and by the 7th century princely tumulus tombs in the San Cerbone necropolis show a powerful elite. Ancient writers disagreed over whether it was founded by Corsicans or by Volaterrae.
populonia.r: Populonia's economy rested on metals: copper and tin from the Campigliese and, from the 6th century BCE, iron ore from Elba smelted in furnaces around the Gulf of Baratti, whose slag heaps later buried the tombs. It was among the first Etruscan cities to mint coins, in the 5th century BCE, often showing the smith god Sethlans or a Gorgon head, and its port linked Etruria to Corsica and Massalia.
populonia.e: Populonia became a Roman ally in the 3rd century BCE and in 205 BCE supplied iron for Scipio's fleet against Carthage. Sacked by Sulla during the civil wars of the 80s BCE, it declined; Strabo found it largely deserted. The slag heaps were mined again for iron in the 20th century, uncovering the necropolis.

powys-wenwynwyn.t: The southern half of Powys, ruled from Welshpool by princes who often sided with England against Gwynedd.
powys-wenwynwyn.o: After Madog ap Maredudd's death in 1160, his nephew Owain Cyfeiliog took the southern part of Powys. It was named after Owain's son Gwenwynwyn ab Owain, who ruled from 1195 and tried to lead the Welsh princes himself.
powys-wenwynwyn.r: Gwenwynwyn's rivalry with Llywelyn the Great of Gwynedd cost him his lands for long periods. His son Gruffydd ap Gwenwynwyn fought and allied with Llywelyn ap Gruffudd in turn, and plotted against him in 1274. Owain Cyfeiliog was a noted poet and founded Strata Marcella Abbey. Welshpool and Powis Castle were its centres.
powys-wenwynwyn.e: Gruffydd supported Edward I in the conquest of 1282 to 1283, and his son Owain surrendered the princely title, holding the lands as an English barony. The heiress married John Charlton, and the lordship of Powis passed to his family.

peoples-republic-of-bulgaria.t: Communist Bulgaria, the Soviet Union's most loyal ally in Eastern Europe, ruled for 35 years by Todor Zhivkov.
peoples-republic-of-bulgaria.o: The Soviet army entered Bulgaria in September 1944, and the communist-led Fatherland Front took power. Opponents were tried by People's Courts, and a referendum in September 1946 abolished the monarchy of the Kingdom of Bulgaria. The People's Republic was proclaimed on 15 September 1946, with Georgi Dimitrov as prime minister, and the Dimitrov Constitution followed in 1947.
peoples-republic-of-bulgaria.r: The Communist Party nationalised industry, collectivised agriculture and crushed opposition, executing the Agrarian leader Nikola Petkov in 1947. Under Todor Zhivkov, party leader from 1954, Bulgaria became the most faithful Soviet ally, industrialising rapidly with Soviet energy and markets. The 1984 to 1989 'Revival Process' forced Bulgarian Turks to take Slavic names, and in 1989 some 300,000 fled to Turkey.
peoples-republic-of-bulgaria.e: On 10 November 1989, the day after the Berlin Wall opened, Zhivkov was ousted by reformers in his own party. Round Table talks led to free elections in 1990, and in November 1990 the country was renamed the Republic of Bulgaria.
