prince-bishopric-of-utrecht.t: The Sticht, a church principality covering much of the northern Netherlands, whose bishops fought Holland and Guelders for five centuries.
prince-bishopric-of-utrecht.o: Utrecht had been the seat of Willibrord's mission to the Frisians since the late 7th century. In the early 11th century the Salian emperors granted Bishop Adalbold and his successors counties and secular rights, including lands in Drenthe and along the IJssel, turning the see into a principality of the Holy Roman Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-utrecht.r: The territory had two parts: the Nedersticht around Utrecht and the Oversticht, today Overijssel and Drenthe. Utrecht was an imperial favourite, where Conrad II and Henry V died. The bishops were elected by chapters but often imposed by neighbours: David of Burgundy, son of Philip the Good, held the see from 1456. Towns such as Deventer and Kampen grew rich in the Hanseatic trade.
prince-bishopric-of-utrecht.e: Weakened by wars with Holland and the Duchy of Guelders, Bishop Henry of Bavaria transferred his temporal power to Charles V in 1528. The lands became the Lordship of Utrecht and Lordship of Overijssel in the Habsburg Netherlands.

portuguese-bahrain.t: Bahrain under Portuguese overlordship, ruled through Hormuz from a rebuilt fort, until Safavid Persia took the island in 1602.
portuguese-bahrain.o: In 1521 a Portuguese and Hormuzi force under Antonio Correia attacked Bahrain, defeating and fatally wounding the Jabrid ruler Muqrin ibn Zamil. The islands passed to the Kingdom of Ormus, a vassal of the Portuguese Empire.
portuguese-bahrain.r: Bahrain was governed by Hormuzi governors, while the Portuguese kept a garrison and rebuilt the fort at Qal'at al-Bahrain. The islands' value lay in their pearls and dates and in their position. Local revolts broke out, notably in 1529, and an Ottoman attempt to take the island in 1559 failed. The Portuguese presence itself was small for most of the period.
portuguese-bahrain.e: In 1602 the local governor was overthrown and the Safavid governor of Fars took Bahrain for the Safavid Empire, which held it for most of the next 120 years. The fort, now part of a World Heritage Site, is the main relic.

principality-of-neuchatel.t: A small principality on Lake Neuchâtel ruled for 150 years by the kings of Prussia while also allied to, and later part of, the Swiss Confederacy.
principality-of-neuchatel.o: Neuchâtel ('new castle') appears in 1011 when King Rudolf III of Burgundy gave the castle to his wife; in 1034 it passed with Burgundy to the Empire. Counts of Neuchâtel ruled from the 12th century, and the county passed to the Hochberg family and in 1504 to the French house of Orléans-Longueville.
principality-of-neuchatel.r: The county became Protestant under Guillaume Farel in 1530 and was closely allied with Bern and other Swiss cantons. Its estates and towns enjoyed liberties. When the Longueville line ended in 1707, the estates chose King Frederick I of Prussia as prince. Watchmaking in the Jura valleys, at La Chaux-de-Fonds and Le Locle, became the chief industry.
principality-of-neuchatel.e: Napoleon gave Neuchâtel to Marshal Berthier from 1806 to 1814. In 1815 it became a Swiss canton while remaining a Prussian principality, an anomaly ended by the republican revolution of 1848. Prussia renounced its claims in 1857.

principality-of-monaco.t: A rock on the Riviera seized by the Grimaldis in 1297 and still ruled by them, now one of the world's smallest and richest sovereign states.
principality-of-monaco.o: In January 1297 François Grimaldi, a Genoese Guelph exile, took the fortress of Monaco disguised as a Franciscan friar, an event recalled in the monk on the family arms. The Grimaldis lost and regained the rock several times before establishing lasting control in the 15th century.
principality-of-monaco.r: The Grimaldis governed as lords, later princes, balancing between Genoa, Spain, France and Savoy. Honoré II placed Monaco under French protection in 1641 and adopted the title of prince. Revenues came from tolls, olive oil and citrus from Menton and Roquebrune, until Charles III founded the Monte Carlo casino in 1863.
principality-of-monaco.e: Monaco was annexed by France in 1793 and restored in 1814 under Sardinian protection. Menton and Roquebrune broke away in 1848 and were sold to France in 1861. Constitutions of 1911 and 1962 limited princely power; under Rainier III and Albert II it became a banking and tourism centre.

principality-of-yaroslavl.t: A Volga principality around the city founded by Yaroslav the Wise, ruled by its own princes until it passed to Moscow in 1463.
principality-of-yaroslavl.o: Yaroslavl was founded in the early 11th century by Yaroslav the Wise at the meeting of the Volga and the Kotorosl; a legend has him killing a bear there. In 1218 Konstantin Vsevolodovich of Rostov gave it to his son Vsevolod, who founded a separate princely line.
principality-of-yaroslavl.r: Its position on the Volga made Yaroslavl a trading town. Vsevolod was killed fighting the Mongols on the Sit in 1238. Fyodor the Black, who ruled from the 1260s, spent years at the court of the Golden Horde, married a daughter of the khan and was later venerated as a saint. The principality later split into many small appanages.
principality-of-yaroslavl.e: Its princes increasingly served the Grand Duchy of Moscow, and in 1463 Ivan III annexed the principality. The Yaroslavl princes survived as noble families such as the Shakhovskoy and Kurbsky. The city became one of Russia's richest commercial centres in the 17th century.

principality-of-kashin.t: An appanage of the Tver lands on the upper Volga, linked with Saint Anna of Kashin and reabsorbed by Tver in 1426.
principality-of-kashin.o: Kashin, north-east of Tver, was part of the Grand Principality of Tver. After Mikhail Yaroslavich was executed at the Golden Horde in 1318, his youngest son Vasily received Kashin as his appanage, founding a separate line of princes.
principality-of-kashin.r: The principality was small, with an economy based on farming and local trade. Mikhail's widow Anna lived her last years in Kashin as a nun and was later venerated as Saint Anna of Kashin. Its princes repeatedly quarrelled with their Tver cousins and sometimes sought the support of Moscow against them.
principality-of-kashin.e: After several periods of union and separation, Kashin was finally merged back into the Grand Principality of Tver in 1426. Together with Tver, it was annexed by the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1485.

principality-of-besleney.t: An eastern Circassian princely tribe on the upper Kuban and Laba, closely related to the Kabardians, whose descendants are the Cherkess of Karachay-Cherkessia.
principality-of-besleney.o: The Besleney lived on the upper Kuban, Laba and Urup rivers, between Kabarda and the western Circassians. Tradition links their princely house to the Kabardian aristocracy, and their speech is close to Kabardian. They appear as a distinct community from the 16th and 17th centuries; earlier history is not separately recorded.
principality-of-besleney.r: Princes and nobles ruled over free peasants and serfs according to the Adyghe code of conduct. The Besleney were horse breeders and herders, and their princes alternately allied with Kabarda, the Crimean Khanate and Russia. Their position on the routes between east and west Circassia gave them influence beyond their size.
principality-of-besleney.e: The Russian Empire brought them under its control in the course of the Russo-Circassian War, completed in 1864. Many emigrated to the Ottoman Empire, but part remained, and their descendants form much of the Cherkess people of Karachay-Cherkessia.

phaistos.t: Greek city-state built on the ruins of the Minoan palace in southern Crete, rival of Gortyn until destroyed by it c. 150 BCE.
phaistos.o: After the Bronze Age palace fell, Phaistos survived as a settlement on its ridge above the Mesara plain. In the early Iron Age Dorian-speaking Greeks dominated it, and by the Archaic period it was an independent polis, one of many on Crete, with Greek temples built over parts of the old palace.
phaistos.r: Phaistos controlled the western Mesara and the harbour of Matala. It minted coins from the 4th century BCE showing Talos, the bronze giant of myth, and Heracles. Like other Cretan cities it had an aristocratic constitution with kosmoi magistrates and men's messes. Its great rival was Gortyn, a few kilometres east.
phaistos.e: Phaistos was destroyed by Gortyn in the mid-2nd century BCE and its territory absorbed. The site was later known chiefly for its Minoan palace, described separately as the Palace State of Phaistos.

prince-bishopric-of-toul.t: The smallest of the Three Bishoprics of Lorraine, an ecclesiastical principality of the Empire that produced a reforming pope and was absorbed by France.
prince-bishopric-of-toul.o: Toul had been a bishopric since late Roman times. In the 10th century, as the German kings sought loyal counterweights to the Lorraine nobility, the bishops received comital rights over the city and its surroundings, traditionally dated to 928 under Henry the Fowler, making them princes of the Holy Roman Empire.
prince-bishopric-of-toul.r: The bishops ruled a small territory on the upper Moselle, often clashing with the dukes of Lorraine and with the citizens of Toul, who won considerable self-government. Bishop Bruno of Egisheim became Pope Leo IX in 1049 and drove the Gregorian reform. The diocese itself was far larger than the temporal principality.
prince-bishopric-of-toul.e: In 1552 Henry II of France occupied Toul, Metz and Verdun as 'protector' during his war with Charles V. French control of the Three Bishoprics was confirmed by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, and Toul became part of the Kingdom of France.

principality-of-gottingen.t: Guelph principality on the upper Leine whose turbulent dukes, including Otto the Bad, struggled with their own town of Göttingen until 1463.
principality-of-gottingen.o: After the death of Albert I of Brunswick in 1279, his sons divided the Principality of Wolfenbüttel, and around 1291 Albert II the Fat received the southern lands around Göttingen, Münden and Uslar, founding a separate Guelph principality on the upper Leine and Weser.
principality-of-gottingen.r: The dukes ruled a land of hills, forests and small towns, with Göttingen the main town. The town grew increasingly independent, joined the Hanseatic League and expelled Duke Otto the Bad, whose feuds and debts weakened the principality in the late 14th century. His son Otto Cocles, the One-Eyed, was nearly blind and handed government to the estates in 1435.
principality-of-gottingen.e: When Otto Cocles died in 1463, the principality passed to the Wolfenbüttel branch and was later joined to the Principality of Calenberg. Göttingen became part of the Electorate of Hanover, where its university was founded in 1734.

principality-of-minden.t: Secularised Westphalian bishopric on the Weser that became a Prussian principality and gave its name to a famous battle of 1759.
principality-of-minden.o: The Bishopric of Minden, founded by Charlemagne around 800, had turned Protestant in the Reformation. At the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 it was secularised and assigned to the Margraviate of Brandenburg as part of its compensation for ceding Western Pomerania to Sweden.
principality-of-minden.r: Brandenburg-Prussia governed Minden through a provincial administration, later combined with the County of Ravensberg in a single chamber of war and domains. The town was fortified and garrisoned, and the region produced grain and linen. During the Seven Years' War an Anglo-German army under Ferdinand of Brunswick defeated the French nearby at the Battle of Minden on 1 August 1759.
principality-of-minden.e: After Prussia's collapse in 1806, Minden was divided between the Kingdom of Westphalia and, from 1810, France. In 1815 it returned to Prussia as part of the Province of Westphalia; the area is now in North Rhine-Westphalia.

principality-of-prosek.t: Short-lived lordship of the adventurer Dobromir Chrysos in the Vardar gorge, carved out during the Bulgarian revolt against Byzantium.
principality-of-prosek.o: Dobromir Chrysos, a Vlach or Bulgarian commander who had served in the Byzantine army, broke away during the Asen revolt that founded the Second Bulgarian Empire. Around 1197 he seized the fortress of Prosek, in the Demir Kapija gorge of the Vardar, and nearby Strumica.
principality-of-prosek.r: Known mainly from the Byzantine historian Niketas Choniates, his realm rested on the near-impregnable fortress of Prosek and on several hundred warriors. The emperor Alexios III failed to take it and recognised him, marrying him to a relative.
principality-of-prosek.e: Chrysos rebelled again, and around 1201–1202 Alexios III defeated him and recovered his lands; Prosek soon passed to Kaloyan of Bulgaria.

philippolis-griqua-state.t: Adam Kok's Griqua captaincy north of the Orange River, squeezed out by Boer settlers until its people trekked to Griqualand East.
philippolis-griqua-state.o: Philippolis began in 1823 as a London Missionary Society station for San. In 1826 Adam Kok II and his Griqua followers, who had split from the community at Griquatown, settled there and made it the centre of their own captaincy.
philippolis-griqua-state.r: The Kok family ruled with a council and a mission-backed legal order, and the Griqua farmed sheep and cattle. From the 1830s Boer trekboers leased and bought Griqua farms. Adam Kok III, kaptein from 1837, sought British support, signing a treaty with the Cape in 1843, but under the Orange River Sovereignty and then the Orange Free State the Griqua steadily lost land.
philippolis-griqua-state.e: In 1861 Adam Kok III sold the remaining land to the Orange Free State and led about 2,000 people across the Drakensberg to Nomansland, where they founded Griqualand East.

principality-of-reuss-lobenstein.t: Tiny Thuringian lordship of the Reuss family, where every male ruler was named Heinrich.
principality-of-reuss-lobenstein.o: The Younger Line of the House of Reuss divided its lands in 1647 into Gera, Schleiz, Lobenstein and Saalburg. Heinrich X received Lobenstein in the Thuringian Highlands, and his descendants later split off Ebersdorf and Hirschberg as further sub-lines.
principality-of-reuss-lobenstein.r: Lobenstein was small, hilly and poor, with some mining and timber. Like all Reuss branches, its counts named every son Heinrich, distinguished by numbers counted across the century. The rulers were Lutheran and governed through a modest court in Lobenstein. They were raised to princely rank in 1790.
principality-of-reuss-lobenstein.e: The Lobenstein line died out in 1824, and its lands passed to the Principality of Reuss-Ebersdorf, which became Reuss-Lobenstein-Ebersdorf. In 1848 all these lands joined the Principality of Reuss-Schleiz to form the Principality of Reuss Younger Line.

principality-of-guria.t: A small principality on Georgia's Black Sea coast, ruled by the Gurieli family between the Kingdom of Imereti and the Ottoman Empire.
principality-of-guria.o: Guria, the land south of the Rioni along the Black Sea coast, was governed by a branch of the Vardanidze family, later called Gurieli, as eristavis of the Kingdom of Georgia. As the kingdom broke apart in the 1460s, the Gurieli became effectively independent princes, nominally owing allegiance to the Kingdom of Imereti.
principality-of-guria.r: The princes ruled from Ozurgeti over a land of maize, vineyards and forested hills. Guria lay on the frontier with the Ottoman Empire, which seized its coastal fortresses and drew tribute; the slave trade through Ottoman ports was a persistent evil. The Gurieli took part in Imereti's dynastic wars, sometimes ruling it themselves, as Mamia I did.
principality-of-guria.e: In 1810 Mamia V accepted a Russian protectorate. After the death of Mamia V's young heir, a revolt in 1828 was crushed, and in 1829 the Russian Empire annexed Guria.

paemani.t: One of the Germani Cisrhenani of the Belgian Ardennes, remembered in the name of the Famenne region.
paemani.o: Caesar lists the Paemani with the Condrusi, Eburones and Caeroesi as Germani living west of the Rhine. Their name is usually linked to the Famenne, in the modern Belgian provinces of Namur and Luxembourg.
paemani.r: Nothing is known of their rulers or settlements.
paemani.e: They joined the Belgic coalition against Caesar in 57 BCE. After the conquest they disappear from the sources, their land absorbed into the civitas of the Tungri.

prince-bishopric-of-speyer.t: A prince-bishopric on the Rhine whose cathedral holds the tombs of Salian emperors, its bishops ruling from Bruchsal until 1803.
prince-bishopric-of-speyer.o: Speyer had been a bishopric since the 7th century, and Salian kings made it their family church; Conrad II began the great cathedral around 1030. In 1111 Emperor Henry V granted the citizens of Speyer privileges, and the bishops' secular rule over their territory developed in the 11th and 12th centuries.
prince-bishopric-of-speyer.r: The bishops ruled a territory on both banks of the Rhine but not the city of Speyer, which became a free imperial city; they moved their residence to Udenheim, renamed Philippsburg, and in 1720 to Bruchsal, where Cardinal Damian Hugo von Schönborn built a baroque palace. The cathedral, burial place of eight emperors and kings, is a World Heritage Site.
prince-bishopric-of-speyer.e: France annexed the left-bank lands during the Revolutionary Wars, and in 1803 the right-bank territory, including Bruchsal, was secularised and given to Baden. The diocese of Speyer was re-founded in 1817 under Bavaria.

principality-of-kakheti.t: An eastern Georgian principality ruled by chorepiscopi, leaders with a churchly title, that resisted the Arab emirs of Tbilisi and the Bagratid kings.
principality-of-kakheti.o: Kakheti, the land east of Tbilisi, broke away from the Principality of Iberia in 786, when the nobleman Grigol took the title chorepiscopus and united its mountain communities. The weakening of central power under Arab rule allowed it to become a separate state.
principality-of-kakheti.r: Its rulers, whose title meant rural bishop although they were lay princes, ruled from Ujarma and later Telavi with the support of the mountain peoples of Tusheti and Pshavi. They fought the Emirate of Tbilisi and the Kingdom of Abkhazia, and in the 10th century absorbed the Principality of Hereti. Viticulture and farming in the Alazani valley sustained it.
principality-of-kakheti.e: Around 1010 Kvirike III took the title king, forming the Kingdom of Kakheti-Hereti, which held out against the united Georgian monarchy until 1104. Kakheti later re-emerged as a separate Georgian kingdom in the 15th century.

principality-of-volhynia.t: A western Rus' principality around Volodymyr whose prince Roman united it with Galicia in 1199.
principality-of-volhynia.o: Volhynia, between the Bug and the upper Pripyat, was an old land of Rus' with its centre at Volodymyr. In the mid 12th century it became the hereditary domain of the descendants of Iziaslav Mstislavich of Kiev, and from 1154 his son Mstislav Iziaslavich ruled it as a separate principality.
principality-of-volhynia.r: Volhynia was a fertile land of towns such as Volodymyr, Lutsk and Berestia, trading with Poland and the West. Its princes, the senior branch of Monomakh's family, were among the strongest in Rus' and frequently fought for Kiev. Roman Mstislavich, who succeeded in 1170, was an energetic warrior who fought the Lithuanians and Cumans.
principality-of-volhynia.e: In 1199 Roman Mstislavich took Halych after its dynasty died out and joined the two lands into the Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia. Volhynia later passed to Lithuania as the Duchy of Volhynia.

pskov-republic.t: A fortified city-republic on Russia's western frontier, which governed itself through its veche until Moscow annexed it in 1510.
pskov-republic.o: Pskov was long a dependency of the Novgorod Republic, though it already had its own princes, among them the Lithuanian exile Daumantas, who defended it in the late 13th century. In 1348 the Treaty of Bolotovo recognised Pskov's self-government, and it became an independent republic.
pskov-republic.r: Power lay with the veche, which met by the Trinity Cathedral in the stone citadel known as the Krom, and with elected posadniks. Pskov hired princes to command its troops, often from Lithuania or Moscow. Its Judicial Charter is one of the most important legal texts of medieval Russia. A frontier fortress, it repeatedly fought the Livonian Order.
pskov-republic.e: In the 15th century Pskov relied increasingly on Moscow for protection. In 1510 Vasily III ended its independence, removed the veche bell and deported hundreds of leading families. The city became a Muscovite fortress and withstood the siege of Stefan Batory in 1581.

prince-archbishopric-of-bremen.t: Archbishopric of the North Sea coast, heir to Ansgar's mission to Scandinavia, which ruled the land between the Weser and Elbe until Sweden took it in 1648.
prince-archbishopric-of-bremen.o: The archdiocese of Hamburg was founded in 831 for Ansgar, apostle of the North, and joined to Bremen after Vikings sacked Hamburg in 845. Under Archbishop Adalbert in the 11th century it claimed authority over all of Scandinavia. After Henry the Lion fell in 1180 the archbishops built a secular principality between the lower Weser and Elbe.
prince-archbishopric-of-bremen.r: The archbishops governed marshland and moor from Stade and Bremervörde, while the wealthy city of Bremen slipped from their control. Free peasant communities in the marshes resisted lordship. The estates, including the cathedral chapter, nobles and towns, shared power. In the 16th century the land became Lutheran, and administrators came from princely houses such as Holstein-Gottorp and Denmark.
prince-archbishopric-of-bremen.e: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 secularised it as the Duchy of Bremen under Sweden, which ruled it with Verden. Denmark took it in 1712 and sold it to the Electorate of Hanover in 1715. The land is now in Lower Saxony.

principality-of-herat.t: The last outpost of Sadozai rule, a frontier city-state whose sieges by Persia drew Britain and Russia into the Great Game.
principality-of-herat.o: When the Barakzai brothers took over most of the Durrani Empire around 1818, the Sadozai prince Mahmud Shah and his son Kamran Shah held on to Herat, ruling it as an independent principality.
principality-of-herat.r: Kamran Shah's vizier Yar Muhammad Khan Alakozai became the real power and in 1842 killed Kamran, ruling himself until 1851. Herat was a walled city on the route between Persia, Central Asia and India, and its strategic value made it central to the Great Game. Persia besieged it in 1837 to 1838, with a young British officer, Eldred Pottinger, helping the defence, and again in 1856, when Britain went to war with Persia to force its withdrawal.
principality-of-herat.e: By the Treaty of Paris in 1857 Persia renounced its claims. Dost Mohammad Khan took Herat in 1863 after a ten-month siege, dying there days later, and Herat joined the Emirate of Afghanistan.

peoples-state-of-hesse.t: Republican successor of the Grand Duchy of Hesse, a Social Democratic state on both sides of the Rhine.
peoples-state-of-hesse.o: Grand Duke Ernest Louis was deposed in November 1918, and Hesse-Darmstadt became the People's State of Hesse, with a democratic constitution adopted in December 1919. It kept the grand duchy's three provinces: Starkenburg, Upper Hesse around Giessen, and Rhenish Hesse with Mainz and Worms.
peoples-state-of-hesse.r: Social Democrats led the state for most of the Weimar years under Carl Ulrich. Rhenish Hesse and Mainz were under French occupation until 1930. Darmstadt had a technical university and the Merck chemical company. The Nazis took power in March 1933 under Reich governor Jakob Sprenger, and the Jewish communities of Mainz and Worms, among the oldest in Germany, were destroyed.
peoples-state-of-hesse.e: In 1945 the parts east of the Rhine were combined with Prussian territories into Greater Hesse in the American zone, now the state of Hesse. Rhenish Hesse went to the French zone and later to Rhineland-Palatinate.

principality-of-soyo.t: A Kongo coastal province at the mouth of the Congo River that broke away to become an independent Catholic principality and defeated Portugal in 1670.
principality-of-soyo.o: Soyo was a province of the Kingdom of Kongo, ruled by a count (Mani Soyo) from Mbanza Soyo, close to the river mouth. Its control of the port of Mpinda and direct trade with the Dutch made it rich, and in 1641 Count Daniel da Silva asserted independence from the Kongo king.
principality-of-soyo.r: Soyo's counts, later styled princes, ruled as Catholic monarchs, hosting Italian Capuchin missionaries and celebrating the feast of St James. Trade in slaves, ivory and copper with Dutch and English merchants funded a strong army. In 1670 Soyo defeated a Portuguese invasion at the Battle of Kitombo, and it later intervened in the Kongo civil wars.
principality-of-soyo.e: Soyo remained autonomous through the 18th and 19th centuries, though its power waned with the end of the slave trade. It was incorporated into Portuguese Angola after the Berlin Conference of 1884–85. The town of Soyo is now an Angolan oil centre.

prince-bishopric-of-freising.t: The Bavarian church state of Saint Corbinian, a small principality on the Isar with scattered estates reaching into Austria and Carniola.
prince-bishopric-of-freising.o: The diocese goes back to Saint Corbinian, who worked at Freising around 720, and was formally organised by Saint Boniface in 739. Over the following centuries the bishops gathered estates across Bavaria, Austria, Tyrol and Carniola. Their territory as an imperial principality took shape around the city and the county of Werdenfels, bought in 1294.
prince-bishopric-of-freising.r: The bishop, elected by the cathedral chapter, ruled as a prince of the Holy Roman Empire, but his small core lands were surrounded by Bavaria and he depended heavily on the Wittelsbach dukes, several of whose sons held the see. Freising's cathedral hill was a centre of learning, and the nearby abbey of Weihenstephan brewed beer. The territory remained Catholic.
prince-bishopric-of-freising.e: In 1802 and 1803 the prince-bishopric was secularised and its lands passed to the Electorate of Bavaria, while estates in Austria went to the Habsburgs. The see moved to Munich in 1821 as the Archdiocese of Munich and Freising.

prince-bishopric-of-cammin.t: Pomeranian church state founded as the bishopric of the newly converted Pomeranians and secularised into a Brandenburg principality in 1650.
prince-bishopric-of-cammin.o: The bishopric of Pomerania was founded in 1140 at Wolin after the mission of Otto of Bamberg, with Adalbert as first bishop, and moved to Cammin by 1176. Exempt from any archbishop, it answered directly to the pope. In 1248 the bishops acquired the land of Kolberg, forming their secular territory with Köslin and Bublitz.
prince-bishopric-of-cammin.r: The bishops ruled a small but distinct territory, with Köslin and Kolberg its main towns and residences. They claimed imperial immediacy, which the dukes of Pomerania contested, and the Pomeranian estates drew the bishopric into ducal politics. After the Reformation in the 1530s the see became Lutheran and was administered by members of the Pomeranian ducal house.
prince-bishopric-of-cammin.e: The last administrator, Ernst Bogislaw of Croÿ, handed it over after the Peace of Westphalia gave Cammin to Brandenburg, which took possession in 1650 as the Principality of Cammin. The region has been part of Poland since 1945.

paracas.t: A culture of Peru's southern desert coast celebrated for the finest embroidered textiles of the ancient Andes, preserved in hundreds of mummy bundles at the Paracas peninsula.
paracas.o: The Paracas culture developed on the south coast of Peru, around the Paracas peninsula and the Ica and Pisco valleys, from about 800 BCE. Early phases show the influence of the Chavín style in pottery and imagery before local traditions took over.
paracas.r: Paracas society was organised in chiefdoms supported by irrigation farming and rich fishing grounds. It is best known from its cemeteries: the necropolis of Wari Kayan, excavated by Julio C. Tello in 1927, held more than 400 mummy bundles wrapped in brilliantly coloured embroidered mantles of cotton and camelid wool. Paracas people practised cranial deformation and trepanation of the skull. Their pottery was painted with resin-based colours after firing.
paracas.e: Around 100 BCE the late Paracas tradition, known as Necropolis, merged gradually into the Nazca culture, which inherited its iconography and textile techniques. The large Paracas Candelabra geoglyph is sometimes attributed to it, though its date is uncertain.

principality-of-samos.t: Autonomous Christian principality on the island of Samos under Ottoman suzerainty, created after the Greek War of Independence and united with Greece in 1912.
principality-of-samos.o: Samos fought in the Greek War of Independence, but the London Protocol of 1830 left it outside the new Greek state. As a compromise the Ottoman Sultan made it an autonomous principality, established in 1834, with a Christian prince appointed by the Porte and paying an annual tribute. Its first prince was Stefanos Vogoridis.
principality-of-samos.r: The prince, usually a Phanariot Greek, governed with an elected assembly and his own administration, flag and later postage stamps, from Vathy. Samians paid low taxes and enjoyed religious freedom. The economy rested on wine, especially muscat, tobacco and shipping. Politics were often turbulent, with clashes between princes and local factions.
principality-of-samos.e: During the First Balkan War, the Samian leader Themistoklis Sofoulis drove out the last Ottoman garrison and the assembly declared union with Greece in November 1912. Greek rule was confirmed in 1913 and Samos joined the Kingdom of Greece.

principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau.t: Short-lived Anhalt principality, a minor appanage whose line went on to rule Anhalt-Köthen.
principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau.o: Plötzkau, a small castle district on the Saale, was assigned in the 1603 partition of Anhalt to August, a younger son of Joachim Ernst. It began as an appanage of limited territory rather than a full share, and was formally set up as a principality in 1611.
principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau.r: Little distinguishes its government from the other Anhalt states: it was a small Calvinist territory administered from Plötzkau castle, with revenues from farming along the Saale. Its prince August acted as regent for the young princes of Anhalt-Köthen and served the joint interests of the Anhalt house during the Thirty Years' War.
principality-of-anhalt-plotzkau.e: In 1665 the Köthen line died out and Lebrecht and Emanuel of Anhalt-Plötzkau inherited Anhalt-Köthen, giving up Plötzkau, which returned to Anhalt-Bernburg. The Plötzkau branch thus continued as the ruling house of Köthen until 1847.

palatinate-birkenfeld.t: A Wittelsbach line in the Hunsrück, from whose descendants came the kings of Bavaria and the dukes in Bavaria.
palatinate-birkenfeld.o: In 1569 Duke Wolfgang of Palatinate-Zweibrücken divided his lands among his sons, and Charles I received Birkenfeld, part of the old County of Sponheim in the Hunsrück, founding the line of Palatinate-Birkenfeld.
palatinate-birkenfeld.r: The dukes ruled a small, scattered territory from Birkenfeld, sharing the Sponheim lands with Baden, and kept a modest Lutheran court. Branches formed at Bischweiler and Gelnhausen. Christian II acquired the lordship of Rappoltstein (Ribeaupierre) in Alsace by marriage in 1673.
palatinate-birkenfeld.e: In 1731 Christian III inherited Palatinate-Zweibrücken, and the line moved there as Zweibrücken-Birkenfeld. His grandson Maximilian Joseph became the first king of the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806, while the Gelnhausen branch became the dukes in Bavaria, family of Empress Elisabeth of Austria.

palace-state-of-knossos.t: The largest Minoan palace centre and later a Mycenaean-ruled capital whose Linear B tablets are the earliest written Greek from Crete.
palace-state-of-knossos.o: Knossos, near modern Heraklion, was occupied from the Neolithic and became Crete's largest settlement. Around 1950 BCE the first palace was built around a central court. Rebuilt after an earthquake c. 1700 BCE, it grew into a complex of more than a thousand rooms, with a town of perhaps several thousand people around it.
palace-state-of-knossos.r: Knossos was the centre of Minoan civilisation, with frescoes such as the bull-leaping scene, light wells, storerooms of pithoi and a theatral area. Administration used Linear A. After c. 1450 BCE Greek-speaking rulers took control and kept records in Linear B, listing sheep, wool, textiles and offerings to gods such as Potnia. The palace then dominated much of central and western Crete.
palace-state-of-knossos.e: The palace was destroyed by fire, traditionally c. 1375 BCE, though the date is debated and some scholars place the final destruction later. Knossos survived as a town and became the Greek city-state described separately as Knossos. Arthur Evans excavated and partly reconstructed the site from 1900.
palace-state-of-knossos.re: Minoan religion; later Mycenaean Greek religion

principality-of-samtskhe.t: A south-west Georgian principality ruled by the Jaqeli atabegs, which broke from the Georgian crown and was finally absorbed by the Ottoman Empire.
principality-of-samtskhe.o: Samtskhe, the upland borderland around Akhaltsikhe, was governed by the Jaqeli family as royal lieutenants. In 1268 Sargis I Jaqeli secured direct recognition from the Mongol Ilkhanate, making his lands effectively separate from the Kingdom of Georgia, and his heirs held the title of atabeg.
principality-of-samtskhe.r: The atabegs ruled from Akhaltsikhe over farming valleys, the cave monastery of Vardzia and routes to Anatolia. Beka I Jaqeli issued a law code in the early 14th century. Samtskhe rejoined Georgia under George V but broke away again in the 15th century, becoming a battleground between the Ottomans and Safavids after 1500 and a vassal of the Ottoman Empire from 1578.
principality-of-samtskhe.e: The Jaqeli rulers converted to Islam, and in 1628 the Ottomans turned Samtskhe into the Childir Eyalet, with Safar Pasha, a Jaqeli, as its first governor. Much of the population was gradually Islamised, and the region returned to Georgian rule only after the Russian conquest of 1829.

principality-of-hersfeld.t: A Benedictine abbey in Hesse founded by a disciple of Saint Boniface, whose abbots ruled a principality until it became part of Hesse-Kassel.
principality-of-hersfeld.o: Hersfeld began as a hermitage of Saint Sturmi around 736 and was refounded as a Benedictine monastery by Archbishop Lullus of Mainz around 769. Charlemagne granted it royal protection in 775, making it an imperial abbey. Its relics of Saint Wigbert made it an important pilgrimage centre.
principality-of-hersfeld.r: Hersfeld held lands across Hesse and Thuringia, recorded in the Breviarium Lulli. Its scholars included the chronicler Lambert of Hersfeld, who wrote a major account of the reign of Henry IV. The abbots were princes of the Empire, but rivalry with the town of Hersfeld and with the landgraves of Hesse slowly weakened them.
principality-of-hersfeld.e: The landgraves of Hesse became protectors of the abbey and, after the Reformation, effectively controlled it. In 1648 the Peace of Westphalia secularised Hersfeld as a principality granted to Hesse-Kassel. The ruins of its Romanesque abbey church are among the largest in Germany.

protectorate-of-bohemia-and-moravia.t: Nazi-occupied Czech lands, nominally autonomous but ruled through terror, deportations and forced labour from 1939 to 1945.
protectorate-of-bohemia-and-moravia.o: After the Munich Agreement and the loss of the Sudetenland in 1938, Germany occupied the rest of Bohemia and Moravia on 15 March 1939, as Slovakia declared independence. The next day Hitler proclaimed the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia from Prague Castle.
protectorate-of-bohemia-and-moravia.r: A Czech government under President Emil Hácha remained in place, but real power lay with the Reich Protector, first Konstantin von Neurath and then Reinhard Heydrich. Czech universities were closed in 1939, and Czech industry, such as the Škoda works, served the German war effort. Heydrich was assassinated by Czech parachutists in 1942, and the Nazis destroyed the villages of Lidice and Ležáky in reprisal. Most Czech Jews were deported via Theresienstadt and murdered.
protectorate-of-bohemia-and-moravia.e: The Prague uprising broke out on 5 May 1945, and the Red Army entered Prague on 9 May. The territory was restored to Czechoslovakia, which expelled most of its German population in the following two years.

principality-of-kandahar.t: The principality ruled by the Barakzai 'Kandahar Sardars', half-brothers of Dost Mohammad Khan, between the fall of the Durranis and Afghan reunification.
principality-of-kandahar.o: As the Durrani Empire fell apart after 1818, the powerful Barakzai brothers divided its lands. Kandahar went to a group of brothers known as the Kandahar Sardars, led by Purdil Khan and later Kohandil Khan, who were half-brothers of Dost Mohammad Khan of Kabul.
principality-of-kandahar.r: The sardars ruled jointly over Kandahar and its Pashtun tribes, relying on tribal levies and revenue from trade on the route to Herat and India. They negotiated with Persia and Russia as well as with their relatives in Kabul. During the First Anglo-Afghan War the British occupied Kandahar from 1839 to 1842, and the sardars took refuge in Persia before returning.
principality-of-kandahar.e: After Kohandil Khan died in 1855, Dost Mohammad Khan seized Kandahar and incorporated it into the Emirate of Afghanistan, a key step towards reuniting the Afghan lands.

puruha.t: A highland people of central Ecuador around Chimborazo who were absorbed by the Incas and later by the Spanish, but whose identity survives today.
puruha.o: The Puruhá occupied the highland basin around the volcano Chimborazo, in the modern provinces of Chimborazo and Bolívar, from around 800. Archaeology shows a sequence of local pottery traditions, with the Puruhá phase often linked to tombs found near Riobamba.
puruha.r: Little is known of their political organisation beyond a series of chiefdoms under local lords. They farmed maize, potatoes and quinoa on the volcanic slopes and herded llamas. Their tombs contained copper ornaments and distinctive pottery, including vessels with modelled human faces. Later chroniclers claimed that Puruhá lords allied by marriage with Quito, but these accounts are doubtful.
puruha.e: The Puruhá were brought under Inca rule around 1470 during the campaigns of Túpac Inca Yupanqui. After the Spanish conquest, Riobamba was founded in their territory in 1534. Their descendants, Kichwa-speaking communities of Chimborazo, keep a strong indigenous identity.

principality-of-kesh.t: A Sogdian principality south of Samarkand, centred on the city later called Shahrisabz, the birthplace of Timur.
principality-of-kesh.o: Kesh lay on the Qashqadarya River in southern Sogdiana. It became one of the Sogdian principalities in the 6th century, under the overlordship of the Western Turkic Khaganate, and was ruled by local lords who issued their own coins.
principality-of-kesh.r: Like its neighbours, Kesh was a town of farmers, craftsmen and merchants governed by a local dynasty and nobility. Chinese sources call it Shi, and it traded through Samarkand and over the Iron Gate pass to Tokharistan. Very little detail survives about its rulers or institutions.
principality-of-kesh.e: Arab armies conquered Kesh during the campaigns of Qutayba ibn Muslim in the early 8th century, and it was absorbed into Umayyad and Abbasid Transoxiana. The city, renamed Shahrisabz, later became the home town of Timur.

pukara.t: The first major political and ceremonial centre of the Lake Titicaca basin, whose stone sculpture and sunken courts foreshadowed the later power of Tiwanaku.
pukara.o: Pukará grew from about 500 BCE on the northern side of the Titicaca basin in Puno, Peru. A large terraced ceremonial complex was built against a red sandstone outcrop, with sunken rectangular courts at its summit. It became the dominant centre of the northern basin.
pukara.r: Pukará is thought to have been a chiefdom or early regional polity whose leaders controlled herding of llamas and alpacas, raised-field farming and trade in obsidian and other goods. It is known for carved stone stelae and statues, including figures holding trophy heads, and for polychrome incised pottery with feline and human images. Its sunken courts and stone sculpture tradition influenced later highland architecture.
pukara.e: The site declined after about 200 CE, and the centre of power in the basin shifted south to Tiwanaku, which absorbed elements of its art and ritual. The modern town of Pucará is known for its ceramic bulls, an unrelated colonial tradition.

principality-of-reuss-greiz.t: The Elder Line of the house of Reuss, ruling from Greiz, one of the smallest states of the German Empire.
principality-of-reuss-greiz.o: In the division of the Reuss lands in 1564, the Elder Line received Greiz and the surrounding part of the Vogtland. After a split into Upper and Lower Greiz, the branches were reunited in 1768, and in 1778 Heinrich XI was raised to prince of the empire.
principality-of-reuss-greiz.r: Like their cousins, all male members were named Heinrich, but the Elder Line numbered them in a sequence that restarted at intervals. The principality was small, Lutheran and agrarian, later with textile mills in Greiz and Zeulenroda. Its upper and lower castles still dominate the town.
principality-of-reuss-greiz.e: Reuss Elder Line sided with Austria in 1866 and was occupied by Prussia, but joined the German Empire in 1871, and Prince Heinrich XXII remained a noted opponent of Prussian policy. After the revolution of 1918 it merged with the Younger Line in 1919 into the People's State of Reuss, part of Thuringia from 1920.

piedmontese-republic.t: The provisional republic set up in Piedmont after the French forced King Charles Emmanuel IV to abandon the mainland in 1798.
piedmontese-republic.o: In December 1798 French troops occupied Turin and forced Charles Emmanuel IV of the Kingdom of Sardinia to give up his mainland states and withdraw to the island of Sardinia. A provisional government of Piedmontese patriots took over in Turin, proclaiming a republic.
piedmontese-republic.r: The provisional government abolished feudal rights and noble titles and held votes in which the Piedmontese communities asked to be annexed to France; the French Directory approved the annexation in early 1799. Real power lay with French commissioners and generals, and French requisitions caused unrest in the countryside.
piedmontese-republic.e: In 1799 the Austro-Russian army under Suvorov drove the French out of Piedmont, ending the regime. After Napoleon's victory at Marengo in 1800, the French set up the Subalpine Republic.

principality-of-mingrelia.t: A western Georgian principality ruled by the Dadiani princes, which under Levan II dominated western Georgia and kept autonomy until 1867.
principality-of-mingrelia.o: Mingrelia, or Odishi, the lowland between the Rioni and the Inguri, had been governed by the Dadiani family as eristavis since the Middle Ages. As the Kingdom of Imereti weakened, the Dadiani became effectively independent, and from 1557 they ruled as sovereign princes, paying tribute to the Ottoman Empire.
principality-of-mingrelia.r: The princes ruled from Zugdidi and other residences over nobles and a largely enserfed peasantry. Levan II Dadiani, from 1611, made Mingrelia the leading power of western Georgia, fighting Imereti and Abkhazia; Catholic missionaries such as Arcangelo Lamberti described his court. The slave trade with Ottoman ports was a lasting curse. The Mingrelian language was spoken alongside Georgian.
principality-of-mingrelia.e: Grigol Dadiani accepted a Russian protectorate in 1803. After the Crimean War and a peasant revolt, Russia took over the administration in 1857 and formally annexed the principality in 1867. Princess Ekaterine Dadiani was the last ruling figure.

principality-of-moldavia.t: Romanian principality between the Carpathians and the Dniester, celebrated for Stephen the Great and its painted monasteries, which merged with Wallachia in 1859.
principality-of-moldavia.o: Around 1346 the Hungarian king sent Dragoș, a Romanian noble from Maramureș, to set up a march east of the Carpathians against the Golden Horde. In 1359 another Maramureș noble, Bogdan I, drove out Dragoș's heirs and made Moldavia independent of Hungary.
principality-of-moldavia.r: The voivode ruled with boyars and the Orthodox Church from Suceava and, after 1564, Iași. Alexander the Good gave the country stable institutions. Stephen the Great (1457–1504) defeated the Ottomans at Vaslui in 1475 and built churches such as Putna and Voroneț, famous for exterior frescoes. From the 16th century Moldavia paid tribute to the Ottomans, and from 1711 to 1821 it was ruled by Phanariot princes.
principality-of-moldavia.e: It lost Bukovina to Austria in 1775 and Bessarabia to Russia in 1812. In 1859 it elected Alexandru Ioan Cuza, as did the Principality of Wallachia, creating the union that became Romania.

peloponnesian-league.t: Sparta's network of alliances, the leading military coalition of classical Greece and Athens' opponent in the Peloponnesian War.
peloponnesian-league.o: The league grew in the mid-6th century BCE when Sparta, after defeating Tegea around 550 BCE, turned from conquest to alliance. City by city, Peloponnesian states such as Tegea, Corinth, Elis and later Megara swore to have the same friends and enemies as the Lacedaemonians and to follow them wherever they led.
peloponnesian-league.r: There was no common treasury or capital beyond Sparta. Each ally was bound to Sparta by its own treaty; from the late 6th century a congress of allies voted on war, each city having one vote, and Sparta commanded the joint army. Sparta favoured friendly oligarchies in member cities. The league formed the core of Greek resistance to Persia in 480-479 BCE.
peloponnesian-league.e: It fought and won the Peloponnesian War against the Delian League (431-404 BCE), but the Theban victory at Leuctra in 371 BCE and invasions of Laconia broke Sparta's hold. The liberation of Messenia and separate peace deals by Corinth and others in 366-365 BCE ended the league.

perge.t: Perge, a Greek city of the Pamphylian plain, famous for its sanctuary of Artemis and the mathematician Apollonius.
perge.o: Greek tradition says Perge was founded after the Trojan War by heroes such as Mopsus and Calchas, and a city called Parha appears in a Hittite treaty. By the 7th century BCE it was a Greek-speaking city near the coast, inland on the Kestros river.
perge.r: Perge was a self-governing city whose patron was Artemis Pergaia, worshipped at a rich temple. It surrendered to Alexander of the Macedonian Empire in 333 BCE and later passed through Seleucid and Attalid rule. The mathematician Apollonius of Perga wrote his work on conic sections in the 3rd century BCE.
perge.e: Perge came under Roman control, and in 25 BCE it became part of the Roman province of Galatia, later Pamphylia. Its finest monuments, including colonnaded streets and a theatre, date from the Roman period.

pagania.t: Slavic principality of the Narentines between the Cetina and Neretva, whose pirate fleets challenged Venice for two centuries.
pagania.o: The Narentines were Slavs who settled the coast between the Cetina and Neretva rivers in the 7th century. By the 9th century they formed a principality, called Pagania by the Byzantines because they accepted Christianity late. Constantine VII lists its towns, including Mokro and Ostrog, and the islands of Brač, Hvar, Korčula and Mljet.
pagania.r: Ruled by its own princes and assembly of clans, Pagania lived largely from the sea, raiding and taxing Adriatic shipping. Venice had to pay for safe passage, and in 887 the Narentines killed Doge Pietro I Candiano in battle. They accepted Byzantine missionaries in the late 9th century.
pagania.e: In 1000 Doge Pietro II Orseolo led a fleet that broke Narentine sea power. Pagania then came under the Kingdom of Croatia (925-1102) and later Zachlumia, and the name fades by the 11th century.

principality-of-montenegro.t: Secular Montenegrin principality of the Petrović-Njegoš dynasty, which won international recognition of its independence at the Congress of Berlin.
principality-of-montenegro.o: In 1852 Danilo Petrović-Njegoš, heir of the Prince-Bishopric of Montenegro, declined to become a bishop and proclaimed himself secular prince with Russian backing. He issued a legal code in 1855, imposed taxes on the clans, and his brother Mirko Petrović defeated the Ottomans at Grahovac in 1858, after which Montenegro's borders were first drawn.
principality-of-montenegro.r: After Danilo's assassination in 1860, his nephew Nikola ruled for over half a century as a patriarchal autocrat from Cetinje, where foreign legations were built. Montenegro remained a poor land of clans and herders, heavily subsidised by Russia. Nikola married his daughters into the royal houses of Italy, Serbia and Russia, and granted a constitution only in 1905.
principality-of-montenegro.e: War against the Ottomans in 1876 to 1878 won recognition of independence at Berlin in 1878, nearly doubling the territory and gaining Nikšić, Podgorica, Bar and later Ulcinj. On his jubilee in 1910 Nikola proclaimed the Kingdom of Montenegro.

paros.t: Cycladic island famed for its fine white marble and its poet Archilochus, and coloniser of Thasos.
paros.o: Paros, in the central Cyclades, was settled by Ionian Greeks in the early Iron Age. Its translucent marble, quarried in underground galleries, became the prized stone of Greek sculptors. By the 7th century BCE Paros was strong enough to colonise Thasos c. 680 BCE and later Parion on the Hellespont.
paros.r: Archilochus, a pioneering lyric and iambic poet, was a Parian who joined the settlement of Thasos. Paros was a commercial and religious centre with a temple of Demeter. It supported Persia in 490 BCE, and the Athenian Miltiades failed to take it in 489 BCE. In the Delian League Paros paid one of the largest island tributes.
paros.e: Paros came under Hellenistic kings and later Roman control by 146 BCE. Its inscribed Parian Chronicle of 264 BCE, now in Oxford, is a key source for Greek chronology, and Parian marble remained in demand.

petrocorii.t: Gallic people of the Dordogne whose name lives on in the Périgord and whose town Vesunna became Périgueux.
petrocorii.o: The Petrocorii lived in the valleys of the Isle and the Dordogne, in the modern Dordogne. Their name is usually read as the four armies, perhaps a league of four communities. Strabo notes their iron workings.
petrocorii.r: Little is known of their rulers. Their main oppidum stood at La Curade near Périgueux.
petrocorii.e: They sent five thousand men to relieve Alesia in 52 BCE. Under Rome their capital was Vesunna, a well-preserved town whose temple tower, the Tour de Vésone, still stands. The city became Périgueux, and the medieval County of Périgord kept their name.

principality-of-reuss-ebersdorf.t: Tiny Reuss lordship in Thuringia that became a stronghold of Pietism and the Moravian Brethren.
principality-of-reuss-ebersdorf.o: Ebersdorf was separated from Reuss-Lobenstein in 1678 for Heinrich X, a younger son of the Lobenstein line, creating a small county within the Younger Line of the House of Reuss in the Thuringian Highlands.
principality-of-reuss-ebersdorf.r: The counts of Ebersdorf were devout Pietists who turned their small residence into a religious centre. Count Nikolaus Ludwig von Zinzendorf, founder of the renewed Moravian Church at Herrnhut, married Erdmuthe Dorothea of Reuss-Ebersdorf in 1722, and a Moravian congregation settled in Ebersdorf. Queen Victoria's maternal grandmother came from the family. The rulers became princes in 1806.
principality-of-reuss-ebersdorf.e: Ebersdorf inherited Reuss-Lobenstein in 1824. Prince Heinrich LXXII, an eccentric absolutist, abdicated during the revolution of 1848, and his lands passed to Reuss-Schleiz, forming the Principality of Reuss Younger Line.

palatinate-veldenz.t: A small Wittelsbach duchy on the Glan and in the northern Vosges, created in 1543 for a younger branch of the Zweibrücken line.
palatinate-veldenz.o: By the Treaty of Marburg in 1543, Count Palatine Rupert, uncle and former guardian of Duke Wolfgang of Palatinate-Zweibrücken, received the old County of Veldenz with Lauterecken and lands in the Vosges, founding the line of Palatinate-Veldenz.
palatinate-veldenz.r: The dukes ruled from Lauterecken and from Lützelstein (La Petite-Pierre) in the northern Vosges, a scattered and poor territory of farming villages. They were Lutheran, and Duke George John founded the town of Phalsbourg in 1570. The Thirty Years' War and Louis XIV's Reunions, which claimed the Vosges lands for France after 1680, devastated the little state.
palatinate-veldenz.e: When Duke Leopold Louis died without male heirs in 1694, a long inheritance dispute followed among the Palatine branches. It was settled only in 1733, when the lands were shared among the Electoral Palatinate and other Wittelsbach lines.

prince-bishopric-of-constance.t: The temporal lordship of the bishops of Germany's largest medieval diocese, ruled from Meersburg after the Reformation drove them from Constance.
prince-bishopric-of-constance.o: Constance became a bishopric around 600, serving the Alemanni, and grew into the largest diocese of the German lands, stretching from the Alps to the Neckar. In 1155 Frederick Barbarossa confirmed the bishop's possessions and rights, the basis of a small secular territory around Lake Constance.
prince-bishopric-of-constance.r: The city of Constance became an imperial city independent of its bishop and hosted the Council of Constance from 1414 to 1418, which ended the Western Schism and burned Jan Hus. The bishops acquired the Reichenau abbey in 1540. After Constance became Protestant in 1527, they moved to Meersburg, where they built a baroque New Palace.
prince-bishopric-of-constance.e: In 1803 the prince-bishopric was secularised and its lands went to Baden. The diocese itself was dissolved in 1821, its parts divided between the new Archdiocese of Freiburg and Swiss dioceses.

principality-of-albania.t: Albania's first internationally recognised state, a principality that survived foreign occupation in the First World War and was rebuilt as a nation in 1920.
principality-of-albania.o: The Conference of Ambassadors in London made Albania an independent principality under the Great Powers' guarantee and chose the German Prince Wilhelm of Wied as ruler. He arrived in Durrës on 7 March 1914, replacing the Provisional Government of Albania and Essad Pasha's Republic of Central Albania.
principality-of-albania.r: Wied's rule collapsed within months amid Essad's intrigues, a Muslim peasant revolt in central Albania and Greek-backed autonomy in the south; he left in September 1914. During the First World War Italian, Austrian, Serbian, Greek and French troops occupied the country. The Congress of Lushnjë in 1920 created a regency council, moved the capital to Tirana and secured League of Nations membership.
principality-of-albania.e: The 1920s saw instability, with Fan Noli's June Revolution of 1924 overthrown by Ahmet Zogu in December. In January 1925 a constituent assembly abolished the principality and created the Albanian Republic, with Zogu as president.
principality-of-albania.re: Sunni Islam, Orthodox and Catholic Christianity

principality-of-schwarzenberg.t: Franconian territory of the Schwarzenberg family, whose princes became some of the greatest landowners and statesmen of the Habsburg monarchy.
principality-of-schwarzenberg.o: The lords of Seinsheim took the name Schwarzenberg from a castle near Scheinfeld in Franconia in the 15th century. In 1599 the family was raised to the rank of imperial counts, and in 1670 Johann Adolf von Schwarzenberg, a senior adviser of Emperor Leopold I, was made a prince of the Empire, with the lands around Scheinfeld forming the core of the family's immediate territory.
principality-of-schwarzenberg.r: The Franconian lands were small, but the family's real weight lay in service to the Habsburgs and in vast estates acquired in Bohemia, including Krumau (Český Krumlov) and Frauenberg (Hluboká), inherited from the Eggenberg family in 1719. The territory was Catholic and administered by officials while the princes lived at court in Vienna or on their Bohemian estates.
principality-of-schwarzenberg.e: In 1806 the Franconian lands were mediatised and placed under the Kingdom of Bavaria. The family remained prominent: Karl Philipp zu Schwarzenberg commanded the allied armies at Leipzig in 1813, and Felix zu Schwarzenberg led the Austrian Empire's government after the 1848 revolution.

political-committee-of-national-liberati.t: The 'Mountain Government' created by the Greek resistance in 1944, which held the first Greek elections in which women voted.
political-committee-of-national-liberati.o: By 1944 the left-wing resistance movement EAM and its army ELAS controlled much of mountainous Greece. On 10 March 1944 EAM created the Political Committee of National Liberation (PEEA) at Viniani in Evrytania, as a rival to both the collaborationist Hellenic State and the government-in-exile in Cairo.
political-committee-of-national-liberati.r: PEEA was led first by Colonel Evripidis Bakirtzis and then by the law professor Alexandros Svolos. It organised local self-government, people's courts and schools in liberated areas, and in April 1944 held elections for a National Council, which met at Koryschades; women voted for the first time in Greece. The Greek forces in Egypt mutinied in its support.
political-committee-of-national-liberati.e: At the Lebanon Conference in May 1944, PEEA agreed to join a government of national unity under Georgios Papandreou, and its ministers entered that government in September. It dissolved after liberation in November 1944, shortly before fighting in Athens began.

principality-of-chach.t: The early medieval principality of the Tashkent oasis, a Sogdian-Turkic borderland whose ruler's execution helped bring about the Battle of Talas.
principality-of-chach.o: Chach, or Shash, was the oasis on the Chirchiq River where Tashkent now stands. It emerged as a principality in the 6th century, closely tied to the Western Turkic Khaganate, whose rulers often installed Turkic tuduns or relatives as local lords alongside a Sogdian-speaking population.
principality-of-chach.r: Chach controlled a fertile irrigated plain at the meeting point of farmland and steppe, trading with Turkic nomads and producing silver and weapons. Its coins blended Sogdian and Turkic features, and the ruling house bore Turkic titles. Chinese sources call it Shi, the 'stone' country.
principality-of-chach.e: In 750 the Tang general Gao Xianzhi executed the ruler of Chach, whose son sought help from the Abbasids; the resulting Battle of Talas in 751 ended Chinese influence west of the Tian Shan. Chach then came under Muslim rule, later as part of the Samanid Empire.

peoples-state-of-reuss.t: Brief Thuringian republic uniting the two old Reuss principalities before they merged into Thuringia.
peoples-state-of-reuss.o: The Principality of Reuss Elder Line at Greiz and the Principality of Reuss Younger Line at Gera both became free states in November 1918 after their princes abdicated. In April 1919 the two united as the People's State of Reuss, with Gera as capital.
peoples-state-of-reuss.r: The state was industrial, with textile and machine-building works around Gera and Greiz, and its politics were dominated by the Social Democrats and Independent Socialists. It existed mainly to manage the transition from monarchy and to negotiate the union of the small Thuringian states.
peoples-state-of-reuss.e: On 1 May 1920 the People's State of Reuss merged with six other states to form the Free State of Thuringia. Gera, its capital, became one of Thuringia's main industrial cities and later a district capital in East Germany.

prince-bishopric-of-verden.t: Small church principality between the Weser and Elbe, rooted in Charlemagne's conquest of the Saxons and handed to Sweden in 1648.
prince-bishopric-of-verden.o: The diocese of Verden was founded around 800 in the wake of Charlemagne's wars against the Saxons. Its bishops acquired estates on the Aller and the lower Weser. After the fall of Henry the Lion in 1180 they ruled a secular territory as imperial princes, though their cathedral city of Verden was largely self-governing and they resided at Rotenburg.
prince-bishopric-of-verden.r: The territory was a thinly settled land of heath and moor. Its bishops were usually drawn from the princely houses of northern Germany, especially Brunswick-Lüneburg. The Reformation spread in the 16th century, and Lutheran administrators such as Philip Sigismund of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel replaced Catholic bishops. In the Thirty Years War the see was held by the Danish prince Frederick, later Frederick III of Denmark.
prince-bishopric-of-verden.e: The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 secularised the see as the Duchy of Verden and gave it to Sweden, which ruled it with Bremen. Denmark seized it in 1712 and sold it to the Electorate of Hanover in 1715. It is now in Lower Saxony.

proto-kingdom-of-nekhen.t: The predynastic chiefdom of Hierakonpolis, home of the falcon god Horus and one of the cradles of Egyptian kingship.
proto-kingdom-of-nekhen.o: Nekhen, the Greek Hierakonpolis, lay on the west bank of the Nile in southern Upper Egypt and was among the largest settlements of the Naqada period. By c. 3500 BCE it had a ceremonial precinct, breweries, pottery kilns and an elite cemetery, and its chiefs controlled trade with Nubia and along desert routes to the south.
proto-kingdom-of-nekhen.r: Nekhen was the cult centre of Horus, the falcon god later embodied by every Egyptian king. Its Tomb 100, the 'Painted Tomb', bears the earliest known Egyptian wall painting, with boats, hunting scenes and a figure smiting captives. Excavations have revealed an oval ceremonial court and an elite cemetery with buried animals, including elephants, hippopotami and baboons, signs of an ambitious ruling ideology.
proto-kingdom-of-nekhen.e: Around 3150 BCE its rulers seem to have merged with, or been overtaken by, the kings of the Proto-kingdom of Thinis. The town remained a royal religious centre: the Narmer Palette and the Scorpion Macehead were found in its temple's Main Deposit, and Nekhen stayed the symbolic capital of Upper Egypt.
